katakana-chart.intro_tr: カタカナ (katakana) is one of two sound-based writing systems in Japanese and represents the exact same sounds as hiragana — the only difference between them is their field of use and shape. Katakana is primarily used for foreign-origin words (外来語[がいらいご]), foreign proper names (person/country/city names), onomatopoeia, scientific terms (plant-animal species) and words that need emphasis. It consists of a total of 46 basic characters (gojūon), by adding dakuten (゛) and handakuten (゜) to these, 25 more sounds are derived, and with small ヤユヨ, 33 compound (yōon) sounds are obtained. Additionally, special extended combinations such as ファ, ティ, ヴ have been developed to write sounds in foreign languages more accurately. This page presents all katakana characters, their derivatives and special usage rules as a single reference.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Katakana (清音[せいおん] — Gojūon Table)
footnotes_tr: シ is pronounced 'shi', チ is pronounced 'chi', ツ is pronounced 'tsu' — written in the way closest to Turkish pronunciation; these are irregular pronunciations.
フ is a sound between 'fu' and 'hu' in Turkish, produced by blowing with the lips.
ヲ is pronounced almost only as 'o' in modern Japanese and is very rarely used in practice (generally not seen in katakana texts either, hiragana を is preferred more).

tables.caption_tr: Dakuten and Handakuten Inflections (濁音[だくおん]・半濁音[はんだくおん])
footnotes_tr: ジ and ヂ are pronounced the same (ji), ズ and ヅ are pronounced the same (zu) — in modern writing, ジ and ズ are preferred almost always, ヂ/ヅ are very rare.
Dakuten (゛) is added as two short lines to the top right of the character, handakuten (゜) is added as a small circle; it can only be applied to the カ・サ・タ・ハ rows.

tables.caption_tr: Compound Sounds (拗音[ようおん] — with small ャュョ)
footnotes_tr: Small ャ/ュ/ョ is written approximately 60-70% smaller than normal-sized characters; it is aligned to the lower-middle level of the line in writing.
These sound combinations are pronounced as a single syllable, not read as two syllables (キャ = 'kya', not 'ki-ya').

tables.caption_tr: Extended Katakana — Special Combinations for Foreign Sounds
footnotes_tr: These combinations are not included in the basic 46 katakana; they were developed later solely to enable writing foreign words closer to their original pronunciation.
ヴ sound is often also pronounced/written as 'b' in speech (e.g. バイオリン is also common instead of ヴァイオリン).

tables.caption_tr: Special Marks: Long Vowel (ー) and Small ッ
rows: Uzatma işareti hiraganadaki gibi あ/い/う/え/お tekrarı değil, düz çizgidir
Sözcük sonunda ani kesilme/ünlem etkisi verir
footnotes_tr: In hiragana, the letters あ/い/う/え/お are written again for long vowels, while in katakana a straight ー line is used instead — this is an important point of difference.
The ー line is shown vertically in vertical writing (tategaki) and horizontally in horizontal writing.

dakuten-handakuten.intro_tr: Dakuten (濁点 ゛) and handakuten (半濁点 ゜) are small marks added to the upper right corner of hiragana and katakana characters and change the pronunciation of that syllable. Dakuten converts a "voiceless" (清音) sound to a "voiced" (濁音) sound: か→が, さ→ざ, た→だ, は→ば, etc. Handakuten, on the other hand, is used only in the は row and produces a "p" sound in the form は→ぱ. These marks can completely change the meaning of a word (かき "persimmon" ≠ かぎ "key"), so they must not be overlooked when reading and writing. The tables below summarize all the transformations, writing rules, and frequently confused じ/ぢ and ず/づ pairs.

tables.caption_tr: Dakuten (゛) Transformation Table — か・さ・た・は rows

footnotes_tr: Handakuten (゜) is used ONLY in the は row (ha/hi/fu/he/ho); it does not appear in any other row.
In katakana, handakuten appears most frequently in words of foreign origin: パン (bread), ピアノ (piano), プール (swimming pool).

Modern Japanese generally prefers じ and ず; ぢ/づ are limited to exceptional cases (Monbushō 1986 rules).

small-kana-combos.title_tr: Small Kana Combinations (拗音[ようおん]) — きゃ, しゅ, ちょ...
small-kana-combos.intro_tr: In Japanese, by adding small-written や, ゆ, よ (゛や、ゅ、ょ゛) next to certain kana such as き, し, ち, に, ひ, み, り, ぎ, じ, ぢ, び, ぴ, single-syllable 'combined sounds' (拗音[ようおん] - yōon) are formed. Although these combinations are written with two kana, they are read as a single mora (sound unit); for example, きゃ is a single syllable pronounced 'kya', not two separate syllables 'ki-ya'. The small や/ゆ/よ are always written smaller than normal size in the lower right of the row; on computers, small characters (ゃゅょ) are used and must not be confused with large characters (やゆよ). The same system works in Katakana (キャ, シュ, チョ...) and additionally, extended katakana combinations (ファ, ティ, ウォ etc.) are used for writing foreign words. This topic is the natural next step for students who know Hiragana and Katakana tables, and forms the foundation of reading and writing at JLPT N5 level.

tables.caption_tr: Hiragana Small Kana Combinations — Plain (清音[せいおん])
footnotes_tr: These combinations are read as A SINGLE MORA (sound unit): きゃ = 'kya', never 'ki-ya'.
し + ゃ = しゃ 'sha' (not shi-ya), ち + ゃ = ちゃ 'cha' (not chi-ya) — in these two rows the consonant sound changes.

tables.caption_tr: Hiragana Small Kana Combinations — Voiced (濁音[だくおん]・半濁音[はんだくおん])
footnotes_tr: ぢゃ/ぢゅ/ぢょ is very rare in modern Japanese, almost never used (pronounced the same as じゃ/じゅ/じょ, appearing only in certain compound words).
じゃ and ぢゃ are pronounced the same ('ja') but have different spellings — the rule distinguishing this difference is related to the 連濁[れんだく] rule in the Dakuten/Handakuten topic.

tables.caption_tr: Katakana Small Kana Combinations (Exactly the Same Logic as Hiragana)
footnotes_tr: Katakana is normally used for foreign words, country/city names, and onomatopoeia.
Example words: キャベツ (cabbage), シャワー (shower), チョコレート (chocolate), ジュース (juice).

tables.caption_tr: Extended Katakana Combinations (For Foreign Sounds — Not in the Standard Hiragana Table)
footnotes_tr: These combinations are NOT in the standard 拗音[ようおん] list; they were developed specifically for katakana only to write foreign words more accurately.
Some authors/publishers may prefer to write with the nearest standard katakana instead of using these extended combinations (e.g., in older texts ハン might appear instead of ファン).

tables.caption_tr: Spelling Rules and Common Mistakes
rows: Büyük や yazılırsa 'ki-ya' (iki hece) olarak okunur, birleşim bozulur.
El yazısında küçük kana belirgin şekilde daha küçük ve satırın alt-sağına yakın yazılmalı.
し + ゃ birleşiminde temel ünsüz korunur ama 'i' sesi düşer, 'sh' + 'a' = 'sha' olur.
Günlük kelimelerin neredeyse tamamında じゃ/じゅ/じょ kullanılır; ぢゃ sadece birkaç özel durumda (連濁[れんだく]) görülür.
っ ile ゃゅょ karıştırma
Küçük っ (sokuon, çift ünsüz) tamamen farklı bir işleve sahiptir — bu konu ayrı olarak 'Uzun Ünlüler ve Küçük っ' başlığında işlenir.
Bilgisayar/telefon klavyesinde birleşimler doğrudan 'kya', 'sha', 'cho' gibi yazılarak otomatik üretilir.

wa-topic-particle.intro_tr: は (written as 'ha', read as わ when used as a particle) is one of the most fundamental particles in Japanese and marks the TOPIC (topic) of the sentence — that is, it adds the meaning of 'I'm talking about...'. は should not be confused with the grammatical subject (subject) in English; the particle that marks the actual subject is が, and は instead establishes the frame of 'what I'm going to say about this topic'. は also establishes contrast/comparison, makes known/given information a topic again, and is also used to emphasize a certain element in negative sentences. It can replace particles like を and が, and is attached on top of particles like に/で/と/から/まで. The most frequently encountered pattern at N5 level is the structure X は Y です (X is Y).

tables.caption_tr: Basic Functions of the は Particle
rows: 私[わたし]は田中[たなか]です。
X は A, Y は B
犬[いぬ]は好[す]きですが、猫[ねこ]は好[す]きではありません。
"Köpekleri severim ama kedileri sevmem." İki は birbirine zıt bilgi verir.
(を/が düşer) X は …ません
肉[にく]は食[た]べません。
"Eti yemiyorum (ama başka şey yiyebilirim)" — を yerine は gelerek belirli bir şey vurgulanır.
その本[ほん]は面白[おもしろ]いです。
Konuşmada daha önce geçmiş veya bağlamdan bilinen bir şey tekrar konu edilir.
Çift konu yapısı (X は Y が …)
象[ぞう]は鼻[はな]が長[なが]い。
"Fillerin hortumu uzundur." は geniş konuyu, が alt-özneyi belirtir.
X は Y だ/です
日本[にほん]は島国[しまぐに]です。
"Japonya bir ada ülkesidir." Genel bilgi/gerçek ifadesi.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Differences Between は and が
rows: Cümlenin geri kalanı (yüklem) hakkında bilgi verir
Bilinen, verilmiş, konuşmada zaten geçen bilgi
Yeni bilgi, ilk kez tanıtılan bilgi
だれは, なには gibi kullanılmaz ✗
だれが、なにが — soru kelimesi genelde が alır ✓
Yan (bağımlı) cümlelerde özne çoğunlukla が alır
私[わたし]は学生[がくせい]です。(Genel tanıtım)
私[わたし]が学生[がくせい]です。("Öğrenci olan BENİM" — vurgulu, seçici)
footnotes_tr: Briefly: は = 'I'm talking about this', and が = 'this exactly (not something else)'

tables.caption_tr: Combining は with Other Particles
rows: を düşer, sadece は kalır
パンを食[た]べる → パンは食[た]べない。
を + は birlikte kullanılmaz, を tamamen kaybolur.
が düşer, sadece は kalır
猫[ねこ]がいる → 猫[ねこ]はいる。
東京[とうきょう]に行[い]く → 東京[とうきょう]には行[い]かない。
に korunur, üzerine は eklenir.
図書館[としょかん]で勉強[べんきょう]する → 図書館[としょかん]では勉強[べんきょう]しない。
で korunur, üzerine は eklenir.
彼[かれ]と話[はな]す → 彼[かれ]とは話[はな]さない。
9時[くじ]から始[はじ]まる → 9時[くじ]からは始[はじ]まらない。
駅[えき]まで歩[ある]く → 駅[えき]までは歩[ある]かない。
も zaten kendi başına 'de/da/aynı zamanda' işlevini üstlenir, は ile yan yana gelmez.

tables.caption_tr: Basic は Patterns with the です Copula
rows: X は Y です (olumlu, şimdiki/geniş)
これは辞書[じしょ]です。
X は Y ではありません (olumsuz)
これは辞書[じしょ]ではありません。
X は Y でした (geçmiş olumlu)
昨日[きのう]は雨[あめ]でした。
X は Y ではありませんでした (geçmiş olumsuz)

X は Y ですか (soru)
これは山田[やまだ]さんのペンですか。
X は Y が好[す]きです (tercih)
私[わたし]は寿司[すし]が好[す]きです。
X は Y があります/います (sahiplik/varlık)
私[わたし]は兄[あに]がいます。

は her zaman özne demektir sanmak ✗
は konu, が genellikle gramatik özne bildirir
は+が bir arada kullanılabilir: 私[わたし]は音楽[おんがく]が好[す]きです (konu: ben, özne: müzik).

examples.reading: わたしはがくせいです。
examples.translation_tr: I am a student.

examples.target: これは本[ほん]です。
examples.reading: これはほんです。

examples.translation_tr: I don't like this (but I might like something else — emphasis on contrast/opposition).
examples.note_tr: The object これ doesn't normally take を, but は makes it an emphasized topic.

examples.target: 東京[とうきょう]には行[い]きません。
examples.reading: とうきょうにはいきません。
examples.translation_tr: I'm not going to Tokyo (but I might go somewhere else).
examples.note_tr: に + は combines to form には; に doesn't disappear, は is attached on top of it.

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんは先生[せんせい]ではありません。
examples.reading: たなかさんはせんせいではありません。
examples.translation_tr: Tanaka is not a teacher.

examples.target: 私[わたし]は日本語[にほんご]を勉強[べんきょう]していますが、彼[かれ]は英語[えいご]を勉強[べんきょう]しています。
examples.reading: わたしはにほんごをべんきょうしていますが、かれはえいごをべんきょうしています。
examples.translation_tr: I am studying Japanese, and he is studying English.
examples.note_tr: Using two は side by side compares two different topics (contrast function).

ga-subject-particle.title_tr: が Subject Particle (Difference with は)
ga-subject-particle.intro_tr: が and は are the two particles most commonly confused in Japanese; although both may sometimes appear as "subject," they actually perform different functions: は indicates the TOPIC of the sentence (what is being talked about), while が marks the grammatical SUBJECT, especially NEW information that the listener does not yet know. While は operates on the logic of "known/old information + broad topic," が emphasizes with the nuance "this is it, exactly this," highlighting a specific element. Question words (誰[だれ], 何[なに], どこ) always use が when they are the subject; in expressions of feeling/ability like 好[す]き, 欲[ほ]しい, わかる, the true "object" is marked with が. Subjects within subordinate clauses (relative clauses, causal clauses) also almost always take が, not は. This page summarizes all the basic rules, mandatory usage areas, and common mistakes of the two particles in table form.

o-object-particle.intro_tr: The を particle is a basic object particle used in Japanese to mark the direct object of a verb (that is, the thing directly affected by an action) and is only used with transitive (他動詞[たどうし]) verbs. Within a sentence, it always comes immediately after the object and immediately before the verb: [Object] + を + [Verb]. The を particle is also used in the meanings of 'a place/path passed through' (with motion verbs like 歩く, 渡る, 飛ぶ) and 'a point departed from/left' (with verbs like 出る, 降りる, 卒業する) — in these cases it is translated not as '-i/-ı' but as '-den/-dan', or as prepositions such as 'inside' or 'on'. In writing, を is always written in hiragana; in katakana texts it can also be written as ヲ, but its pronunciation is always 'o' (not 'wo'). In everyday speech, especially with objects that are well-known/easily guessed, を is sometimes completely dropped.

tables.caption_tr: 1. Basic Usage: を + Transitive Verb (Direct Object)
rows: 日本語[にほんご]を勉強する
にほんごをべんきょうする
footnotes_tr: Sentence order is always: [Object] + を + [Verb]. The noun before を is the thing that directly receives/is affected by the action.

tables.caption_tr: 2. Special Uses of を: With Motion Verbs (Path/Passage, Point of Departure)
rows: 歩[ある]く, 渡[わた]る, 通[とお]る, 飛[と]ぶ, 走[はし]る
出[で]る, 降[お]りる, 卒業[そつぎょう]する
電車[でんしゃ]を降りる
大学[だいがく]を卒業する
だいがくをそつぎょうする
footnotes_tr: In these uses, を translates to Turkish as '-de/-da' (passage) or '-den/-dan' (departure), not as '-i/-ı'.
These verbs are generally considered intransitive (自動詞[じどうし]) but they take を; this is an exceptional structure and must be memorized.

tables.caption_tr: 3. Comparison with Confusing Particles: を / が / に / で
rows: Özne, ya da beğenme/isteme fiillerinde nesne (好き, 欲しい, わかる)
が duygu/algı/yeterlilik fiilleriyle kullanılır, を değil
Hedef, yön, varış noktası, zaman noktası
に hareketin yöneldiği/ulaştığı noktayı gösterir, を geçilen yolu gösterir
公園[こうえん]で遊[あそ]ぶ (parkta oynamak)
で eylemin yapıldığı sabit yeri, を bazı hareket fiilleriyle geçilen yolu gösterir
footnotes_tr: Common mistake: 公園を散歩[さんぽ]する (walking around inside the park) and 公園で遊ぶ (playing in the park) are different — one is passage/strolling, the other is an action in a fixed place.

tables.caption_tr: 4. Omission of を in Everyday Spoken Language
rows: Rahat/samimi konuşmada, özellikle nesne cümle başındaysa を sıkça düşürülür
Soru cümlelerinde de düşürülebilir, tonlama nesneyi belirginleştirir
footnotes_tr: In formal writing or N5 exam questions, を should never be omitted; this only occurs in spoken/casual recordings.

ni-particle.intro_tr: The に particle is one of the most frequently used particles with the most functions at N5 level; therefore, it can be thought of as "a versatile multi-purpose particle that works for everything." Fundamentally, it is used to indicate a point in time (hour, day, date), the destination of movement (with 行く/来る/帰る), the location where something is (with ある/いる), the target/indirect object of an action (giving something to someone, saying, teaching), and the result of a change. The confusion of に with other particles such as へ, で, を is a very common mistake among Turkish learners; therefore, these particles are compared with each other in the tables below. The logic behind the rule is as follows: に generally indicates "a fixed point" (a moment in time, a destination/location in space), while で generally indicates "the area where the action takes place." Instead of memorizing the tables on this page, first look at which verb it is used with and try to identify its function.

mo-also-particle.intro_tr: The も particle corresponds to the Turkish suffix "de/da"; it is used to add something that shares the same property or state as the previous one. It completely replaces the particles は, が, を (and is never used together with them), but can be used together with particles like に, で, へ, から, まで. When combined with question words (だれ, なに, どこ etc.), it carries the meaning of "no one/nothing/nowhere" in negative sentences, and in some patterns, "everyone/everything/everywhere" in positive sentences. The も...も structure gives the meaning of "both...and" or in negatives "neither...nor"; when used with numbers, it emphasizes that there are more than expected ("even...as many as").

te-kudasai.title_tr: 〜てください (Request) — Expressing a Polite Request with a Verb
te-kudasai.intro_tr: 〜てください is a basic N5-level pattern used for requesting something from another person or giving polite instructions. It is formed by adding ください to the て-form of a verb: 食[た]べてください (please eat), 書[か]いてください (please write), and so on. For negative requests, でください is added to the ない-form: 〜ないでください (please don't do). This pattern expresses a neutral-polite request; the bare て-form (e.g., 待って) is more intimate/imperative, while お〜ください is a more formal and respectful version. In the tables below, the rules for forming the て-form, affirmative/negative usage, and politeness levels are presented comparatively.

tables.caption_tr: Rules for Forming the て-Form (Comprehensive, by Verb Groups)
rows: İstisna: いて değil って olur!
Kökten değişir, okunuş きて olur

tables.caption_tr: 〜てください: Affirmative and Negative Request Structure
rows: 食[た]べる → 食[た]べて
書[か]く → 書[か]かない
書[か]かないでください。
食[た]べる → 食[た]べない
食[た]べないでください。
心配[しんぱい]しないでください。
footnotes_tr: In negative requests, the ない-form is used, not the て-form: ない + で + ください.
Instead of 〜ないでください, in more formal contexts 〜ないようにしてください can also be used (with a softer suggestion tone).

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of Politeness Levels in Request Expressions
rows: Yakın arkadaş, aile; bazen emir gibi algılanabilir
ちょっと待[ま]って。(Biraz bekle.)
Öğretmen→öğrenci, günlük talimat, tanıdık yetişkinler arası
ちょっと待[ま]ってください。(Biraz bekleyin.)
Daha resmi rica, ilk kez tanışılan biri
ちょっと待[ま]ってくださいませんか。(Biraz bekler misiniz?)
〜ていただけますか / 〜ていただけませんか
İş ortamı, müşteri hizmeti, üst makam
少[すこ]々[しょう]お待[ま]ちいただけますか。(Biraz bekleyebilir misiniz?)
お〜ください (尊敬語 kalıbı)
少[すこ]々[しょう]お待[ま]ちください。(Lütfen biraz bekleyiniz.)
footnotes_tr: The お〜ください pattern is only used with verbs whose ます-stem is not a single syllable; with する verbs, the ご〜ください form is generally preferred (e.g., ご利用[りよう]ください).

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used 〜てください Patterns from Daily Life
rows: もう一度[いちど]言[い]ってください。
こちらに来[き]てください。

to-particle.intro_tr: The と particle is one of the most basic and frequently used particles in Japanese; it has three main functions: (1) it connects two or more nouns completely to each other and gives the meaning of 'and', (2) it specifies the person doing an action together and gives the meaning of 'with', (3) it serves as a quotation function by directly conveying a word, thought, or name (like と言う, と思う). When listing nouns, unlike や, と covers EVERYTHING listed, nothing is left out. In the quotation function, と comes directly after (within 「」) or immediately after indirect narration and is generally used together with verbs like 言う, 思う, 聞く, 書く. Because of this versatility, using と correctly is one of the building blocks at the N5 level.

tables.caption_tr: Three Basic Functions of と
rows: 友達[ともだち]と行[い]く
Cümle/Kelime + と + 言う/思う/聞く/書く
İsim + と + 同[おな]じ / 違[ちが]う
春[はる]になると花[はな]が咲[さ]く
footnotes_tr: The 5th function (conditional と) is handled in detail under the 'Conditional Forms' section as a separate topic; here it is only a reminder.

tables.caption_tr: Noun Linking: Comparison of と vs や vs とか
rows: Sayılan HER ŞEY dahildir, liste tamdır
りんごとバナナを買[か]った
'Sadece elma ve muz aldım' — başka bir şey yok
Örnek olarak birkaçı sayılır, liste EKSİKTİR
りんごやバナナを買[か]った
'Elma, muz vb. aldım' — başka şeyler de olabilir
りんごとかバナナとか買[か]った
Günlük konuşmada çok sık, resmî yazıda az kullanılır

tables.caption_tr: Verbs Frequently Used with Quotation と
rows: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ると思[おも]う
彼[かれ]は忙[いそが]しいと聞[き]いた
ここに名前[なまえ]と書[か]いてある
彼[かれ]を先生[せんせい]と呼[よ]ぶ
難[むずか]しいと感[かん]じた
footnotes_tr: This pattern connects indirect or direct narration to the next verb; the part before と is left unchanged (verb in dictionary/negative/past form) and is not conjugated.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of と in Togetherness with で and に
rows: 友達[ともだち]と話[はな]す
İki taraf da eylemi birlikte yapar (konuşmak, gitmek, evlenmek vb.)
友達[ともだち]に話[はな]す
Araç veya yer bildirir, kişi bildirmez
footnotes_tr: The verb '話[はな]す' can be used with both と and に, but the meaning nuance changes: と = mutual conversation, に = telling someone.

tables.caption_tr: Notes on Writing and Usage of と

Fiil sözlük/た/ない formunda, çekimlenmeden と'ya bağlanır

En az 2 isim gerekir; sonuncu isimden sonra と KOYULMAZ (günlük dilde bazen koyulur ama temel kural budur)
肉[にく]と魚[さかな]（を食[た]べる）
İki fiili bağlamak için と değil、て formu kullanılır
食[た]べて飲[の]む（doğru） / 食[た]べると飲[の]む（yanlış anlam）

tai-form.intro_tr: 〜たい is a very basic pattern used to express the desire to perform an action, and describes the speaker's (and sometimes the addressee's in questions) own inner desire. It is added to the masu-stem (ます-kökü) of a verb and then conjugates just like an い-adjective (たい → たくない → たかった → たくなかった). たい is naturally used only for the 1st person (and 2nd person in questions); to express the desire of a 3rd person, the form 〜たがる/〜たがっている is preferred. Either が or を can be used to mark the desired object; が is more natural in everyday speech. This topic is directly connected to the masu Form, い-adjective conjugation, and the 〜がる topics.

tables.caption_tr: Formation of the 〜たい Form (According to Verb Groups)
footnotes_tr: Rule: Remove ます from the masu-form of a verb, and add たい in its place.

tables.caption_tr: 〜たい Conjugation Table (conjugates like an い-adjective) — Example: 食[た]べる
rows: 〜たくないです / 〜たくありません
〜たくなかったです / 〜たくありませんでした
食[た]べたくなかったです
footnotes_tr: 〜たい can also function as an い-adjective to modify a noun: 食[た]べたいもの (something I want to eat).

tables.caption_tr: Particle Usage: が or を?
rows: En doğal ve yaygın kullanım; istek doğrudan nesneye odaklanır
Dilbilgisel olarak da doğru; özellikle nesne ile fiil arasına başka öğeler girdiğinde veya vurgu fiildeyse tercih edilir
Birden fazla たい fiili varsa
何[なに]かを食[た]べたいし、飲[の]みたい
İki eylem art arda sayılırken を kullanmak cümleyi netleştirir

彼[かれ]は行[い]きたがる

O şu an gitmek istiyor(muş) (dışarıdan gözlemlenen)
〜たいと言[い]っている / 〜たいらしい / 〜たいそうだ
彼[かれ]は行[い]きたいと言[い]っている
footnotes_tr: 〜たい only expresses the speaker's (or the person being asked) direct inner world; saying another person's desire directly with たい is not natural, and たがる should be used.

新[あたら]しい車[くるま]が欲[ほ]しい

i-adjectives.intro_tr: い-adjectives (形容詞) are a type of adjective in Japanese that can directly modify nouns and perform tense/negation conjugation on their own; their dictionary forms always end with い (e.g., 高[たか]い, 寒[さむ]い, おいしい). Conjugation is done by adding suffixes to the adjective's "stem" (the form with the final い removed): for example, 高い → 高く (adverbial), 高くない (negative), 高かった (past). The most important exception is いい/よい: although the present tense positive form is いい, in all other conjugations the stem よい is used (よくない, よかった, etc.). Unlike な-adjectives, い-adjectives do not need a copula like だ/な before nouns and have a complete conjugation system within themselves. This page summarizes all basic conjugation forms, derived structures, and common mistakes in tabular format.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Conjugation Table (基本活用[きほんかつよう]) — example: 高[たか]い (expensive/high)
rows: 高[たか]くないです / 高[たか]くありません
高[たか]くなかったです / 高[たか]くありませんでした
footnotes_tr: Rule: Stem (the part excluding い) + かった/くない/くなかった. Example: 高い → 高(stem).
The word くない that appears in the negative is also an い-adjective, so its past form is くなかった (not くないかった).

tables.caption_tr: Derived Forms (派生形[はせいけい]) — usage and patterns
rows: Fiili nitelemek için zarf yapma (~く/~にの い-sıfat karşılığı)
仮定形[かていけい] ば (koşul)
名詞修飾[めいししゅうしょく] (isim niteleme)
辞書形[じしょけい] + isim
Sıfat doğrudan isimden önce gelir, ek gerekmez
footnotes_tr: When すぎる and そう are added, there are irregularities such as ない → なさそう, いい → よさそう.

tables.caption_tr: Exception Conjugation: いい / よい (good)
rows: いい (ii) — ayrıca よい de kullanılır (daha resmî/yazılı)
Tek istisna form; diğer tüm çekimlerde よい gövdesi kullanılır
footnotes_tr: Compound adjectives containing いい like 格好[かっこう]いい (handsome/cool) also follow the same irregularity: 格好よくない, 格好よかった.

tables.caption_tr: Other Usage Areas of い-Adjectives
rows: この部屋[へや]は広[ひろ]くて明[あか]るいです (bu oda geniş ve aydınlık)
寒[さむ]がる (üşüyormuş gibi davranmak/üşümek — başkası için)
footnotes_tr: 〜がる is used only with adjectives expressing emotions/sensations: 寒い→寒がる, 痛い→痛がる, ほしい→ほしがる.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Points to Pay Attention To
rows: 綺麗[きれい]です / 綺麗[きれい]な
綺麗 bir な-sıfatıdır, い ile bitse de kural dışıdır
高[たか]いだ (isim önünde だ kullanma)
い-sıfatları isim niteleme için だ/な gerektirmez
高[たか]いに走[はし]る (zarf yapımında に kullanma)
高[たか]く走[はし]る (yanlış anlam ama örnek: 速[はや]く走[はし]る doğru)
い-sıfatlarında zarf eki 〜く'dur, 〜に な-sıfatları içindir

よくない / よかった
いい istisnası: çekimlerde よい gövdesi kullanılır
高[たか]くないかった (çifte geçmiş)
くない zaten い-sıfat gibi çeker: くない → くなかった

personal-pronouns.title_tr: Personal Pronouns (わたし, あなた, 彼[かれ]…)
personal-pronouns.intro_tr: In Japanese, personal pronouns work very differently from Turkish or English: there is no single fixed word for "I" or "you"; depending on the speaker's gender, age, politeness level, and relationship with the person being addressed, one chooses from dozens of different pronouns. Additionally, in Japanese, if the subject is understood from context, it is almost always dropped; instead of using a pronoun, adding "〜さん" to the person's name is much more polite and natural — especially the second person (あなた) is rarely used in everyday speech and can sometimes even be considered rude. This page summarizes first, second, and third person pronouns, plural markers, and usage nuances in table form. At the N5 level, わたし, あなた, 彼[かれ], 彼女[かのじょ] are most commonly seen; however, there are many more variants in actual speech.

tables.caption_tr: First Person Pronouns (I) — By Formality and Gender
rows: En kibar form; günlük konuşmada nadir
En güvenli ve yaygın form, ders kitaplarının standardı
Resmî ortamda kullanılmaz, sert/erkeksi hava verir
Aslında 'kendisi' anlamına gelir, bazı erkekler 'ben' yerine kullanır
footnotes_tr: In Japanese speech, if the subject is known, the pronoun is generally completely omitted: instead of '(私は)学生です', one simply says '学生[がくせい]です'.

tables.caption_tr: Second Person Pronouns (You) — With Usage Warnings
rows: Karşıdakine doğrudan hitap etmek Japoncada az yapılır; yakın olmayanlara garip gelebilir. Eşler arası 'sevgilim' anlamında da kullanılır
Eşitler veya alt konumdakilere; üste kullanılmaz
Yanlış bağlamda kaba veya küçümseyici olabilir

Japoncada ikinci şahıs yerine genelde karşıdakinin ADI + さん/様 kullanılır
footnotes_tr: General rule: When speaking with someone you don't know or someone in a higher position, using the person's name + さん instead of あなた is much safer and considered more polite.

tables.caption_tr: Third Person Pronouns (He/She)
rows: Resmî/kibar bağlamda 'o kişi' demenin nazik yolu

Sürekli あなた kullanmak yapay ve bazen kaba durur

kara-made.intro_tr: から and まで are basic particles in Japanese that indicate the start and end points of a range: から means "...from, ...starting from" (beginning), while まで means "...until, ...up to" (end). These two particles can be used in both time and place/location expressions, and are often used together as から〜まで to indicate both ends of a range. から can also be used alone as a conjunction meaning "because" (this is a different topic and should not be confused). The difference between まで's meaning of "...up to a continuous state" and までに's meaning of "...by, ...until (one-time, deadline)" is the most commonly confused point at the N5 level, and is also addressed separately on this page.

family-terms.title_tr: Family Terms: My Family and Someone Else's Family
family-terms.intro_tr: In Japanese, when talking about family members, two separate sets of words are used: when referring to your own family (or a person within a group, "uchi" 内) to others, HUMBLE (kenjōgo style, no suffix) terms are used; when referring to someone else's family ("soto" 外), RESPECTFUL (sonkeigo style, typically お〜さん pattern) terms are used. This distinction reflects the Japanese society's "inside-outside" (内・外) logic in family terms. An interesting exception: when addressing your own family DIRECTLY (for example, when calling to mother), you generally use the respectful form (お母さん), while the humble form (母) is used only when talking about your family to OTHERS. This page summarizes basic nuclear family and extended family terms and usage rules in table format.

masu-form.title_tr: ます Form (Polite Present/General Present Tense)
masu-form.intro_tr: ます形[ますけい] is the polite (teineigo[ていねいご]) conjugation of Japanese verbs and is the standard level of politeness used in daily life when speaking with foreigners, at work, at school, or with people you don't know. It combines present, general present, and near future meanings into a single form — In Japanese, the distinction between "I am doing now" and "I usually/will do" is made not with ます形 but with the 〜ている form. The conjugation rules change depending on the verb group (godan, ichidan, irregular); therefore, it is essential to know which group the verb belongs to. ます形 has four basic conjugations: affirmative-present (〜ます), negative-present (〜ません), affirmative-past (〜ました), and negative-past (〜ませんでした). Because it is more polite than the dictionary form, it is taught first in beginner textbooks and in formal speech.

The ます form can mean both 'now' and 'generally/in the future'; 〜ている is used for ongoing actions.

desu-copula.intro_tr: です is a basic copula in Japanese that politely ends sentences with nouns and な-adjectives (similar to the English "to be" verb, but it does not change according to person or number). With the pattern "A は B です", the meaning "A is B" is constructed, and this pattern is the most fundamental sentence structure at the N5 level. です has its own affirmative/negative and present/past tense conjugations; these apply to nouns and な-adjectives, but when used with い-adjectives, です does not change; the conjugation occurs on the adjective itself. In everyday conversation, the plain form of です is だ; the difference between these two determines the politeness level. On this page, all tense/negation conjugations of です, its uses, and common mistakes are summarized in table form.

tables.caption_tr: です Basic Conjugation Table (Noun/な-Adjective + です)

学生[がくせい]じゃなかったです / じゃありませんでした
footnotes_tr: ではありません is somewhat more formal than じゃありません; both are correct and common.
When asking a question, only か is added to the end of the sentence; です does not change at all.
By adding ね or よ to です (学生[がくせい]ですね/よ), you can ask for confirmation or add emphasis.

numbers-dates-time.intro_tr: Japanese has two separate number systems: the 漢語[かんご] numbers of Chinese origin (一[いち], 二[に], 三[さん]...) and the 和語[わご] numbers of Japanese origin (ひとつ, ふたつ, みっつ...). When expressing date, time, and age, various suffixes are added to these numbers, and in some combinations, irregular pronunciations that need to be memorized emerge (e.g., 4時[よじ], 9月[くがつ], 20歳[はたち]). Additionally, in some counters like 分[ふん/ぷん], voicing changes (連濁[れんだく] and っ hardening) are seen. This page brings together in a single reference the numbers, days of the month, days of the week, months, hours, minutes, age, and relative time expressions (like yesterday/today/tomorrow). At the N5 level, the vast majority of these patterns require memorization, so it is beneficial to return to the tables frequently and practice.

basic-word-order.intro_tr: Japanese, just like Turkish, has SOV (Subject-Object-Verb) word order; therefore, the verb appearing at the end of the sentence is not actually a strange logic for Turkish students — you have a big advantage compared to those learning English (SVO). In Japanese, the role of nouns in the sentence (subject, object, place, time, etc.) is determined by particles (助詞[じょし]), so the order of elements BEFORE the verb is actually quite flexible; the only firm rule is that the inflected verb or adjective/copula must appear at the VERY END of the sentence. Nevertheless, for natural and fluent Japanese, there is a preferred "default" word order: Time → Place → Subject → Indirect Object → Direct Object → Verb. Question words (何, だれ, いつ, etc.) occupy the position of a normal element in the sentence, as in Turkish, and are not moved to the beginning of the sentence. On this page, you will find the basic template, particle-element matches, flexibility rules, and common mistakes made by Turkish students in table format.

sentence-ending-particles.title_tr: Sentence-Final Particles: ね, よ, な
sentence-ending-particles.intro_tr: ね, よ and な are small but extremely important particles (終助詞[しゅうじょし]) added to the very end of sentences in Japanese to determine the speaker's attitude, emotion, and relationship with the listener. ね generally seeks shared knowledge or confirmation with the meaning of 'isn't it?', while よ conveys information that the listener is assumed not to know in an emphatic manner. な, on the other hand, takes on two completely different functions depending on context: after a verb's dictionary form it is a strict prohibition ('don't do it!'), and after an adjective/noun it is similar to ね but carries a more masculine and intimate exclamation/confirmation tone. These particles do not change the grammatical meaning of the sentence but only shape its tone and the speaker-listener relationship; therefore they must certainly be learned to speak natural and intimate Japanese. Their usage varies greatly depending on gender, age, and level of formality (register), which is why these distinctions are particularly noted in the tables below.

tables.caption_tr: Three Main Sentence-Final Particles: Basic Functions
rows: Konuşmacı, bilginin dinleyiciyle ortak olduğunu varsayar; onay/empati arar. Türkçe 'değil mi?' karşılığı.

Günlük konuşma, her yaş ve cinsiyet.
もう時間[じかん]ですよ。
Fiilin sözlük (辞書形[じしょけい]) formundan sonra: sert, doğrudan yasaklama '…-me!'
Emir kipinin olumsuzu; kaba/direkt, genelde erkeksi veya acil durumlar.
Sıfat/isim + な: ね'ye benzer ama daha erkeksi, samimi bir ünlem/onay tonu.
Konuşma dili, çoğunlukla erkekler; resmî dilde kullanılmaz.
footnotes_tr: The two uses of な are completely different from each other; which one it is is determined by the type of the preceding word (whether it's a verb's dictionary form or an adjective/noun).

dictionary-form.title_tr: Dictionary Form (辞書形) and Everyday Conversation
dictionary-form.intro_tr: 辞書形[じしょけい] (dictionary form) is the basic form of a verb as it appears in a dictionary, without any conjugation suffix; it also represents the verb's "present tense/future tense, affirmative, informal (plain)" form. This form, which is the polite equivalent of ます form, is used when speaking with family and close friends, in inner voice/thought sentences, and as the base structure to which many grammar patterns (〜前に, 〜ことがある, 〜と思う, 〜つもりだ etc.) are attached. Each verb group (godan, ichidan, irregular) has its own rules for forming the dictionary form. At the N5 level, it is crucial to know both how to produce this form and the abbreviations and variations encountered in everyday/casual speech (てる, じゃない, んだ etc.). This page summarizes the structure of the dictionary form, its usage areas, and the register differences specific to everyday conversation in tables.

tables.caption_tr: Formation of the Dictionary Form (By Verb Groups)
column_headers: 辞書形[じしょけい] (Sözlük Formu)
footnotes_tr: Rule: In godan verbs, the い-row syllable (i-row) in ます form changes to the u-row (u-row): き→く, ぎ→ぐ, し→す, ち→つ, に→ぬ, び→ぶ, み→む, い→う.
In ichidan verbs, only the ます suffix is removed and る is added: 食[た]べ+ます → 食[た]べる.
する and 来[く]る are completely irregular and must be memorized.

tables.caption_tr: Major Grammar Patterns Where the Dictionary Form Is Used

Sentence-final particles such as わ, さ, ぜ, ぞ vary depending on the speaker's gender/style; they are not taught in textbook Japanese but are frequently heard in everyday life.

no-possessive.intro_tr: の is one of the most frequently used particles in Japanese, and its primary function is to connect two nouns to each other — this connection corresponds to both the "-in/-ın" possessive suffix in Turkish and the noun phrase structure (noun modifier). The structure A の B means "A's B"; but this relationship does not always have to be actual possession; it also creates descriptive links such as origin, material, topic, profession. の can also function like a pronoun with the meaning "…that which is" when used alone at the end of a sentence, and it is also used to nominalize verb/adjective clauses (it can partially be replaced with こと). Additionally, in everyday speech it can come to the end of sentences and function like a question particle. On this page you will find all these uses of の and common mistakes presented in table form.

footnotes_tr: In the structure A の B, A is the modifier and B is the modified (main) element; in Turkish translation the order is generally preserved: 'A's B'.

past-tense.intro_tr: In Japanese, the past tense is constructed in two different ways depending on speech level (register): in polite speech, the past form of ます形, which is 〜ました / 〜ませんでした, and in intimate/casual speech, the form obtained by modifying the dictionary form, 〜た / 〜なかった (briefly called "た形"), is used. The rule for forming た形 in verbs varies depending on which group the verb belongs to (godan, ichidan, irregular), and especially in godan verbs, sound changes (音便[おんびん]) come into play. Adjectives (い-adjective, な-adjective) and the です copula also have their own past tense rules; these are conjugated differently from verbs. On this page, all affirmative/negative variations of both polite and casual past tense forms are presented in table format, along with their exceptions.

tables.caption_tr: 1. Past Tense with ます形 (Polite Register)
rows: ません → ませんでした
footnotes_tr: ませんでした always ends with でした, which is the past tense of です; a form like 'ませんだ' DOES NOT EXIST — this is a common mistake.

tables.caption_tr: 2. Rules for Forming た形 — Godan Verbs (Sound Change / 音便[おんびん])
footnotes_tr: These rules are exactly the same as て形: if you know て形, you can reach た形 by the て→た, で→だ change (例: 話[はな]して → 話[はな]した).

tables.caption_tr: 3. た形 — Ichidan and Irregular Verbs
rows: なかった (あなかった DEĞİL!)
footnotes_tr: The negative of the verb ある is always ない/なかった, not derived from its own root — this is the most frequently confused exception at the N5 level.

tables.caption_tr: 4. Past Tense in Adjectives and the です Copula
rows: 高[たか]くなかったです / 高[たか]くありませんでした
元気[げんき]じゃなかった
元気[げんき]じゃありませんでした
学生[がくせい]じゃなかった
学生[がくせい]じゃありませんでした
footnotes_tr: In い-adjectives, the past tense is added not to a verb, but to the adjective itself: い → かった. 'でした' is never directly attached to an い-adjective (高いでした is WRONG).

tables.caption_tr: 5. Polite (丁寧[ていねい]) vs Casual (普通[ふつう]) Past Tense — General Summary
footnotes_tr: The casual form is used in everyday conversation, everyday/inner speech, chatting with friends, and written language (except である体); the polite form, on the other hand, is preferred in any situation that requires politeness.

negative-form.intro_tr: In Japanese, there are two basic register levels for verb negation: 〜ません (the negative of ます形) used in polite speech, and 〜ない (the ない形 derived from the dictionary form) used in daily/casual speech. Both forms carry present/future tense and negation simultaneously; for past tense, the forms 〜ませんでした and 〜なかった are additionally used. The formation rule of ない形 varies depending on the verb group (五段[ごだん], 一段[いちだん], 不規則[ふきそく]), and some consonant harmony rules must be memorized. On this page, you will find complete conjugation tables for both registers, vowel change rules for godan verbs, comparative examples across groups, and a quick overview of common patterns derived from ない形.

tables.caption_tr: ます形 (敬体/丁寧体) — Polite Register Conjugation Table
rows: 食[た]べませんでした (tabemasen deshita)
footnotes_tr: ます形 is always conjugated in the same pattern: ます/ません/ました/ませんでした. The rule is fixed regardless of the verb group, because only the verb stem before the ます-root changes.

tables.caption_tr: ない形 (普通体/casual) — Daily/Casual Register Conjugation Table
footnotes_tr: The なかった form comes from ない behaving like an い-adjective: ない → なかった (just like 高[たか]い → 高[たか]かった).

tables.caption_tr: Rule for Forming ない形 in 五段[ごだん] Verbs — Final Sound Change (u-row → a-row)
footnotes_tr: Verbs ending in う change to わ, not to あ (あない is incorrect) — this is one of the most common mistakes.
Some verbs ending in -る like 帰[かえ]る appear to be 一段[いちだん] but are actually 五段[ごだん]; these verbs are called 'apparently ichidan (見[み]せかけの一段)' verbs.

tables.caption_tr: Comparative Negative Table by Verb Groups (ます形 vs ない形)
footnotes_tr: The ある verb is the only irregular negating verb in Japanese: breaking the rule, it becomes ない instead of あらない.
The reading changes in the 来[く]る verb: positive 来[く]る → negative 来[こ]ない (kanji is the same, reading is different).

tables.caption_tr: Common Patterns Derived from ない形 — Quick Reference
rows: 時間[じかん]がなくて、行[い]けなかった。 (Zaman olmadığı için gidemedim.)
…-meden, bir şey yapmadan başka bir şey yapmak
朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べないで学校[がっこう]へ行[い]った。 (Kahvaltı etmeden okula gittim.)

心配[しんぱい]しなくてもいい。 (Endişelenmene gerek yok.)
無理[むり]をしないほうがいい。 (Zorlamaman iyi olur.)
footnotes_tr: Each of these patterns is detailed as a separate grammar topic; here they are summarized only to see how they derive from the foundation of ない形.

kosoado.title_tr: こそあど System (これ/それ/あれ/どれ) — Demonstrative Words
kosoado.intro_tr: The こそあど system is the general name for demonstrative words (this/that/that over there/which) in Japanese and consists of four word groups (こ-, そ-, あ-, ど-). こ- refers to things close to the speaker, そ- refers to things close to the listener or recently mentioned, あ- refers to things far from both or commonly known, and ど- carries a question meaning. These four roots are used in six different categories: nouns (これ/それ/あれ/どれ), adjectives (この/その/あの/どの), places (ここ/そこ/あそこ/どこ), directions (こちら/そちら/あちら/どちら), qualities (こんな/そんな/あんな/どんな), and manner (こう/そう/ああ/どう). In spoken language, the rules depend not only on physical distance but also on the information flow in the discourse (textual/anaphoric usage) — especially the difference between そ- and あ- can be confusing at first.

tables.caption_tr: General Structure of the こそあど System — Six Categories
rows: Nesne (isim yerine geçer, tek başına kullanılır)
Tarz / şekil (副詞[ふくし] gibi kullanılır)
footnotes_tr: これ/それ/あれ/どれ are used as nouns by themselves, and no other noun can come directly after them.
この/その/あの/どの, on the other hand, can NEVER be used alone; they must always come before a noun: この本 (this book), *この (wrong).
こちら/そちら/あちら/どちら can be used both as 'direction' and politely as 'this/that/that person' (polite form of これ/それ/あれ).

tables.caption_tr: これ / それ / あれ / どれ — Demonstrative Pronouns (Objects)
rows: これは ペンです。(Bu bir kalem.)
Dinleyicinin elinde/yanında olan şey, ya da az önce sözü edilen konu
それは 何[なん]ですか。(O şey nedir?)
Hem konuşandan hem dinleyiciden uzak olan, ikisinin de görebildiği şey
あれは 山[やま]です。(Şu, dağdır.)
Üç veya daha fazla seçenek arasından soru sorarken
どれが いいですか。(Hangisi iyi?)
footnotes_tr: If asking a question between two options, use どちら instead of どれ: どちらが いいですか (Which of the two is better?).
あれ is also used as an exclamation in everyday speech when you can't remember something: あれ、財布[さいふ]がない！(Oh no, my wallet is gone!)

tables.caption_tr: この / その / あの / どの — Usage as Adjectives (+ Noun)
rows: この 人[ひと]は 先生[せんせい]です。(Bu kişi öğretmendir.)
その 話[はなし]は 本当[ほんとう]ですか。(O hikâye gerçek mi?)
あの 店[みせ]は おいしいです。(Şu dükkânın yemekleri lezzetli.)
どの 席[せき]が 空[あ]いていますか。(Hangi koltuk boş?)
footnotes_tr: あの is also used as an exclamation showing hesitation when starting to speak: あの…すみません。(Um... excuse me.)

tables.caption_tr: ここ / そこ / あそこ / どこ and こちら / そちら / あちら / どちら — Places and Directions
rows: Genel yer belirtir: ここに 座[すわ]ってください。(Buraya oturun.)
Daha nazik ve resmî; ayrıca kibarca 'bu/şu/o kişi' anlamında kullanılır
Arkadaşlar arası, gündelik konuşma; iki seçenek sorusu için de kullanılır
footnotes_tr: When introducing oneself politely on the phone, one says こちらは〜です (I am ...).
どちら can be used both as a direction question and politely as a 'who' question: どちら様[さま]ですか (Who are you, politely).

tables.caption_tr: こんな / そんな / あんな / どんな — Adjectives Describing Quality/Type
rows: bu tür / bu kadar (konuşana yakın nitelik)
こんな 服[ふく]が 欲[ほ]しいです。(Böyle bir kıyafet istiyorum.)
そんな こと 言[い]わないでください。(Öyle bir şey söylemeyin.)
şu tür / öyle (ikisinden de uzak nitelik)
あんな 映画[えいが]は 見[み]たくない。(Öyle bir filmi izlemek istemiyorum.)
どんな 音楽[おんがく]が 好[す]きですか。(Ne tür müzik seversin?)
footnotes_tr: こんな/そんな/あんな/どんな behave like な-adjectives and come directly before nouns; they are not used as nouns (unlike この).

tables.caption_tr: こう / そう / ああ / どう — Manner/Way Adverbs
rows: こう 書[か]いてください。(Böyle yazın.)
öyle (bahsedilen şekilde); aynı zamanda 'öyle mi?' onayı
そうですね。(Öyle, doğru / Hımm, düşüneyim.)
ああ すれば いいですよ。(Şöyle yaparsan iyi olur.)
これは どうですか。(Bu nasıl?)
footnotes_tr: そう is very frequently used alone as an aizuchi (response word) meaning 'I see, I understand.'
どうも is a fixed expression meaning both 'thank you very much' and 'somehow/anyway.'

temo-ii-dame.title_tr: 〜てもいい / 〜てはだめ (Expressing Permission and Prohibition)
temo-ii-dame.intro_tr: 〜てもいい is added to the て(で) form of verbs/adjectives/nouns to express PERMISSION or to ask for permission with the meaning '…-se/can be okay, …-can'. Its opposite, 〜てはいけない / 〜てはだめ, conveys the meaning of PROHIBITION with '…-ing is forbidden, …-must not'; in colloquial speech, てはいけない is often shortened to ちゃいけない/じゃいけない, and てはだめ to ちゃだめ/じゃだめ. This pattern can be used not only with verbs, but also with い-adjectives (くて), な-adjectives/nouns (で). When asking for permission, 〜てもいいですか is the most common pattern; in more polite speech, 〜てもよろしいですか or 〜てもかまいませんか are preferred. Note: 〜てもいい should not be confused with 〜なくてもいい (not mandatory) which has the meaning '…-ing is not necessary' — the two carry different meanings.

tables.caption_tr: Formation of the て/で Form and Adding 〜てもいい / 〜てはだめ
rows: 待[ま]って・帰[かえ]って
学生[がくせい]でもいい

〜ちゃ(ん)いけない / 〜じゃいけない
footnotes_tr: In colloquial speech, ては→ちゃ and では→じゃ are contracted: 食べては→食べちゃ, 飲んでは→飲んじゃ.

honorific-titles.title_tr: Honorific Suffixes: さん・くん・ちゃん・様
honorific-titles.intro_tr: In Japanese, suffixes like さん, くん, ちゃん, and 様[さま] added to a person's name or title indicate the degree of politeness, age, gender, and closeness between the speaker and the other person. These suffixes can be thought of like "Mr./Ms." in Turkish, but they contain much finer distinctions; which one is chosen depends on the type of relationship (work, family, friendship, customer-seller, etc.). The most important rule: these suffixes are NEVER added to your own name; they are only used when referring to someone else or addressing someone. Also, occupation/title names like 先生[せんせい], 部長[ぶちょう] already carry respect within themselves, so adding さん once more on top of them is a common mistake. On this page, the usage areas of four basic suffixes, who addresses whom and how, and common mistakes are summarized in table format.

greetings-expressions.title_tr: Greetings and Set Phrases (挨拶[あいさつ]と決[き]まり文句[もんく])
greetings-expressions.intro_tr: In Japanese, throughout almost every moment of daily life (from waking up in the morning to eating meals, leaving and entering home, thanking someone, etc.), specific, nearly unchangeable set phrases are used. These expressions function not as grammar rules but as rules of social etiquette; using them in the right place and at the right time is very important. At the N5 level, it is necessary to memorize these phrases less for their meaning and more by 'when and to whom they are said.' In the tables below, greetings according to the time of day, coming and going phrases, thanks/apology expressions, meal phrases, and meeting sentences are presented together, with both casual and polite (formal) equivalents. This page can be used like a dictionary; you can come back and check it whenever you need.

footnotes_tr: こんにちは and こんばんは are generally used alone, not with suffixes like さん/くん, and are suitable for mid to late day.

de-particle.title_tr: The で Particle (Place, Tool, Reason, Material, Limit)
de-particle.intro_tr: The で particle is a very versatile particle in Japanese and is one of the most frequently encountered particles at the N5 level. Its primary function is to indicate the place where an action takes place (unlike に which is used with あります/います). Besides that, it is also used to express which tool, method, or material we use to do something, the reason for a situation, and the total limit of a whole (duration, quantity, price). It is used without conjugation in the form of Noun + で and comes before the verb. The following tables summarize all basic uses of で and the points that are confused with に.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Functions of the で Particle
rows: 公園[こうえん]で 遊[あそ]びます
Bir eylemin (oynamak, çalışmak, yemek yemek vb.) gerçekleştiği yeri gösterir. Statik varlık bildiren あります/います ile kullanılmaz, onun yerine に kullanılır.
はさみで 紙[かみ]を 切[き]ります
Bir işi hangi alet, taşıt veya yöntemle yaptığımızı belirtir.
malzeme + で + 作[つく]る / できている
米[こめ]で 酒[さけ]を 作[つく]る
Ham madde son üründe artık gözle görülmüyorsa で kullanılır; görünüyorsa の tercih edilir.
台風[たいふう]で 電車[でんしゃ]が 止[と]まりました
Bir durumun nesnel/somut sebebini bildirir; çünkü/ので'ye yakın ama daha kısadır ve isimle biter.
全部[ぜんぶ]で 三千円[さんぜんえん]です
Bir bütünün toplam miktarını, süresini veya kapsamını belirtir: toplamda, içinde.
dil + で + 話す / 書く
英語[えいご]で 話[はな]します
Hangi dilde konuşulduğunu veya yazıldığını belirtir; bir tür araç kullanımıdır.
一人[ひとり]で 行[い]きます
Bir işin hangi durumda (yalnız, grup halinde vb.) yapıldığını belirtir.

tables.caption_tr: で vs に: Comparison of Two Particles Indicating Place
rows: Eylem fiilleriyle: 食[た]べる, 勉強[べんきょう]する, 遊[あそ]ぶ, 働[はたら]く
教室[きょうしつ]で 昼[ひる]ご 飯[はん]を 食[た]べます
Varoluş/durum fiilleriyle: あります, います, 住[す]む, 座[すわ]る
教室[きょうしつ]に 学生[がくせい]が います
Hedef/varış noktası bildiren fiillerle: 行[い]く, 来[く]る, 着[つ]く, 入[はい]る
学校[がっこう]に 行[い]きます
Hareketin gerçekleştiği alan bildiren fiillerle (行く/来る hariç çoğu fiil)
公園[こうえん]で テニスを します
footnotes_tr: Quick rule: に is used to answer 'What/Who is there?'; で is used to answer 'What are you doing there?'

tables.caption_tr: Other Meanings of で: Reason, Material, Limit, Price
rows: 雨[あめ]で 試合[しあい]が 中止[ちゅうし]に なりました
malzeme + で + 作る/できる
この 机[つくえ]は 木[き]で できています
みんなで 五人[ごにん]です
一時間[いちじかん]で 終[お]わります
千円[せんえん]で 買[か]いました

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes: で or に?
rows: 図書館[としょかん]に 勉強[べんきょう]します
図書館[としょかん]で 勉強[べんきょう]します
勉強する bir eylem fiilidir; yer için で gerekir, statik konum bildiren に değil.
教室[きょうしつ]で 先生[せんせい]が います

います varoluş fiilidir; konum için に kullanılır.
学校[がっこう]で 行きます (varış noktası anlamında)
学校[がっこう]に 行[い]きます
Varış noktası için に kullanılır; で sadece hareketin geçtiği alanı belirtir, hedefi değil.
三日[みっか]に 終わります (süre sınırı anlamında)
三日[みっか]で 終[お]わります
Bir işin tamamlanma süresi/sınırı için で kullanılır, に değil.

ga-kedo-contrast.intro_tr: が and けど are contrast conjunctions that connect two sentences with the meaning of "but, however, yet," and unlike in Turkish, they are not placed at the beginning of a sentence but rather attached to the END of the FIRST sentence (A-sentence + が/けど + B-sentence). Whereas が is more formal/suitable for written language, けど is used very frequently in everyday spoken language; けれど and けれども are intermediate politeness levels between the two. Additionally, が and けど do not always create a true contrast; they are often used to soften a request, question, or command by providing a polite introduction (すみませんが…). Note: this が is written the same as the particle が that marks the subject (a separate topic) but has a completely different function — here it is attached to the end of a sentence as a conjunction.

tables.caption_tr: が / けれども / けれど / けど — Politeness Levels
rows: Yazı dili, iş Japoncası, kibar konuşma (です/ます + が)
Cümle başında yeni cümle başlatmak için (でも yerine de kullanılır)
footnotes_tr: In written language しかし also serves a similar function but is a separate conjunction and is generally used at the beginning of a sentence.

rows: 安[やす]いですが、おいしくないです。

Çoğu zaman sadece kibarca giriş yapar, gerçek çelişki içermez

e-direction-particle.intro_tr: へ is a basic particle in Japanese that indicates the direction of movement or destination point, and is generally used together with verbs expressing movement such as 行[い]く (to go), 来[く]る (to come), 帰[かえ]る (to return), and 向[む]かう (to head toward). Its meaning is similar to the Turkish suffix "…'e" or "…'e doğru". Although its written form is the hiragana へ (normally pronounced "he"), when used as a particle in a sentence, it is always pronounced "e" — this is an important exception that follows the same logic as the particle は being pronounced "wa". In most sentences, it can be substituted directly with the particle に; however, へ more emphasizes the idea of "toward that direction", while に emphasizes arriving "at exactly that point". It is one of the most frequently encountered particles at the N5 level and must be memorized.

tables.caption_tr: へ Particle's Basic Usage
rows: 学校[がっこう]へ 行[い]きます
友達[ともだち]の 家[いえ]へ 来[き]てください
右[みぎ]へ 曲[ま]がってください
どこへ 行[い]きますか
footnotes_tr: へ is always used together with verbs that express movement; it does not indicate static states (being, sitting, etc.).

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of へ and に
rows: Kullanılır ama に kadar sık değil
着[つ]く, 住[す]む, 入[はい]る gibi fiillerle doğal değil
着[つ]く, 住[す]む, 入[はい]る ile doğal
Yön fiilleriyle (行く/来る/帰る/向かう)
東京[とうきょう]へ 行[い]きます
東京[とうきょう]に 行[い]きます (anlamca hemen hemen aynı)
footnotes_tr: In short: with movement verbs (行く/来る/帰る), へ and に can almost always be used interchangeably. However, with verbs that carry the meaning of 'entering/arriving/living' (着く, 住む, 入る), only に is natural.

tables.caption_tr: Verbs Frequently Used with へ
rows: Daha az doğal, に tercih edilir
Daha az doğal, に tercih edilir

tables.caption_tr: Writing and Pronunciation Note
rows: Cümlede yön/hedef belirten edat olduğunda 'he' değil 'e' okunur.
Kelimenin kendi hecesi olduğunda normal 'he' sesiyle okunur, edat değildir.
footnotes_tr: This exception belongs to the same group as the particle は being pronounced 'wa' and the particle を being pronounced 'o' — in Japanese, these three are the classic 'particles whose pronunciation changes': は, へ, を.

examples.target: 学校[がっこう]へ 行[い]きます。
examples.reading: がっこうへ いきます。
examples.translation_tr: I am going to school.
examples.note_tr: The most basic usage: destination + へ + movement verb.

examples.target: 明日[あした]、東京[とうきょう]へ 行[い]く 予定[よてい]です。
examples.reading: あした、とうきょうへ いく よていです。
examples.translation_tr: I have a plan to go to Tokyo tomorrow.

examples.target: 友達[ともだち]の 家[いえ]へ 来[き]てください。
examples.reading: ともだちの いえへ きてください。
examples.translation_tr: Please come to my friend's house.

examples.target: 家族[かぞく]は 来週[らいしゅう] 田舎[いなか]へ 帰[かえ]ります。
examples.reading: かぞくは らいしゅう いなかへ かえります。
examples.translation_tr: My family is returning to the homeland next week.

examples.target: 右[みぎ]へ 曲[ま]がってください。
examples.reading: みぎへ まがってください。
examples.translation_tr: Please turn right.
examples.note_tr: When indicating direction (right/left/forward/backward), へ is very natural, and に can also be used.

examples.target: 電車[でんしゃ]は 大阪[おおさか]へ 向[む]かっています。
examples.reading: でんしゃは おおさかへ むかっています。

examples.target: どこへ 行[い]きますか。
examples.reading: どこへ いきますか。

examples.note_tr: This is a very frequently used pattern together with the question word どこ.

examples.target: 母[はは]へ 手紙[てがみ]を 書[か]きました。

examples.note_tr: Here, へ indicates to whom the letter is being sent; in this usage に is also possible, but へ is more common when writing on envelopes (例: 母へ).

te-form.intro_tr: The て form is one of the most basic and most frequently used structures in Japanese verb conjugation; it forms the foundation of dozens of different grammar patterns such as connecting verbs together, making polite requests, granting permission, and expressing continuity/state. Each verb group (godan, ichidan, irregular) has its own te-form rules, and these rules operate by exactly the same logic as た-form (past tense) — only the た at the end changes to て. The て form by itself does not indicate a tense; its meaning changes depending on the auxiliary verb attached after it or the context. This page presents both the formation rules and the most frequently used て-patterns as a single reference.

tables.caption_tr: て Form Rules in Godan (Group I) Verbs
footnotes_tr: EXCEPTION: 行[い]く (to go) → 行[い]って (irregular, takes って not いて).
The た-form (past tense) uses exactly the same rules; た comes instead of て (例: 買[か]った, 飲[の]んだ, 書[か]いた).

tables.caption_tr: て Form in Ichidan (Group II) and Irregular Verbs
footnotes_tr: Ichidan verbs are easily recognized: they end in る and the preceding syllable has え-row or い-row vowels (exceptions excluded: some る-ending verbs like 帰[かえ]る, 入[はい]る are actually godan).
For い-adjectives there is no て-form; instead 〜くて is used (例: 大[おお]きくて → being large).

Yağmur yağdığı için maç iptal oldu.

写真[しゃしん]を撮[と]ってもいいです
ここでたばこを吸[す]ってはいけません
荷物[にもつ]を持[も]ってあげました
日本語[にほんご]が上手[じょうず]になってきました
宿題[しゅくだい]をしてから、遊[あそ]びます

る-biten ama aslında godan olan fiiller
て formu ichidan gibi değil, godan kuralına göre って alır

adjective-adverbs.intro_tr: In Japanese, adjectives undergo special conjugation to modify a verb (i.e., to be used as an adverb). In い-adjectives, the final い is dropped and く is added in its place (e.g., 早い[はやい] → 早く[はやく]). In な-adjectives, only に is added directly to the end of the word, with the な suffix dropped (e.g., 静か[しずか] → 静かに[しずかに]). These adverbial forms are placed before a verb to describe "how something is done" and are particularly frequently used with verbs like なる (to become) and する (to do). The most important exception is that the adverbial form of the adjective いい/よい is not いく but よく. This structure is fundamental at the N5 level and is encountered continuously, so it should be well reinforced.

tables.caption_tr: Making Adverbs from い-Adjectives (〜く)
rows: İSTİSNA: いい değil よい esas alınır
footnotes_tr: Rule: The final 'い' syllable of an い-adjective is dropped and 'く' is added in its place.
The root of the adjective いい is actually 良い[よい]; therefore its adverbial form is 'よく', not 'いく'.

tables.caption_tr: Making Adverbs from な-Adjectives (〜に)
footnotes_tr: Rule: The 'な' suffix of a な-adjective is dropped and 'に' is added directly to the end of the word.
Some words like きれい and きらい that appear to end in い are actually な-adjectives; for these as well, the rule is to add に, not く.

tables.caption_tr: Exceptions and Points to Note
rows: いい'nin gerçek kökü 良い[よい]'dir, zarf ondan türer.
ない de bir い-sıfat gibi çekilir: なく + て/なる vb.
きれい い ile bitse de aslında な-sıfattır, kural に'dir.
同じ özel bir な-sıfattır; zarf hali genelde 同じく şeklinde kullanılır.
きらい de い ile bitse de な-sıfattır, に alır.

tables.caption_tr: The Patterns 〜くなる/〜になる (Change) and 〜くする/〜にする (Making)
rows: 部屋[へや]を明るく[あかるく]する (odayı aydınlatmak)
部屋をきれいにする (odayı temizlemek)
先生[せんせい]になる (öğretmen olmak)
footnotes_tr: These patterns are very frequently encountered at the N5-N4 boundary and are among the fundamental building blocks of daily conversation.

counters.title_tr: Counters (助数詞[じょすうし]): 〜つ, 〜人, 〜本, 〜枚 and Others
counters.intro_tr: In Japanese, when expressing the quantity of something, a bare number (一、二、三...) is not enough; after the number, a special "counter" (助数詞[じょすうし]) suffix is added that changes depending on the shape, size, or type of the object being counted. For example, 〜人[にん] is used for people, 〜本[ほん] for long thin objects (bottles, pens), and 〜枚[まい] for thin flat objects (paper, plates). The most general and "lifesaver" counter is 〜つ, a special series from 1 to 10; when unsure which counter to use, it can be used for most concrete objects. In counters, when combined with certain numbers like 1, 3, 6, 8, 10, consonant gemination (っ) or vowel changes (は→ぱ/ば for example) are common; these changes are irregularities that must be memorized. This page compiles complete 1-10 inflection tables, irregularities, and sentence usage patterns of the most frequently used counters at N5 level in one place.

tables.caption_tr: 〜つ — General counter (native Japanese numerals, 1-10)
rows: İSTİSNA: つ eki yoktur, sadece とお
footnotes_tr: The つ series is not used for numbers 11 and above; instead, Chinese-origin numerals (十一、十二...) + appropriate special counter are used.
つ is the 'lifesaver' counter for any concrete object with an unclear category, such as kanji, animals, people.

tables.caption_tr: 〜人 — Human counter
rows: 七人[しちにん]／七人[ななにん]
footnotes_tr: For 1 and 2 people, special native Japanese remnant readings (ひとり, ふたり) are used; from 3 onwards, the regular 〜にん structure is used.

tables.caption_tr: 〜本 — Long thin objects (bottles, pens, trees, films, etc.)
rows: 十本[じゅっぽん]／十本[じっぽん]
footnotes_tr: At numbers 1, 6, 8, 10, the ほん sound changes to ぽん; at 3, it changes to ぼん. This pattern is a repeated sound change pattern in many other counters (匹, 個, 冊, 階...).

tables.caption_tr: 〜枚 — Thin, flat objects (paper, plates, shirts, tickets, etc.)
footnotes_tr: The 枚 counter has no sound changes and is completely regular — therefore it is one of the easiest counters to memorize at the beginner level.

tables.caption_tr: 〜匹 — Small animals (cats, dogs, fish, insects, etc.)
rows: 十匹[じゅっぴき]／十匹[じっぴき]
footnotes_tr: For large animals (cows, horses, elephants, etc.), 〜頭[とう] counter is used instead of 匹; for birds and rabbits, 〜羽[わ] is used.

tables.caption_tr: 〜個 — Small general objects (apples, boxes, stones, etc.)
rows: 十個[じゅっこ]／十個[じっこ]
footnotes_tr: 個 is very close in meaning to つ; つ is preferred more in spoken language, while 個 is preferred somewhat more in written/formal language and in larger numbers (11 and above).

tables.caption_tr: 〜台 — Machines and vehicles (cars, computers, TVs, etc.)
footnotes_tr: There are no sound changes in the 台 counter; it is used for all mechanical/motorized objects such as cars, bicycles, machines, and electronic appliances.

tables.caption_tr: 〜冊 — Books and bound materials (books, magazines, notebooks, etc.)
rows: 十冊[じゅっさつ]／十冊[じっさつ]
footnotes_tr: Consonant gemination is seen only at 1, 8, and 10; the others are completely regular.

tables.caption_tr: 〜階 — Building floors/stories
rows: 三階[さんがい]／三階[さんかい]
十階[じゅっかい]／十階[じっかい]
何階[なんがい]／何階[なんかい]
footnotes_tr: The reading of the 3rd floor shows regional/personal variation (さんがい is the most common standard).

tables.caption_tr: 〜歳／〜才 — Age counter
rows: İSTİSNA — さんじゅっさい değil, tamamen düzensiz okunur
footnotes_tr: 歳 and 才 are read the same and have the same meaning; 才 is preferred more in daily/informal writing, while 歳 is preferred in official documents.
Age 20 (はたち) is especially important because it is the age of legal adulthood in Japan and its irregular reading must definitely be memorized.

tables.caption_tr: Which counter is used for which object? — Summary table
rows: 学生[がくせい]、友達[ともだち]
ペン、瓶[びん]、木[き]、映画[えいが]
紙[かみ]、皿[さら]、シャツ、切符[きっぷ]
猫[ねこ]、犬[いぬ]、魚[さかな]
りんご、箱[はこ]、消しゴム
車[くるま]、パソコン、テレビ
本[ほん]、雑誌[ざっし]、ノート

tables.caption_tr: Counter word order in sentences (word order patterns)
rows: 学生[がくせい]が三人[さんにん]います。
En doğal ve en yaygın dizilim; sayaç isimden ayrı, fiilden hemen önce gelir.
三人[さんにん]の学生[がくせい]
İsim tamlaması gibi kullanılır; yazılı/resmî dilde ve isim öbeğini vurgulamak istendiğinde tercih edilir.
りんごを三[みっ]つ買[か]いました。
Nesne(を ile işaretli) önce gelir, sayaç fiile bitişik olarak sonra gelir; günlük konuşmada en doğal kalıptır.
footnotes_tr: The second pattern (with の) carries a somewhat more formal/written tone; in daily conversation, the first and third patterns are much more frequently used.

relative-clauses.title_tr: Adjectival Clauses (Modifying Nouns) — 連体修飾[れんたいしゅうしょく]
relative-clauses.intro_tr: In Japanese, to modify a noun, unlike Turkish, you don't use a separate relative pronoun ("ki", "-en/-an") or "which/that"; instead, the modifying clause (verb, adjective, or noun+の) is placed directly BEFORE the noun it modifies. In other words, the structure "the book I bought yesterday" is constructed in Japanese as "昨日[きのう]買[か]った本[ほん]" (literally: yesterday bought book). The verbs and adjectives within the modifying clause ALWAYS use plain form (plain/futsūkei) — the です・ます form is not used in noun modification sections. Additionally, if there is a subject within the clause, が is used instead of は. This is a very frequently encountered pattern at N4 level and is fundamental in daily conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Noun Modification According to Word Type (Adjective Clause Structure)
rows: Fiil - なかった hali (olumsuz geçmiş)
食[た]べなかった人[ひと]
静[しず]かじゃない部屋[へや]
学生[がくせい]の時[とき]
学生[がくせい]じゃない人[ひと]
footnotes_tr: だ/です can never come directly before a noun to modify it; instead, な (for な-adjectives/nouns) or の (for nouns, in certain patterns) is used.

tables.caption_tr: Verb Tense: 'Relative Time' within Modifying Clauses
rows: Ana cümleye göre gelecekte olan veya genel/süregelen bir eylem
来[く]る人[ひと] — gelecek olan kişi
Ana cümleye göre daha önce tamamlanmış eylem
来[き]た人[ひと] — gelmiş olan kişi
O anda / o dönemde sürmekte olan eylem
走[はし]っている人[ひと] — koşmakta olan kişi
Geçmişte bir noktada sürmekte olan eylem
走[はし]っていた人[ひと] — (o sırada) koşmakta olan kişi
来[こ]ない人[ひと] — gelmeyen kişi
来[こ]なかった人[ひと] — gelmemiş olan kişi
footnotes_tr: The tense within a modifying clause is INDEPENDENT of the main clause's tense — it shows the sequence between two actions, not absolute calendar time.

Cümlecik içindeki özne は değil が alır

comparatives-superlatives.title_tr: Comparison and Superiority (より / ほど / 一番)
comparatives-superlatives.intro_tr: In Japanese, unlike Turkish, there is no separate "comparison" or "superiority" suffix added to the adjective itself (like -er/-est in English); instead, comparison is done with particles and adverbs such as より (…more than), ほど (…as much as, with negation), 同[おな]じくらい (to the same degree) and 一番[いちばん]/最[もっと]も (most). The adjective itself does not change; it is used only with normal い or な conjugation. When comparing two things, どちら is used; when asking for the highest among three or more things, the question words どれ/だれ are used. The より phrase can change position in the sentence because Japanese is an SOV language and stress generally falls on the element immediately before the verb/adjective. This page summarizes the most frequently used comparison and superiority patterns at N4 level in table form.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Comparison Patterns (Between Two Things)
rows: 日本[にほん]は トルコより 小[ちい]さいです。
A tarafı daha ... (vurgu A üzerinde, より'li kısım atlanabilir)

A, B kadar ... değil (sıfat olumsuz çekilir)
トルコは 日本[にほん]ほど 小[ちい]さくないです。
AはBと同[おな]じくらい〜です
兄[あに]は 父[ちち]と 同[おな]じくらい 背[せ]が 高[たか]いです。
Hem A hem B ... (ikisi de aynı özellikte)
兄[あに]も 弟[おとうと]も 背[せ]が 高[たか]いです。

クラスで 一番[いちばん] 背[せ]が 高[たか]いです。
富士山[ふじさん]は 日本[にほん]で最[もっと]も 高[たか]い 山[やま]だ。
どれが一番[いちばん]〜ですか
どれが 一番[いちばん] 好[す]きですか。
誰[だれ]が一番[いちばん]〜ですか
クラスで 誰[だれ]が 一番[いちばん] 頭[あたま]が いいですか。
いつが一番[いちばん]〜ですか

AとBでは、どちらが〜ですか
Yukarıdakiyle aynı, では ile de kurulabilir

conditional-forms.title_tr: Conditional Forms (〜たら / 〜ば / 〜と / なら)
conditional-forms.intro_tr: In Japanese, there are four main conditional patterns meaning "if/then/-when": 〜たら, 〜ば, 〜と, and なら. Although they are all roughly translated into Turkish as "-sa/-se, -ınca, ise", they differ in terms of usage areas, repeatability, past-present relationship, and which verbs can come at the end of the sentence. 〜たら is the most flexible and most frequently used in spoken language; it is ideal for specific, one-time events. 〜ば and 〜と are used more for general truths, automatic results, and repeated situations; in particular, the use of 〜と and 〜ば with imperative/request/plea-like structures at the end of a sentence is restricted. なら, on the other hand, unlike the others, is used when reacting to information that the speaker heard/assumed, or when giving advice/suggestions, and the time order can be reversed (the result can come first, then the conditional clause in the sentence). This page summarizes the conjugation patterns of the four forms and their usage differences in a table; for detailed comparison, you can refer to the topic "Conditional Forms Comparison Table".

potential-form.title_tr: Capability Form (〜られる / 〜える) — "…-ebilmek" Structure in Verbs
potential-form.intro_tr: The capability form (可能形[かのうけい]) is used to transform a verb into the meaning of "…-ebilmek / …-abilmek" and corresponds to the capability suffix (-ebil-, -abil-) in Turkish. How it is formed varies depending on the verb group: in Godan verbs, the final syllable is changed to the e-row and る is added, in Ichidan verbs る is removed and られる is added, and in irregular verbs special forms (できる, 来[こ]られる) are used. Verbs in the capability form are considered intransitive in meaning, and generally が is used instead of を which marks the object. Additionally, the newly formed verb is now always conjugated like an Ichidan verb (〜ます, 〜ない, 〜た etc.). In spoken language, the dropping of ら in Ichidan verbs (ら抜[ぬ]き言葉[ことば]) is very common, but is not recommended in formal writing.

conj-i-adjective-full.intro_tr: い-adjectives are the only group in Japanese where adjectives inflect on their own (without requiring a copula); the root (語幹[ごかん]) stays fixed, only the final 「い」 character changes. This page brings together present/past tense, negation, te-form, adverbial form, conditional forms, and politeness levels in a single reference table. The only exception is the いい/よい adjective: in dictionary form いい is used, but in all other inflections it reverts to the よい root (よくない, よかった, etc. — never いくない/いかった). When い-adjectives modify nouns, they are used in the same bare form (高い山[たかいやま]), meaning unlike な-adjectives, no extra な is needed. This table covers nearly all い-adjective forms you will encounter in N4-level exams and daily conversation.

footnotes_tr: 語幹[ごかん] (root) is the fixed part of the adjective before the 「い」 character: 高い → 高(たか).

「〜くありません」 and 「〜くありませんでした」 are considered more formal/written and somewhat old-fashioned; in daily conversation 「〜くないです」 is preferred.

ya-toka-listing.title_tr: や / とか for Exemplary Counting (Creating a List)
ya-toka-listing.intro_tr: や and とか are particles used when counting only ONE PART as an example from among multiple things; unlike と, they carry the meaning 'these and probably other things too'. や generally goes between two or more nouns and is comfortably used in written language; it is often seen together with 〜など ('like, and so forth') to emphasize that the list is open-ended. とか, on the other hand, is a typical part of everyday, casual speech; it can be used not only with nouns but also with verb and adjective phrases, and can be repeated after each item (とか〜とか). Both of these particles are very frequently encountered at the JLPT N4 level and are indispensable patterns in daily conversation.

koto-nominalizer.intro_tr: こと and の are two fundamental nominalizing suffixes that allow you to nominalize verbs (and verb clauses) so that they can be used as subjects, objects, or predicates within a sentence; they serve a function similar to the Turkish infinitive "-mak/-mek" or the participle "-diği". Both are attached directly to the dictionary (rentaikei) form of a verb: 食[た]べる → 食[た]べること / 食[た]べるの. As a general rule, こと is used for abstract, indirect, definitional, or events described as "facts", while の is preferred for concrete, immediate events directly perceived by the five senses (seen, heard). Some set phrases and verbs use only こと, while others use only の, and these requirements are exceptions that must be memorized. This page summarizes the fundamental differences between the two suffixes, mandatory usage patterns, and common mistakes in table form.

giving-receiving.title_tr: あげる / くれる / もらう (Give-Receive Verbs)
giving-receiving.intro_tr: あげる, くれる and もらう are three basic "give-receive" verbs in Japanese that describe the transfer of something (or a favor) from one person to another. Which of these verbs to use depends not simply on the meaning of "give/receive" as in English or Turkish, but on the speaker's perspective (who is giving, who is receiving, is the recipient part of the "in-group"). あげる is used when the speaker or in-group gives something to someone else; くれる is used when someone else gives something to the speaker or in-group; もらう is used when the speaker receives something from someone else. These three verbs also have levels of politeness depending on age/status differences (やる, さしあげる, くださる, いただく). This page covers usage with basic noun + の objects; the 〜てあげる/くれる/もらう structure added to verbs is a separate topic.

conj-copula-full.title_tr: です/だ Copula Conjugation Table (All Registers and Tenses)
conj-copula-full.intro_tr: です/だ is the "copula" that forms nominative and na-adjective sentences in Japanese (it performs a function similar to the "to be" verb in English, but it is not a true verb). だ is the basic form of casual (intimate) speech, while です is the basic form of standard polite speech. These two forms take different shapes along the axes of tense (present/past), polarity (affirmative/negative), and register (register: casual, polite, formal written language である). This page collects ALL conjugations of です/だ — including plain, polite, negative, past, conditional, presumptive, and formal written forms — in a single reference table. At the N4 level, the most frequently confused point is when じゃない/ではない and だ/です are dropped; special attention should be paid to these points.

ta-koto-ga-aru.intro_tr: 〜たことがある is used to express a PAST EXPERIENCE that a person has had one or several times in the past, which has been completed, and means "have you ever …, I have …ed before". The structure is formed as the た-form (past plain form) of a verb + ことがある (to exist); the ある part is conjugated normally to transform into negative, question, and polite forms. Unlike the 〜た form which describes a one-time past event at a specific time, this pattern emphasizes an experience acquired over a lifetime, so it is not naturally used with very recent/specific time expressions such as "yesterday". If only ことがある is used without the た-form, the meaning changes completely to "sometimes …-s, it happens occasionally" (something unusual but occurring from time to time) — these two structures are often confused. Frequency adverbs such as 一度[いちど]、二度[にど]、何度[なんど]も、一度[いちど]も are very frequently used together with this pattern.

mae-ato-nagara.title_tr: まえに / あとで / ながら — Temporal Conjunctions
mae-ato-nagara.intro_tr: まえに (before), あとで (after) and ながら (-ing, at the same time) are basic conjunctions in Japanese that establish temporal relationships between two actions. まえに is always used with the DICTIONARY FORM of the verb — this rule does not change even if the sentence as a whole is in past tense, because the action before まえに is a reference point that has not yet occurred. あとで, on the other hand, is used with the TA-FORM (た形) of the verb because it refers to an action that has already been completed. ながら is attached to the MASU-STEM and indicates that two actions are performed BY THE SAME SUBJECT AT THE SAME TIME; the emphasis is generally on the second (main) verb. When used with nouns, の comes between them: 食事のまえに, 授業のあとで, etc.

tables.caption_tr: まえに (...-before) — Usage Patterns
rows: 食事[しょくじ]のまえに
授業[じゅぎょう]のまえに
üç yıl önce (bu kullanımda まえに zaman ifadesine eklenir, cümle bağlaçı değildir)
footnotes_tr: RULE: The verb before まえに is ALWAYS in dictionary form — it does not change even if the main sentence is in past tense.
When used with nouns, の is mandatory: not 食事まえに but 食事のまえに.

tables.caption_tr: あとで (...-after) — Usage Patterns
rows: 宿題[しゅくだい]をしたあとで
授業[じゅぎょう]のあとで
食事[しょくじ]のあとで
あとで電話[でんわ]します。
footnotes_tr: RULE: The verb before あとで ALWAYS takes た形 (past/completed form) because it refers to an action that has already ended.
あとで can also be used alone as an adverb with the meaning 'later, afterwards'.

tables.caption_tr: ながら (...-ing, at the same time) — Usage Patterns
footnotes_tr: RULE 1: The subject of the two actions must be the SAME person.
RULE 2: The emphasis is usually on the SECOND (main) verb of the sentence; the verb with ながら is an accompanying/side action.
ながら can also be used in patterns like 残念[ざんねん]ながら (unfortunately) with the meaning 'although/-in spite of', this is a separate topic (〜ながらも).

tables.caption_tr: まえに / あとで / ながら / とき Comparison Table

İkinci eylemden ÖNCE gerçekleşen ilk eylem
İkinci eylemden SONRA, ilk eylem biter bitmez değil, bir süre sonra da olabilir
Vurgu ikinci (ana) fiilde; birlikte yapılan eylemler
Eylemler art arda veya aynı anda olabilir
'…-dığında' genel zaman noktası, まえに/あとで kadar kesin sıra belirtmez

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes

İsimden sonra まえに/あとで gelirken の zorunludur.

causative-form.intro_tr: 〜させる (causative form / 使役形[しえきけい]) is a verb conjugation that expresses that one person MADE someone else do something or ALLOWED them to do it; it corresponds to the Turkish "-tir/-dir" suffix (yedirmek, okutmak) or the "permission" structure in Turkish. The meaning is derived from context: the same sentence can be read as both "forced to do" and "allowed to do." The sentence structure varies depending on whether the verb is transitive or intransitive: while intransitive verbs use "yaptıran に," transitive verbs mark the object with 〜を and the person with 〜に. When this form combines with the passive form, it creates the meaning 使役受身形[しえきうけみけい] (〜させられる) of "being forced to do against one's will" (a separate topic). The tables below summarize conjugation rules, particle usage, semantic nuances, and common patterns in detail.

tables.caption_tr: Causative Form (〜させる) Conjugation Rules — By Verb Groups
footnotes_tr: In spoken language, an abbreviated form 〜さす is also heard in some Ichidan and する verbs (食[た]べさす), but this is not considered standard at the N4 level.
In Godan verbs, the rule can always be summarized as 'negative root (あ-row) + せる'; knowing the あ-row in the negative form makes this conjugation easier.

tables.caption_tr: Sentence Structure and Particle Usage: Transitive vs Intransitive Verbs
rows: 母[はは]は子供[こども]を公園[こうえん]に行[い]かせた。
Nesne yok, kişi 〜に ile işaretlenir (bazen 〜を da olabilir, özellikle 'zorlama' anlamı güçlüyse)
Yaptıran-は/が + Yapan-に + Nesne-を + Fiil(ettirgen)
先生[せんせい]は学生[がくせい]に漢字[かんじ]を書[か]かせた。
Nesne zaten 〜を aldığından, yapan kişi mutlaka 〜に ile işaretlenir (aynı cümlede iki 〜を olamaz)
監督[かんとく]は選手[せんしゅ]を走[はし]らせた。
Bazı geçişsiz fiillerde zorlama vurgusu için 〜を tercih edilebilir (özellikle beden hareketi fiillerinde: 立[た]つ, 座[すわ]る, 泣[な]く, 笑[わら]う)
footnotes_tr: Rule in short: if there is already a 〜を in the sentence (object), the person performing the action MUST be marked with 〜に.

tables.caption_tr: Semantic Nuances: Coercion, Permission, and Emotional Causation
rows: Yaptıran kişi karşı taraf istemese de yaptırır
子供[こども]に薬[くすり]を飲[の]ませた。
Yaptıran kişi karşı tarafın isteğine izin verir, engellemez
子供[こども]を公園[こうえん]で遊[あそ]ばせた。
感情[かんじょう]の使役 (Duygusal sebep olma)
Bir davranışın başkasında yarattığı duygu/tepkiyi anlatır (istemli değildir)

自己使役[じこしえき] (Kendini ifade)
Konuşan kişinin kendi davranışı için izin/istek belirtmesi
私[わたし]にやらせてください。
Bunu yapmama izin verin (kendim yapmak istiyorum).

tables.caption_tr: Common Patterns with Causative Form
