来週[らいしゅう]休[やす]ませていただけますか。
Gelecek hafta izin almama müsaade eder misiniz?
発表[はっぴょう]させていただきます。
資料[しりょう]を準備[じゅんび]させておいた。

〜させてあげる/くれる/もらう
先生[せんせい]は私[わたし]に発表[はっぴょう]させてくれた。
Öğretmen benim sunum yapmama izin verdi (bana lütfetti).

tables.caption_tr: Comparison: Causative (〜させる) vs Passive (〜られる) vs Causative-Passive (〜させられる)
rows: Özne, başkasına bir şey yaptırır/izin verir
母[はは]は私[わたし]に野菜[やさい]を食[た]べさせた。
Özne, bir eylemden etkilenir (eylemi kendi yapmaz)
私[わたし]は母[はは]に叱[しか]られた。
Ettirgen-Edilgen (使役受身[しえきうけみ])
Özne, istemediği halde bir şey yapmaya zorlanır
私[わたし]は母[はは]に野菜[やさい]を食[た]べさせられた。
Annem tarafından sebze yemek zorunda bırakıldım (istemeden yedim).
footnotes_tr: The 〜させられる structure is handled in detail under a separate topic 'Causative-Passive (使役受身形[しえきうけみけい])'; here it is provided solely for comparison purposes.
In Godan verbs, 〜させられる can be abbreviated to take the form 〜される (e.g., 話[はな]させられる → 話[はな]される); this is a detail beyond N4.

examples.reading: ぶちょう は わたし に プレゼン を させました。

examples.target: 妹[いもうと]を一人[ひとり]で買[か]い物[もの]に行[い]かせる。

toki-when.title_tr: とき (when... / at the time when...)
toki-when.intro_tr: とき (時) meaning "when..., at the time when..." is a very useful conjunction that connects two sentences with a time relationship, and is actually a noun meaning "time, moment"; because of this, the word that precedes it is inflected according to noun compounding rules (verb/adjective clause + とき, just like こと). The most critical point: whether the verb before とき is in dictionary form or た form does not depend on the GENERAL time of the sentence, but rather on whether that action is completed at the same time as the action in the main clause or BEFORE it — this is the most frequently confused point for Turkish learners. Besides verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives, and nouns can also be attached to とき with their respective attachment rules. On this page, attachment patterns, the nuance difference between dictionary-form/た-form, and comparisons with similar time expressions are provided in table format.

tables.caption_tr: Attachment Patterns of とき (According to Word Type)

Japonya'ya vardıktan sonra (zaten gitmişken) pasaportunu kaybetti

examples.reading: にほんへいくとき、パスポートをとりました。

conj-conditional-table.title_tr: Conditional Forms Comparison Table (と / ば / たら / なら)
conj-conditional-table.intro_tr: In Japanese, there are four different conditional (conditional) forms meaning "-se/-sa": と, ば, たら, and なら. While all of these can be translated into Turkish in a similar way, the context in which they are used, what can and cannot come in the next sentence, and the meanings they emphasize are quite different from each other. と is used more for automatic/natural results, ば for general rules and logical conditions, たら for one-time events and the most flexible daily use, and なら for advice/assumption based on the other person's words or current situation. This page combines the conjugations of the four forms, usage restrictions, and subtle meaning differences between them in a single reference table; at the N4 level, distinguishing these four forms is one of the most critical topics for Japanese learners.

tables.caption_tr: Conjugation Table — と / ば / たら / なら in Verbs, Adjectives, and Nouns
rows: あったら / なかったら
あるなら / ないなら
学生[がくせい]だったら
footnotes_tr: In the ば form, 'ならば' can be used with な-adjectives and nouns, but in daily conversation, usually only 'なら' is preferred (this can also be confused with the 'なら' column, be careful!).
The たら form is always formed as the base of the verb's た-form + ら: if you know the た-form, the たら form comes out automatically.

tables.caption_tr: Usage Areas and Meaning Differences
rows: Otomatik, doğal, değişmez sonuç; genel kural, tekrar eden olay
Fiziksel kurallar, mekanizmalar, yol tarifi, alışkanlıklar
Genel şart, mantıksal sonuç, ölçüt, atasözü
Sınırlı — çoğunlukla olmaz, ama 〜ばいい/〜ばよかった gibi kalıplarda olur
Genel kural, koşullu tercih, öneri kalıpları
En esnek koşul; tek seferlik, somut, sıralı olaylar; geçmişe dayalı 'olduğunda'
Belirli, tek seferlik olay; sonuç genelde sürpriz olabilir
Günlük konuşma, kişisel planlar, beklenmedik sonuçlar
Karşı tarafın sözünü/mevcut durumu temel alan varsayım, henüz gerçekleşmemiş konu
Evet — tavsiye ve öneri için en doğal seçim
Sıralama serbest; önce sonuç, sonra şart da gelebilir
Tavsiye verme, karşılaştırma, konu odaklı şart (bu konuya gelince...)

tables.caption_tr: Grammar Restrictions — What to Pay Attention to
rows: Emir (〜なさい/〜て), istek (〜たい), teklif (〜ましょう), izin (〜てもいい) gibi iradi/kişisel ifadeler yasaktır
Sadece kesin, otomatik, kontrol edilemeyen sonuçlar için kullanılır
Sonuç cümlesi iradi ve özne 1. şahıssa genelde yasaktır; istisna: 〜ばいい, 〜ばよかった, 〜ば〜ほど kalıpları
Geçmiş, tamamlanmış tek olayları anlatmak için uygun değildir
Pratik olarak hiçbir sınırlama yoktur — en serbest ve en sık kullanılan koşul formudur
Konuşma dilinde diğer üç formun neredeyse hepsinin yerine geçebilir
Şart kısmı zaten gerçekleşmiş/tamamlanmış geçmiş bir olay olamaz; genelde konuşmacının duyduğu/bildiği bir bilgiye tepkidir
Diğer formlardan farklı olarak şart ve sonuç sırası değiştirilebilir: 結果+なら+条件

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of Four Forms in the Same Context: 電気[でんき]をつける (turning on the light)
rows: 電気[でんき]をつけると、明[あか]るくなる。
Işığı açınca (her zaman, otomatik olarak) aydınlanır — doğal sonuç
電気[でんき]をつければ、明[あか]るくなる。
Işığı açarsan aydınlanır — genel şart, hafif öneri tonu
電気[でんき]をつけたら、猫[ねこ]がいた。
Işığı açtığımda (bir kere) meğer kedi varmış — beklenmedik, tek seferlik sonuç
電気[でんき]をつけるなら、スイッチはここです。
Işığı açacaksan (öyle bir niyetin varsa), anahtar burada — karşı tarafın niyetine tepki
footnotes_tr: This table shows how the same verb gains completely different meanings and contexts with four different forms; it is the most confused point in exams.

examples.target: 春[はる]になると、桜[さくら]が咲[さ]きます。
examples.translation_tr: When spring comes (every time) cherry blossoms bloom.
examples.note_tr: と: natural/automatic result. A rule repeated every spring.

examples.target: ボタンを押[お]すと、ドアが開[ひら]きます。
examples.translation_tr: When (you) press the button, the door opens.
examples.note_tr: と: used for definite, unchanging results like machines/mechanisms.

examples.target: 安[やす]ければ買[か]います。
examples.translation_tr: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.
examples.note_tr: ば: general condition, logical decision. It is possible to use an intentional result clause with ば, albeit limited.

examples.target: お金[かね]があれば、旅行[りょこう]に行[い]きたいです。
examples.translation_tr: If I had money, I would want to go traveling.
examples.note_tr: ば: hypothetical/unrealized situation + desire (たい) — typical usage of ば.

examples.target: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ったら、行[い]きません。
examples.translation_tr: If it rains, I won't go.
examples.note_tr: たら: one-time, concrete event; the most flexible conditional form.

examples.target: 春[はる]になったら、花見[はなみ]に行[い]きましょう。
examples.translation_tr: When spring comes, let's go to view flowers.
examples.note_tr: たら: suggestion/request (〜ましょう) can be used in the result clause, which is not possible with と/ば.

examples.target: 疲[つか]れているなら、休[やす]んでください。
examples.translation_tr: If you're tired, please rest.
examples.note_tr: なら: advice based on the other person's situation/words; reaction to information that has not yet occurred.

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんが行[い]くなら、私[わたし]も行[い]きます。

examples.note_tr: なら: topic/situation-based condition; the conditional clause is not a past action, but current information/intention.

tsumori-yotei.title_tr: つもり / 予定[よてい] — Expressing Intention and Plan
tsumori-yotei.intro_tr: つもり and 予定[よてい] are two fundamental structures in Japanese used to express future intentions and plans. つもり shows a decision or intention made by the speaker of their own volition; its certainty is low and it can change. 予定[よてい], on the other hand, expresses a pre-arranged, scheduled, or objective plan; it is generally used in contexts such as calendar, appointments, travel, and is more concrete/formal. Both structures are generally used together with the dictionary form of the verb (辞書形[じしょけい]) or the negative (ない形[けい]) and are completed with だ/です. Additionally, when つもり combines with the past tense (た形[けい]), it gains a special and frequently used meaning like "even though it's not actually like that, I think that I did/was it that way myself."

conj-transitivity-pairs.title_tr: Transitive–Intransitive Verb Pairs Table (Comprehensive) — 自動詞[じどうし]・他動詞[たどうし]
conj-transitivity-pairs.intro_tr: In Japanese, many verbs express the same meaning in two separate forms: transitive (他動詞[たどうし]) and intransitive (自動詞[じどうし]). Intransitive verbs describe an event occurring spontaneously, without an agent, and are typically used with が (the window opens - 窓が開く). Transitive verbs, on the other hand, show that a conscious subject is affecting an object and are used with を (I am opening the window - 窓を開ける). This distinction is fundamental for correctly using structures like 〜ている (state/continuity) and 〜てある (state resulting from someone's conscious preparation), as well as for understanding passive and causative voices. This page compiles the most frequently used pairs, sound patterns (patterns), and exceptions in table form.

tables.caption_tr: Main Sound Patterns (Intransitive ↔ Transitive Patterns)
footnotes_tr: These patterns are not absolute rules, but general tendencies that make memorization easier; each verb must be learned individually.

tables.caption_tr: Comprehensive Transitive–Intransitive Verb Pairs List

conj-na-adjective-full.title_tr: Adjective Conjugation Table: な-Adjectives + Copula (All Forms)
conj-na-adjective-full.intro_tr: な-adjectives (noun-like adjectives), unlike い-adjectives, do not conjugate on their own; the meaning and tense information is carried by the です/だ copula. The adjective's "root" (e.g., 静か[しずか]) remains fixed, the part that changes is the copula: だ→だった→じゃない→じゃなかった and the like. When directly modifying a noun, な is added to the end of the root (静か[しずか]な部屋[へや]), and when modifying a verb or adjective, the adverbial marker 〜に is used (静か[しずか]に). Some words like きれい and 嫌い[きらい] end in い but are actually な-adjectives — this is a classic trap. The tables below gather all tense/politeness combinations, adverbial forms, and common exceptions on a single page.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Conjugation: 静[しず]かな (quiet) — Plain and Polite Forms

静[しず]かじゃありませんでした / 静[しず]かではありませんでした
footnotes_tr: じゃ is the colloquial abbreviation of では; では is more formal/written style.
In polite negation, 静[しず]かじゃないです is often heard in colloquial speech, but 静[しず]かじゃありません is more standard.

yori-comparison.intro_tr: より is the basic comparative particle in Japanese used when comparing two things with the meaning "...from/than" and is typically used in the pattern "A は B より [adjective] です" (A is more... than B). To clarify the emphasis, it is often constructed together with の方[ほう]が as "B より A の方[ほう]が...", which means "the A side is more...". より is not only used with adjectives but also with nouns and verbs (e.g., 思[おも]ったより). For negative comparison, ほど is used instead of より (〜ほど〜ない = not as... as...). On this page, the basic structures of より, question patterns, differences with related particles, and common mistakes are summarized in table form.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Comparative Structures with より
rows: A は B より [い-sıfat] です
夏[なつ]は 冬[ふゆ]より 暑[あつ]いです。
A は B より [な-sıfat] です
この町[まち]は あの町[まち]より 静[しず]かです。
Bu şehir o şehirden daha sakindir.
B より A の方[ほう]が [sıfat] です
冬[ふゆ]より 夏[なつ]の方[ほう]が 好[す]きです。
Kıştan çok yazı severim. (yaz tarafı daha…)
A は B ほど [sıfat] ではない
今日[きょう]は 昨日[きのう]ほど 寒[さむ]くない。
Bugün dün kadar soğuk değil. (olumsuz karşılaştırma)
N より N の方[ほう]が V
電車[でんしゃ]より 車[くるま]の方[ほう]が 便利[べんり]です。
思[おも]ったより 難[むずか]しいです。
footnotes_tr: Adding の方[ほう]が is not mandatory but clarifies which side is being compared; it is frequently used in everyday conversation.
For negative comparison, use ほど, not より: 〜ほど〜ない.

tables.caption_tr: Different Usage Areas of the より Particle
rows: 犬[いぬ]より 猫[ねこ]が好[す]きです。
思[おも]ったより 簡単[かんたん]でした。
受付[うけつけ]は9時[くじ]よりです。

運動[うんどう]より 休息[きゅうそく]の方[ほう]が大切[たいせつ]だ。
B'nin A'ya göre üstün/tercih edilir olduğunu belirtir.
より + もっと/はるかに (derece pekiştirme)
A は B より もっと/はるかに〜
彼[かれ]は 私[わたし]より はるかに 背[せ]が高[たか]い。
footnotes_tr: The meaning of より as '...from' (time/place starting point) is particularly seen in formal writing and announcements; から is preferred instead in everyday conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison Questions: どちら / どっち Patterns
rows: A と B と、どちら（どっち）が 〜ですか
コーヒーと お茶[ちゃ]と、どちらが好[す]きですか。
お茶[ちゃ]の方[ほう]が 好[す]きです。
Kahve mi çay mı, hangisini seversin? → Çayı daha çok severim.
どちらの方[ほう]が 安[やす]いですか。
こちらの方[ほう]が 安[やす]いです。
Hangisi daha ucuz? → Bu taraf daha ucuz.
A の方[ほう]が B より〜
電車[でんしゃ]の方[ほう]が バスより 速[はや]いです。
Cevapta より, kıyaslanan diğer tarafı belirtmek için kullanılır.
footnotes_tr: どちら is formal/polite, どっち is colloquial speech.
It is used to ask between two options; for three or more options, どれ is used (not どちら).

tables.caption_tr: より vs ほど vs くらい: Difference Between Comparative Particles
rows: 山[やま]は 海[うみ]より 好[す]きです。
山[やま]は 海[うみ]ほど 好[す]きではない。
妹[いもうと]は 兄[あに]くらい 背[せ]が高[たか]い。
涙[なみだ]が出[で]るほど 嬉[うれ]しかった。
footnotes_tr: より is only used in affirmative superiority sentences; ほど is used almost always with negative predicates.
くらい indicates equality/approximation, not superiority — should not be confused with より.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Their Corrections
rows: 日本[にほん]は トルコより大[おお]きいほど です。
日本[にほん]は トルコより 大[おお]きいです。
より ile ほど aynı cümlede aynı işlev için birlikte kullanılmaz; より olumlu, ほど olumsuz karşılaştırmada kullanılır.
トルコより 日本[にほん] 大[おお]きいです。
日本[にほん]は トルコより 大[おお]きいです。
は konu edatı unutulmamalı; より kıyas edatıdır, cümlenin öznesini işaretlemez.
夏[なつ]より 冬[ふゆ]が 好[す]きだ。（belirsiz vurgu）
夏[なつ]より 冬[ふゆ]の方[ほう]が 好[す]きだ。
Doğal ve net konuşma dilinde の方[ほう]が eklemek tercih edilir; gramer olarak yanlış değildir ama daha az doğal.
今日[きょう]は 昨日[きのう]より 寒[さむ]くない。（yanlış değil ama zayıf vurgu）
今日[きょう]は 昨日[きのう]ほど 寒[さむ]くない。
Olumsuz karşılaştırmada より yerine ほど kullanmak daha doğal ve yaygındır.
footnotes_tr: より + くない (negative adjective) is grammatically possible but semantically weak; ほど is preferred in N4 exams.

politeness-levels.intro_tr: In Japanese, speech 'politeness level' changes depending on your age, status, and closeness relationship with the person in front of you; the same sentence can be spoken in three different ways. The most basic distinction is between casual (普通体[ふつうたい], 'plain form') and polite (丁寧語[ていねいご], ます/です form); above that is 敬語[けいご] (respectful/humble language) directed toward superiors and customers. Among family and close friends, the casual form is natural; with newly acquainted people at school or work, teineigo is standard; in work environments and formal situations, keigo is required. Using the wrong level (for example, speaking casually to a boss) can come across as rude, while constantly using です/ます with a close friend can be perceived as distant/cold. This page provides a general framework at N4 level; for detailed keigo conjugations, refer to relevant topics.

deshou-kamoshirenai.title_tr: でしょう / かもしれない — Probability and Supposition Expressions
deshou-kamoshirenai.intro_tr: でしょう and かもしれない are two fundamental structures in Japanese that express "probability, supposition," but their degrees of certainty differ. でしょう (plain form: だろう) expresses a guess of which the speaker is 70-90% confident, and is generally used together with the adverbs きっと (surely) or たぶん (probably); moreover, when said with rising intonation, it also serves the function of seeking confirmation with the meaning "isn't it?" かもしれない, on the other hand, expresses a weaker probability of around 30-50%, that is, the meaning "perhaps, might" and is generally strengthened with もしかしたら (maybe). Both structures are attached to the simple form (普通形) of verbs, nouns, い-adjectives, and な-adjectives; for politeness, でしょう is already in polite form, while the polite form of かもしれない is かもしれません. On this page, connection rules, degrees of certainty, and register differences are summarized in tables.

te-ageru-kureru-morau.title_tr: 〜てあげる / 〜てくれる / 〜てもらう (Kindness Verbs: Give-Receive Auxiliary Verbs)
te-ageru-kureru-morau.intro_tr: 〜てあげる, 〜てくれる and 〜てもらう are auxiliary verbs that, when added to the て-form of a verb, carry information about "who did a kindness to whom / what was received from whom". In Japanese, this triple does not simply mean "give/receive", but also reflects the speaker's perspective and the relationship between in-group (uchi) and out-group (soto): the action of あげる goes outward, the action of くれる goes toward me/my in-group, and もらう expresses the direction of "obtaining something from someone". Additionally, depending on the status of the person with whom each verb is used, there are polite (さしあげる/くださる/いただく) or casual/informal (やる) variants. Using these patterns correctly is critical for understanding politeness and directionality (from whom to whom) logic in Japanese. The tables below summarize the basic meanings, politeness levels, sentence patterns, and common mistakes.

to-shite-role.title_tr: として — as, in the capacity of
to-shite-role.intro_tr: として specifies in what "role, quality, identity, or category" a person, thing, or situation is evaluated, and corresponds to the "...as" expression in Turkish. It is attached directly after a noun and generally indicates profession, status, duty, category, or assumption. Although used in spoken language, it is particularly frequent in formal speech, written texts, and news. It should not be confused with にとって (from someone's perspective, for someone): として refers to the role itself, while にとって indicates evaluation/perspective according to that role. として, としては, としても, としての and similar derivatives provide different nuances.

causative-passive.intro_tr: The causative-passive voice (〜させられる) in Japanese expresses that a person is FORCED by someone else to do something, typically unwillingly or with reluctance. The structure is formed from the combination of the causative (〜させる) and passive (〜られる) voices; it means "to be made to do." A shortened form (〜される) is also commonly used in godan verbs, but verbs ending in す do not take this abbreviation. This pattern typically carries nuances of complaint, obligation, or "it was beyond my control, I was forced to do it." The most challenging point for students is the verb conjugation and abbreviation rules that change according to verb groups.

koso.intro_tr: こそ is a particle that emphasizes a word or phrase strongly, and is usually translated into English as "exactly", "indeed", or "precisely this/that, not something else". It takes the place of the は particle, bringing the topic to the forefront with the meaning "not the others, definitely this". It usually comes after nouns, time expressions, and adverbs; it is also very frequently used in fixed expressions like からこそ, てこそ, and こちらこそ. When こそ is used, it adds a tone of strong certainty, determination, or comparative emphasis to the sentence. On this page, the basic uses of こそ, its relationship with other particles, and the most frequently occurring idiomatic expressions are summarized in tables.

tables.caption_tr: Basic usage patterns of こそ
rows: あなたこそ天才[てんさい]だ
今度[こんど]こそ勝[か]つ
努力[どりょく]したからこそ成功[せいこう]した
Tam da çaba gösterdiğim için başarılı oldum
経験[けいけん]してこそわかる
こちらこそよろしくお願[ねが]いします
これ/それ/あれ + こそ
それこそ問題[もんだい]だ
İşte asıl mesele tam da bu
footnotes_tr: こそ is attached immediately after the word being emphasized; the rest of the sentence continues normally.

tables.caption_tr: How does こそ combine with other particles?
rows: は yerine doğrudan こそ gelir: 私はこそ değil, 私こそ
今[いま]にこそ行動[こうどう]すべきだ
ここでこそ力[ちから]を発揮[はっき]する
彼[かれ]とこそ話[はな]したい (daha az yaygın)
footnotes_tr: Basic particles like は, が, and を are not used together with こそ; こそ takes their place or replaces them.
Particles like に, で, and と, however, come before こそ: 場所[ばしょ]でこそ, 時[とき]にこそ.

bakari-verb.title_tr: 〜たばかり / 〜てばかり — Just (newly) did… / Keep doing…
bakari-verb.intro_tr: 〜たばかり and 〜てばかり, although they look quite similar in form, are two completely different patterns in meaning. 〜たばかり is added to a verb's た-form and carries the meaning 'something was just done / newly done' — in other words, a (subjectively) short time has passed between the end of the action and the moment of speaking. 〜てばかり(いる) on the other hand is added to a verb's て-form and means 'keep doing / always doing the same thing'; it is usually used with a negative, critical, or complaining tone. To avoid mixing the two up, paying attention to whether the た-form or て-form is used is the most practical way. On this page, the structure of both patterns, their semantic differences, and frequently used patterns are summarized in tables.

koto-ni-naru-suru.title_tr: 〜ことになる / 〜ことにする — Patterns for Expressing Decisions and Results
koto-ni-naru-suru.intro_tr: 〜ことにする and 〜ことになる are two fundamental N3 patterns added to the dictionary or negative form of a verb to express a "decision" or "result". 〜ことにする expresses a decision made by the speaker with THEIR OWN will ("I decide to…"). 〜ことになる, on the other hand, conveys that the decision was made by an external factor (institution, rule, natural development, someone else) or that a result has emerged ("It was decided that… / It will be…"). The forms ことにしている and ことになっている indicate a continuous/established rule or habit. Because these two structures allow the subject to be hidden in Japanese, they are used very frequently, especially in formal and polite speech.

Dış etken: kurum, kural, kader, başkası, doğal sonuç

行[い]くことにする / 行[い]くことになる
footnotes_tr: In Japanese, even if it is one's own decision, ことになる can be preferred to show humility (especially in topics like marriage, moving).

nara-baai.title_tr: なら / 場合[ばあい] — Conditional '-sa/-se' Patterns Expressing Condition and Situation
nara-baai.intro_tr: なら is a conditional suffix used to take a topic or assumption mentioned by the person in front of you and give advice, commentary, or a counter-proposal in the sense of 'if that is so / given that'; it generally points to a situation that has not yet materialized, only come up in conversation, and is very common in spoken language. 場合[ばあい], on the other hand, is a noun meaning 'situation, condition, case' and is used to describe more neutral, formal, and general rules, instructions, or scenarios like '…if it occurs, …when it is the case'. なら is generally more suited to personal advice and natural conversation, while 場合 is more appropriate for rules, warnings, procedures, and written/formal narration. Both can be attached to verbs, adjectives, and nouns in different ways; the tables below summarize all attachment forms and usage differences.

tables.caption_tr: なら Attachment Forms (Verb / Adjective / Noun)
footnotes_tr: For な-adjectives and nouns, 'だ/な' is not used; なら is attached directly to the stem: ×静かだなら, ×学生だなら is incorrect.

sugiru.intro_tr: 〜すぎる is an auxiliary verb that expresses that an action, situation, or quality is WELL BEYOND the normal, expected, or appropriate limit; it is generally translated into English as "too much to ...", "excessively ..." etc. It is attached directly to the ます-root of verbs, the root without い of い-adjectives, and the root without な of な-adjectives; it itself conjugates completely regularly like an 上一段(ichidan) verb (すぎます, すぎた, すぎて, すぎない...). 〜すぎる usually carries a negative judgment or complaining tone: something being more than necessary generally leads to an undesirable outcome. Irregular attachment is seen with some adjectives like いい/よい and ない (よすぎる, なさすぎる); these exceptions must be learned carefully. It is also frequently used as a noun in the form すぎ (in everyday expressions like 食べ過ぎ, 飲み過ぎ).

you-ni-naru-suru.title_tr: 〜ようになる / 〜ようにする — Expressing Change and Effort
you-ni-naru-suru.intro_tr: 〜ようになる and 〜ようにする are two patterns that appear similar on the surface but have different functions. 〜ようになる describes a CHANGE that occurs naturally over time or as a result of effort: it means "I couldn't/didn't do it before, but now I can/do it" and is generally used in the past tense (〜ようになりました/〜ようになった). 〜ようにする, on the other hand, expresses a deliberate EFFORT, developing a habit, or setting a rule: it means "I am making an effort to do... / I am trying to do..." and frequently indicates continuity in the form 〜ようにしています. Both patterns attach to either the dictionary form or the negative (ない) form of the verb; additionally, 〜ようになる most commonly goes with ability (可能形) verbs and carries the meaning of "come to be able to...". On this page, you can find binding rules, all tense/negative variations, and comparisons with similar patterns that are often confused in a table format.

yasui-nikui.title_tr: 〜やすい / 〜にくい (Easy to Do / Hard to Do)
yasui-nikui.intro_tr: 〜やすい and 〜にくい are two patterns frequently used in spoken Japanese that are added to the ます-stem (masu-stem) of a verb to convey the meanings of "…-ing is easy" and "…-ing is difficult." After being attached, the newly formed word behaves entirely like an い-adjective and is subject to normal い-adjective conjugation rules (negative, past, て-form, etc.). 〜やすい is not only "easy to do" but sometimes also carries the meaning of "a tendency to occur frequently/easily …is" (e.g., 壊[こわ]れやすい = easily broken, fragile). 〜にくい, on the other hand, generally expresses structural or physical difficulty of the object, and for more abstract/emotional difficulties, 〜がたい or 〜づらい are preferred. At the N3 level, this pattern appears frequently both in everyday conversation and in written Japanese.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Rule: ます-stem + やすい / にくい According to Verb Group
footnotes_tr: Don't think of it like the て-form of the verb; the ます-stem (not the 辞書形 dictionary form) always comes here.
The resulting word is now an い-adjective: the やすい/にくい part is conjugated.

sae-demo.title_tr: さえ / でも — Particles Meaning "Even"
sae-demo.intro_tr: さえ and でも are two basic particles corresponding to the meaning 'even' in Turkish, and by generally emphasizing an extreme/edge example, they convey the message 'there's no need to ask about others.' While さえ is used more in written language and in negative sentences ('...even none/can't do'), でも is a structure that can appear in both affirmative and negative sentences and is much more common in everyday conversation. でも also combines with question words like 何でも, 誰でも, どこでも to create universal expressions with the meaning 'whatever/whoever/wherever', and in patterns like お茶でも飲みませんか it also carries a polite suggestion meaning of 'like/for example'. On this page, the particle attachment rules, nuance differences, and frequently used patterns of both structures are summarized in table form.

hou-ga-ii.intro_tr: 〜ほうがいい is a pattern used when giving advice to the person in front of us or indicating that one behavior would be better than another, and it is a pattern frequently encountered in daily conversation. In positive suggestions, the past (た) form of the verb is used, and in negative suggestions, the negative (ない) form of the verb is used — however, the meaning is not related to the past, it simply means "if you do/don't do that, it would be better." Compared to べき, it carries a softer, more personal tone of suggestion; it is used in a wide range of contexts from doctor's advice to friend's advice. The tone of the suggestion can be softened or emphasized by adding particles like よ or と思います at the end of the sentence.

setsuzoku-conjunctions.title_tr: Conjunctions: それで / そこで / すると / ところが
setsuzoku-conjunctions.intro_tr: These four conjunctions are used at the BEGINNING of a sentence when connecting two sentences together, and typically a period (。) is placed first, then the conjunction comes. それで and そこで indicate a result or an action taken, while すると indicates an unexpected/automatic development in the narrative, and ところが indicates that the opposite of what was expected occurs (surprising contrast). All of them appear frequently in written and spoken language, but each has a different nuance: それで='for this reason', そこで='upon this (I/he did something)', すると='just then, at that very moment', ところが='but on the contrary'. At the N3 level, distinguishing these differences is very important in reading comprehension and JLPT listening passages. You can find the meaning, usage context, and comparisons with frequently confused structures in the tables below.

nante-nanka.title_tr: なんて / なんか — ...like things, expressions of belittlement and surprise
nante-nanka.intro_tr: なんて and なんか are two particles frequently used in spoken language, and fundamentally mean 'like things, such things, something like that.' Their most common uses are to belittle, trivialize, or make light of something (for example, 勉強なんて嫌いだ - 'I don't like studying and stuff like that'). Moreover, なんて is also used in exclamatory sentences expressing surprise or wonder (なんて〜だろう - 'how...!'). なんか, on the other hand, is more casual and has a softer tone; it can function both as a way to provide examples (この辺で食事なんかどう？) and as a meaningless filler or hesitation word (なんか、疲れた). The two are largely synonymous, but while なんて can appear in written language, なんか is entirely specific to spoken language.

to-iu-koto.title_tr: 〜ということ (...that it is, indirect narration)
to-iu-koto.intro_tr: 「〜ということ」is a highly versatile and multifunctional pattern attached to the end of a verb, adjective, or noun sentence, adding meanings such as "that it is," "that it is being," "that it means," and is used for the purpose of conveying information and defining. Fundamentally, it is composed of the combination of the quotation particle と and the nominalization particle こと; therefore, it serves both the function of "specifying the content of something" and "defining a concept." When used at the end of a sentence in the form 〜ということだ, it becomes an indirect narration (hearsay) structure that conveys information heard from others, and in this form it is similar in meaning to そうだ and とのことだ. At the N3 level, it is a multifaceted and important pattern frequently encountered both in everyday conversation and in news/written language.

tara-dou.title_tr: 〜たらどう / 〜ばいい — Giving Advice, Expressing "What Should Be Done"
tara-dou.intro_tr: 〜たらどう(ですか) and 〜ばいい are two basic patterns used for offering advice to the other person or giving "what should be done" guidance. 〜たらどう(ですか) is formed by adding the question どう (how) to the たら conditional form and carries the meaning "how would it be if you did it like this?" 〜ばいい is formed by adding the adjective いい (good) to the ば conditional form and offers a more relaxed solution suggestion like "just ... is enough, ... would be fine." 〜たらどう should be used carefully when speaking to superiors as it can sometimes be perceived as commanding or directive; in formal situations 〜たらいかがですか should be preferred. Both patterns have different variations and additional nuances (regret, wishes, etc.) depending on the politeness level.

hodo-kurai.title_tr: ほど / くらい（ぐらい） — Particles Indicating Degree and Approximate Amount
hodo-kurai.intro_tr: ほど and くらい（ぐらい） are two basic particles used in Japanese to indicate degree and approximate amount, and they can often be used interchangeably. Both come after nouns, numbers, and the dictionary form or negative form of verbs, adding meanings like 'about,' 'around,' or 'that degree.' The main difference is this: ほど is generally preferred when making comparisons in negative sentences ("...like... not") and when expressing superiority ("nothing like..."), while くらい/ぐらい can be used more freely in both positive and negative sentences and is very common in spoken language. Additionally, the pattern 〜ば〜ほど is an important grammatical structure meaning 'the more... the more...' and is constructed only with ほど; くらい is not used in this pattern. This page presents the usage areas, conjugation tables, and commonly used fixed expressions of both particles together.

noni-contrast.intro_tr: 〜のに is used to express a fact followed by a result that CONTRADICTS or is unexpected in relation to that fact; it corresponds to the Turkish patterns "…-diği halde" (although), "…-mesine rağmen" (despite), and "oysa ki" (yet). Unlike neutral conjunctions like が or けど meaning "but", のに also carries the speaker's surprise, disappointment, or resentment — that is, it contains emotional weight. It attaches directly to the inflected (plain/futsū) form of verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives, and nouns; with な-adjectives and nouns, な is inserted between them. A main clause ending in のに generally CANNOT take the form of an imperative, request, desire, or invitation, because のに describes an accomplished or actual state, not a suggestion or request. It can also be left incomplete at the end of a sentence as 「〜のに。」to express resentment or regret in the sense of "if only it had been so."

to-iu-wake.title_tr: 〜というわけ (namely, that is to say)
to-iu-wake.intro_tr: 〜というわけ, used to draw a logical conclusion based on information previously mentioned in speech or writing, to summarize a situation, or to provide an explanation in the sense of "namely, that is to say." The word わけ by itself expresses a concept like "reason, logic, meaning"; という connects the previous sentence or thought as "this means that." This pattern is especially common with its derivatives like 〜というわけではない (that doesn't necessarily mean so) and 〜というわけにはいかない (it's not possible to do so) in everyday conversation. It is an important pattern at the N3 level because it fulfills the functions of inference, explanation, and polite rejection in spoken language. For beginning-level learners, the most critical point is to distinguish well between the semantic differences among というわけだ (positive conclusion), というわけではない (partial/soft negation), and というわけにはいかない (impossibility/social hindrance).

tokoro.title_tr: 〜ところ (about to / in the middle of / just after) — Temporal Expression
tokoro.intro_tr: 〜ところ is actually a noun meaning "point, moment, place"; when combined with verbs, it is used to mark the exact position of an action on a timeline: the action has not yet started (is about to start), is occurring at that very moment, or has just finished. Depending on the verb form used (辞書形[じしょけい] / ている / た), the meaning changes completely, making it very important to clearly distinguish these three forms. ところだ typically emphasizes a point in time like "right now, this moment, just recently" and is used very frequently in spoken language. When used with the past tense (〜ところだった), it can also convey a nuance of narrow escape, like "almost happened". On this page, the basic usages of ところだ, its patterns with time adverbs, and the differences from similar expressions (〜ている, 〜たばかり, つもり) are summarized in table form.

hazu-beki.title_tr: はず / べき — Expectation and Obligation Expressions
hazu-beki.intro_tr: はず and べき are two obligation/expectation patterns that are frequently confused at the N3 level, but their meanings are fundamentally different. はず, based on the information we have or logic, expresses a prediction/expectation in the form of "...should, ...must (I think so)"; it is the speaker's opinion, not definite knowledge. べき, on the other hand, expresses a moral, social, or logical necessity/recommendation: like "...should, ...must be done," it is a subjective value judgment. While はず can attach to verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives, and nouns, べき attaches only to the dictionary form of verbs (with the exception of する: すべき/するべき). Both have different nuances in their negative and past uses; the tables below show these differences in detail.

行った[いった] + はず
彼[かれ]は行く[いく]はずです。
高くない[たかくない] + はず
高かった[たかかった] + はず
この本[ほん]は高い[たかい]はずです。
元気[げんき] な + はず
元気[げんき] じゃない + はず
元気[げんき] だった + はず
彼女[かのじょ]は元気[げんき]なはずです。
学生[がくせい] の + はず
学生[がくせい] じゃない + はず
学生[がくせい] だった + はず
彼[かれ]は学生[がくせい]のはずです。
footnotes_tr: はず always behaves like a noun; therefore, な / の is required for attachment to な-adjectives and nouns.
After はず, だ / です typically follows: 〜はずだ (neutral/written), 〜はずです (polite).

tables.caption_tr: Negative Patterns of はず: はずがない vs 〜ないはずだ
rows: V/Adj/İsim (olumlu sözlük şekli) + はずがない
"...olması kesinlikle imkânsız/mümkün değil" — güçlü, kesin bir red
彼[かれ]が犯人[はんにん]のはずがない。(Onun suçlu olması imkânsız.)
"...olmaması bekleniyor" — daha nötr, sadece olumsuz bir tahmin
今日[きょう]は誰[だれ]も来[こ]ないはずだ。(Bugün kimsenin gelmemesi bekleniyor.)
footnotes_tr: はずがない carries strong emphasis to the degree of 'impossible'; in daily conversation it expresses surprise/objection.
〜ないはずだ is a softer negative expectation and does not carry a definite rejection meaning.

tables.caption_tr: べき: Conjugation and Usage Patterns
rows: もっと勉強[べんきょう]するべきだ。(Daha çok çalışmalı.)
する → すべき (veya するべき)
Her ikisi de doğru ve yaygındır, すべき biraz daha yazı diline yakındır
すべきことを先[さき]にしなさい。(Yapılması gerekeni önce yap.)
Fiil sözlük şekli + べきではない
嘘[うそ]をつくべきではない。(Yalan söylenmemeli.)
Fiil sözlük şekli + べきだった
もっと早[はや]く言[い]うべきだった。(Daha erken söylemeliydim.)
Fiil sözlük şekli + べきではなかった
そんなことを言[い]うべきではなかった。(Öyle bir şey söylememeliydim.)
footnotes_tr: べき attaches only to verbs and is not directly added to adjectives or nouns.
べき can sound somewhat harsh/formal in spoken language; in daily speech 〜たほうがいい is softer.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of はず and べき
rows: Ahlaki, toplumsal veya mantıksal zorunluluk ("...meli, yapılmalı")
Öznel değer yargısı, tavsiye veya eleştiri
〜たはずだ = "...mış olmalı" (gerçekleşmiş olduğuna dair tahmin)
〜べきだった = "...meliydi" (yapılmadı, pişmanlık); 〜べきではなかった = "...memeliydi" (yapıldı, pişmanlık)
彼[かれ]は来[く]るはずだ。(Gelmesi bekleniyor / gelecek sanıyorum.)
彼[かれ]は来[く]るべきだ。(Onun gelmesi gerekir / gelmeli.)
footnotes_tr: はず is a prediction independent of whether the expectation is fulfilled or not; べき, on the other hand, is a requirement of a rule/morality.
The two can sometimes be used together in the same sentence: 彼[かれ]は謝[あやま]るべきだが、しないはずだ。(He should apologize, but (I expect) he won't.)

examples.target: 彼[かれ]はもうすぐ着[つ]くはずです。
examples.reading: かれはもうすぐつくはずです。
examples.translation_tr: He should be almost there by now (that's my expectation/prediction).
examples.note_tr: Expectation based on logical inference: there is information at hand (e.g., time, distance) and the speaker makes a prediction accordingly.

examples.target: こんな時間[じかん]に彼[かれ]が家[いえ]にいるはずがない。
examples.reading: こんなじかんにかれがいえにいるはずがない。
examples.translation_tr: At this time, it's impossible / he can't be at home.
examples.note_tr: はずがない = strong, definite rejection meaning ("...is not possible").

examples.target: 明日[あした]は休[やす]みのはずだ。
examples.reading: あしたはやすみのはずだ。
examples.translation_tr: Tomorrow must be a holiday (that's what I know/think).
examples.note_tr: Noun + の + はず structure.

examples.target: 今日[きょう]は雨[あめ]が降[ふ]らないはずだ。
examples.reading: きょうはあめがふらないはずだ。
examples.translation_tr: It is expected that it won't rain today.
examples.note_tr: Negative verb + はずだ: neutral negative expectation (softer than はずがない).

examples.target: 学生[がくせい]は毎日[まいにち]勉強[べんきょう]するべきだ。
examples.reading: がくせいはまいにちべんきょうするべきだ。
examples.translation_tr: Students should study every day.
examples.note_tr: べき = indicates general moral/social necessity, recommendation; すべき can also be written instead of する.

examples.target: もっと早[はや]く病院[びょういん]に行[い]くべきだった。
examples.reading: もっとはやくびょういんにいくべきだった。
examples.translation_tr: I should have gone to the hospital earlier (but I didn't).
examples.note_tr: べきだった = regret for something not done in the past.

examples.target: そんなことを言[い]うべきではなかった。
examples.reading: そんなことをいうべきではなかった。
examples.translation_tr: I shouldn't have said such a thing (but I did).
examples.note_tr: べきではなかった = regret for an action that was done, opposite to べきだった.

examples.target: 約束[やくそく]は守[まも]るべきだ。
examples.reading: やくそくはまもるべきだ。
examples.translation_tr: Words/promises must be kept.
examples.note_tr: Usage of べき expressing a general moral rule.

keigo-teichougo.title_tr: 丁重語[ていちょうご] (Teichōgo) — Formal Humble/Polite Language
keigo-teichougo.intro_tr: 丁重語[ていちょうご], in the modern keigo system, is mentioned together with kenjōgo (謙譲語) but is a different category: in kenjōgo, the speaker lowers their action TOWARD A RESPECTED PERSON, but in teichōgo, there is no such specific target — the speaker simply expresses their own action/existence humbly in order to make their speech FORMAL AND POLITE TOWARD THE LISTENER. This is why verbs like 参[まい]る, いたす, 申[もう]す, おる, 存[ぞん]じる can be used both "respectfully to someone" and "only for formality, regardless of whom it is said to"; the second usage is teichōgo. Patterns like でございます, ございます are also the most common examples of teichōgo and are more formal versions of です/あります. Teichōgo typically appears in business Japanese, announcements, formal introductions, and customer service. This category is also called 謙譲語II in the 5-part keigo system defined by the 2007 Bunka Shingikai (文化審議会).

tables.caption_tr: Basic Teichōgo Verbs (used regardless of whom it is said to)
rows: 参[まい]る / 参[まい]ります
En yaygın teichōgo fiili; hem gitme hem gelme için kullanılır
いたす / いたします
申[もう]す / 申[もう]します
Kenjōgo I'deki 'おる' ile aynı kelime, hedefsiz kullanılır
存[ぞん]じる / 存[ぞん]じます
ござる → ございます
En sık görülen teichōgo kalıplarından biri
です'in en resmî hali, mağaza/anons dilinde yaygın
footnotes_tr: These verbs are generally marked as 謙譲語 (kenjōgo) in dictionaries; the distinction is made according to the usage CONTEXT: if the action is directed toward a specific respected person, it is kenjōgo I; if it is only for general formality, it is teichōgo.

casual-speech.intro_tr: Japanese encountered in anime, manga, and daily conversations can look quite different from the "proper" grammar in textbooks: verbs shorten, sounds drop out, and small particles that add emotion are attached to the ends of sentences. This page collects abbreviations like 〜てる/〜ちゃう/〜とく, sound-dropping patterns like ら抜き言葉/い抜き言葉, sentence-ending particles that vary by gender and character (わ・ぜ・ぞ・さ・もん), and common pronoun/address types used in daily conversation all together. The aim is to enable you to recognize the standard forms you've learned in books in anime or street Japanese. Each abbreviation is actually nothing other than a quick pronunciation of a grammar structure (ている, てしまう, なければ etc.) that you already know; that's why knowing the base form is the key to solving abbreviations.

aizuchi.title_tr: Aizuchi (相槌[あいづち]) — Listener Responses: ええ / うん / そうですね
aizuchi.intro_tr: 相槌[あいづち] are short response words that convey the message "I'm listening to you, I understand, continue" while listening to the person in front of us; in Japanese conversation, remaining silent is perceived as rude or disinterested, so using aizuchi is almost mandatory. うん is used at the most intimate level (friends, family), ええ at a mid-polite level, and そうですね/はい are preferred in formal and business settings. Aizuchi does not only indicate agreement; it also has different functions such as surprise (へえ, まさか), doubt (そうかな), understanding (なるほど), or encouraging speech (それで?). These expressions are generally said while the other party is speaking, before the sentence ends, at short intervals, and with a low intonation. Using aizuchi at the correct level and frequency is one of the keys to leaving a natural and fluent Japanese impression.

masu-stem-uses.title_tr: ます-root Uses (〜ながら, 〜やすい, 〜すぎる)
masu-stem-uses.intro_tr: The ます-root (連用形[れんようけい]) is the form obtained by removing the ます suffix from a verb's ます form and constitutes the foundation of dozens of grammar patterns in Japanese. In this lesson, we focus particularly on three frequently used patterns: 〜ながら (doing two actions simultaneously), 〜やすい/〜にくい (expressing that something is easy or difficult) and 〜すぎる (excess, more than necessary). Additionally, you can see other common uses of the ます-root together in a single table. These structures appear extremely frequently in both everyday conversation and written language, which is why they need to be learned solidly at the N3 level.

tables.caption_tr: How is the ます-root Formed?
footnotes_tr: In godan verbs, the final syllable's ウ段 (u-row) sound changes to イ段 (i-row) sound: く→き, む→み, す→し, つ→ち, ぬ→に, ぶ→び, ぐ→ぎ, る→り, う→い.
In ichidan verbs, only the final る is dropped, and the root does not change.

tables.caption_tr: Main Patterns Made with the ます-root (General Overview)
rows: 食[た]べながら話[はな]す
働[はたら]き続[つづ]ける
働[はたら]きつつ学[まな]ぶ
勉強[べんきょう]しなさすぎる

tables.caption_tr: 〜ながら: Usage Types
rows: İki eylem aynı anda yapılır; ana eylem V2'dir
音楽[おんがく]を聞[き]きながら勉強[べんきょう]する
知[し]っていながら教[おし]えなかった
小[ちい]さいながらも立派[りっぱ]な家[いえ]だ
生[う]まれながらの才能[さいのう]
footnotes_tr: When using ながら, the subject of both actions must be the SAME person.
The main emphasis is always on the second (following) verb; the first verb is the background action.

tables.caption_tr: 〜やすい / 〜にくい: Conjugation and Usage
rows: 食[た]べやすくなかった
食[た]べにくくなかった
食[た]べやすい料理[りょうり]
食[た]べにくい料理[りょうり]
footnotes_tr: After やすい and にくい are added, the word conjugates exactly like an い-adjective.
Instead of にくい, 〜がたい can also be used in more literary/written language, but it carries a stronger meaning and expresses 'difficulty approaching impossibility'.
難[むずか]しい is not used in this pattern — にくい/やすい is attached directly to the ます-root of the verb, not to nouns/adjectives.

tables.caption_tr: 〜すぎる: Usage Rules and Exceptions

高[たか]い→高[たか]すぎる
静[しず]かだ→静[しず]かすぎる
食[た]べない→食[た]べなさすぎる

食[た]べ過[す]ぎ、飲[の]み過[す]ぎ
footnotes_tr: すぎる generally carries a negative/excessive judgment: 'more than necessary'.
It can also be written in kanji form as 過[す]ぎる.

ni-taishite.intro_tr: に対して is a particle pattern used to express an attitude, feeling, behavior, or action directed toward a person, object, or situation, and is generally translated as 'toward/against…', 'directed at…', or 'in response to…'. It clearly marks the target/recipient of the action or feeling in the sentence; generally a reaction, attitude, or behavior toward that target is involved (for example, getting angry, respecting, opposing, being rude, etc.). When directly modifying a noun, に対する is used (noun + に対する + noun). It should not be confused with について or に関して, which carry the meaning of providing information/explanation about a topic; に対して more conveys 'directed attitude/reaction', while について/に関して only convey 'topic, about'.

tables.caption_tr: Attachment Patterns
rows: 名詞[めいし] + に対[たい]して
先生[せんせい]に対[たい]して (öğretmene karşı)
動詞[どうし]普通形[ふつうけい] + の + に対[たい]して
働[はたら]くのに対[たい]して (çalışmaya karşılık)
な-sıfat + な/である + の

高[たか]いのに対[たい]して (pahalı olmasına karşılık)
名詞[めいし] + に対[たい]する + 名詞[めいし]
子供[こども]に対[たい]する愛情[あいじょう] (çocuğa karşı sevgi)
footnotes_tr: に対して is generally used with nouns; in verb/adjective clauses, the の に対して pattern often appears, carrying the meaning of 'comparison/contrast' (see example 4).

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of に対して with Similar Particles
rows: Hedefe yönelik aktif tavır veya eylem
彼[かれ]に対[たい]して怒[おこ]る (ona kızmak)

footnotes_tr: に対して should not be confused with について: 'talk about A' → Aについて話す; 'get angry at A' → Aに対して怒る.

sou-you-rashii.title_tr: そう / よう / らしい — Appearance and Hearsay Expressions
sou-you-rashii.intro_tr: そう, よう and らしい are three basic constructions in Japanese that convey the meanings 'according to appearance,' 'seemingly,' and 'as if...,' but their sources and degrees of certainty differ. 様態[ようたい]そう expresses an instantaneous visual impression ('appears to be...'), while 伝聞[でんぶん]そう conveys information heard from others ('they say it's...') — even though both use the same word, their connection patterns are completely different. よう is a softer, more subjective prediction based on the speaker's own observation and reasoning; らしい, on the other hand, is an inference based on information or signs from outside sources, where the speaker maintains some distance, and it is also used to mean '...befits, typical...'. Since these four constructions are often confused, the tables below show their connection patterns, exceptions, and meaning differences separately.

tables.caption_tr: 1. 様態[ようたい]そう — Visual impression: 'appears to be..., seems to have been...'
rows: 降[ふ]り + そう → 降[ふ]りそう
おいし(い) + そう → おいしそう
元気[げんき] + そう → 元気[げんき]そう
お金[かね]がない → お金[かね]がなさそう
高[たか]い → 高[たか]くなさそう
そうな+isim / そうに+fiil / そうだ
降[ふ]りそうな空[そら] / 降[ふ]りそうに見[み]える
footnotes_tr: 様態そう always relies on a sign observed in front of one's eyes at that moment; it is used for events that have not yet happened.
Should not be confused with 伝聞そう — their connection patterns are completely different (see table 2 below).

tables.caption_tr: 2. 伝聞[でんぶん]そう — Heard information (hearsay): 'they say it's..., I heard...'
rows: 普通形[ふつうけい] + そうだ
降[ふ]る → 降[ふ]るそうです / 降[ふ]った → 降[ふ]ったそうです
忙[いそが]しい → 忙[いそが]しいそうです
元気[げんき] → 元気[げんき]だそうです
学生[がくせい] → 学生[がくせい]だそうです
SADECE そうだ/そうです — çekimlenmez
そうな(X) yanlış, そうに(X) yanlış
footnotes_tr: 伝聞そう conveys information heard from others (news, person, announcement), not the speaker's own observation.
It is often used together with 〜によると (according to...) or 〜の話[はなし]では: 天気予報によると〜そうです。

tables.caption_tr: 3. よう(だ) — Soft prediction based on observation/reasoning: 'resembles..., I think...'
rows: 降[ふ]る → 降[ふ]るようです
忙[いそが]しい → 忙[いそが]しいようです
静[しず]か → 静[しず]かなようです
先生[せんせい] → 先生[せんせい]のようです
夢[ゆめ]のような話[はなし]
分[わ]かるように話[はな]す
〜みたい(だ) (isim/na-sıfat doğrudan bağlanır, の gerekmez)
footnotes_tr: よう is based on the speaker's own reasoning, comparison, or impression gained through the senses; it is not 伝聞 (hearing from others).
It conjugates fully like な-adjectives: ようだ/ようです, ような+N, ように+V/Adj/Adv.

tables.caption_tr: 4. らしい — Externally-sourced inference ('appears to be...') and the meaning 'typical...'
rows: 降[ふ]る → 降[ふ]るらしいです
忙[いそが]しい → 忙[いそが]しいらしいです
元気[げんき] → 元気[げんき]らしいです
学生[がくせい] → 学生[がくせい]らしいです
男[おとこ]らしい, 子供[こども]らしい
らしい→らしく(ない)/らしかった
footnotes_tr: The らしい with the meaning of inference is typically based on heard information, signs, or observation, and the speaker takes a somewhat distant/uncertain attitude.
The second meaning ('typical...') is added directly to nouns and conjugates fully like a normal い-adjective, and does not carry the meaning of inference.

tables.caption_tr: 5. Comparison: そう(様態) / そう(伝聞) / よう / らしい together
rows: ます-kökü / sıfat kökü + そう
な-sıfat gibi (そうな/そうに/そうだ)
普通形/な+な/isim+の + ようだ
footnotes_tr: Common error: Attempting to conjugate 伝聞そう like な-adjectives (×そうな, ×そうに) — this is incorrect; only そうだ/そうです is used.
Common error: Combining い-adjectives いい and ない regularly with そう (×いいそう, ×ないそう) — the correct forms are よさそう, なさそう.

te-shimau-chau.title_tr: 〜てしまう / 〜ちゃう — Completion and Regret Expression
te-shimau-chau.intro_tr: 〜てしまう is formed by attaching しまう (auxiliary verb) to the て-form of a verb, and it carries two main meanings: (1) to complete an action entirely, to the end (neutral/positive emphasis on completion) and (2) to describe something done unintentionally, accidentally, or with regret ('oh well, it's done' feeling). In everyday spoken Japanese, てしまう is almost always shortened to ちゃう (でしまう → じゃう); this abbreviation appears especially frequently in anime, dramas, and conversations between friends. ちゃう itself is conjugated like a う-verb (ちゃう→ちゃわない→ちゃった). This pattern is very critical at the N3 level and is one of the fundamental building blocks in both written and spoken Japanese.

rows: 食べてしまう[たべてしまう]
飲んでしまう[のんでしまう]
忘れてしまう[わすれてしまう]
死んでしまう[しんでしまう]
読んでしまう[よんでしまう]
来てしまう[きてしまう]
footnotes_tr: If the て-form ends in ん/む/ぶ (like のんで, よんで, しんで), でしまう is used instead of しまう; this also makes the ちゃう abbreviation じゃう.

tables.caption_tr: Abbreviated Spoken Form: てしまう → ちゃう
rows: 食べてしまう[たべてしまう]
食べちゃう[たべちゃう]
飲んでしまう[のんでしまう]
飲んじゃう[のんじゃう]

忘れてしまわない[わすれてしまわない]

Kibar (nadir, genelde tam form tercih edilir)

tables.caption_tr: ちゃう's Own Conjugation (behaves like a う-verb)
rows: 食べちゃう[たべちゃう]
食べちゃわない[たべちゃわない]

mitai-da.intro_tr: 〜みたい is one of the most frequently used comparison and inference expressions in everyday conversational language; in meaning it is very similar to 〜よう(だ) but it is more informal and specific to spoken language. It attaches directly to nouns, な-adjectives, い-adjectives, and verbs (without putting の or な in between), so structurally it is simpler than よう. It has three main functions: (1) to compare one thing to another (猫[ねこ]みたい = like a cat), (2) to make inferences based on what one sees, hears, or feels (雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るみたいだ = it looks like it will rain), (3) to make generalizations by giving examples (〜みたいな = which is like ...). みたい itself conjugates like a な-adjective: みたいだ, みたいな+noun, みたいに+verb/adjective.

tables.caption_tr: Attachment Rules — How みたい attaches to different word types
rows: Sıfat gövdesi (な düşer) + みたい
ない形[けい] + みたい
footnotes_tr: Unlike よう, みたい does not require の with nouns or な with な-adjectives; it attaches directly.
みたい always attaches to the end of the plain (casual) form, never to the ます-form.

tables.caption_tr: みたい Conjugation Table (behaves like a な-adjective)
rows: 学生[がくせい]みたいだ
学生[がくせい]みたいです
学生[がくせい]みたいじゃない
学生[がくせい]みたいじゃないです
学生[がくせい]みたいだった

kke.intro_tr: 〜っけ is a highly casual and intimate sentence-final particle used when the speaker asks themselves or others about information they knew previously but cannot quite remember now. It conveys the sense of 'what was that, I forgot' or 'wasn't it?'; it is generally used together with question words (何[なに]、いつ、どこ、誰[だれ]、どう). For verbs and い-adjectives, it is attached to the past (た) form; for nouns and な-adjectives, it is attached to the だ/だった form. It is quite an intimate expression; in formal settings, polite forms such as でしたっけ/ましたっけ are preferred. It is almost never used in written language and is entirely unique to spoken language.

footnotes_tr: The present tense form (such as 行くっけ) is very rarely used; in everyday conversation, it is almost always attached to the past (た) base because what is being queried is information that was previously known but has now been forgotten.
The んだっけ / んでしたっけ form becomes even more widely used when combined with の(ん), which indicates explanation/emphasis: 何[なに]て言[い]うんだっけ？

garu.intro_tr: 〜がる is used to express the internal emotion, desire, or sensory state of another person (3rd person) that we cannot directly observe, based on the outward behavior and signs that person displays. In Japanese, emotion/sensation adjectives such as 嬉[うれ]しい, 痛[いた]い, 欲[ほ]しい normally express only the feeling of the speaker (1st person); when used for another person, the suffix がる is added to the adjective stem to add the meaning 'they are acting like that / they seem like that.' The adjective with がる attached transforms into a godan verb and is typically used in the 〜ている form (がっている) to convey the meaning 'they are displaying that state right now.' When combined with たい (to want), たがる (the desire of another person) emerges. This structure is similar to the Turkish expression '…mず gibi görünmek / …ıyormuş' and carries a non-empathetic, outside-observer perspective.

keigo-sonkeigo.title_tr: Honorific Language: 尊敬語[そんけいご] (Sonkeigo)
keigo-sonkeigo.intro_tr: 尊敬語[そんけいご] (sonkeigo) is the honorific language that the speaker uses to elevate the actions and existence of the person they are listening to or speaking about (generally a teacher, superior, customer, elder, etc.) by honoring them. The important point here is: sonkeigo is used ONLY for the actions of the other party or a respected third person — you never express your own actions with sonkeigo (for your own actions, 謙譲語[けんじょうご] is used). Sonkeigo is formed in three main ways: (1) special honorific verbs (completely different words like いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, なさる), (2) the お〜になる / ご〜になる pattern, (3) the passive (られる/れる) form of the verb — this third one is the weakest degree of honorific. Additionally, お/ご is added to the beginning of nouns, and respectful suffixes like 様[さま] are attached to personal names. Although this topic is at the N3 level, it is beneficial to learn it early because it forms the foundation of daily business and formal Japanese.

お休[やす]みになります

footnotes_tr: According to the いらっしゃる, おっしゃる, なさる, くださる group, they conjugate like godan verbs but show a special shortening in the ます-form (いらっしゃいます instead of いらっしゃります).

footnotes_tr: These four verbs are actually in the godan group, but 〜います is used instead of 〜ります — this irregularity only appears in the ます-form, other conjugations follow normal godan rules (いらっしゃらない, いらっしゃれば, etc.).

footnotes_tr: General rule: お〜になる is used with kun-yomi (Japanese origin) verbs, and ご〜になる is used with on-yomi (Chinese origin, ending with 〜する) verbs.
This pattern is the standard production method for verbs that do not have a special honorific verb form.

Advantage: can be applied to any verb, requires no memorization; disadvantage: can be confused with passive/ability.

onomatopoeia.intro_tr: オノマトペ (onomatopoeia) is a special group of words in Japanese that imitate sounds, states, and emotions; it is extremely frequently used in everyday conversation and in manga/anime. It is divided into three main types: 擬音語[ぎおんご] (words that imitate real sounds — "sound words"), 擬態語[ぎたいご] (words that describe appearance, movement, or state — "state words"), and 擬情語[ぎじょうご] (words that express emotions and physical sensations). Most onomatopoeia consists of the repetition of a two-syllable root (e.g. きらきら, どきどき) and this repetition generally emphasizes continuity or intensity. In sentences, they can be used with に + する/なる, と + verb, or directly as adverbs. These words appear very frequently in N3-N2 level reading and listening materials, so memorizing them is important, because it is an entirely sound/feeling-based system with no kanji equivalent.

dokoro-dewanai.title_tr: 〜どころではない (cannot be in a state to…)
dokoro-dewanai.intro_tr: 〜どころではない is an N2-level pattern that expresses a situation where something is too difficult, intense, or serious to be done. It means "is not in a state to…", "far from being able to…, there's no possibility at all" and similar meanings; it generally emphasizes that the speaker's current circumstances (fatigue, busyness, crisis, natural disaster, etc.) make that action impossible. It is attached to the dictionary form of verbs, nouns, or pronouns like それ. In spoken language どころじゃない is used, while in formal writing どころではありません/ございません forms are used. It should not be confused with the 〜どころか pattern; the two have different functions.

dokoro-ka.intro_tr: 〜どころか is used to strongly reject an expectation or claim and emphasize the complete opposite or something much more extreme instead; it corresponds to the Turkish expressions "…şöyle dursun" (far from...) or "…bir yana" (aside from...). It has two basic uses: (1) to state that A is not true, but actually the opposite (B) is true, (2) to create an exaggerated contrast by emphasizing that even A has not happened, let alone something smaller/more basic like B. It is attached directly to nouns, な-adjectives, い-adjectives, and verbs in plain form. It typically carries the speaker's surprise, disappointment, or ironic emphasis and has a wide range of usage from everyday conversation to written language. It should not be confused with similar patterns like 〜はおろか and 〜どころではない.

mono-dakara.title_tr: 〜ものだから / 〜もので (because, excuse/justification expressing reason pattern)
mono-dakara.intro_tr: 〜ものだから and 〜もので are speech-like patterns used when explaining an "excusable" reason for a behavior or situation. They typically appear in the context of apologizing, offering an excuse, or justifying an unexpected/unwanted result; the speaker conveys the sense of "it was beyond my control, that's why this happened." 〜ものだから carries a more emotional and casual conversational tone, while 〜もので is a somewhat more polite version also suitable for written language. Both indicate cause-and-effect similarly to から/ので, but the second sentence usually contains a past, unwanted, or uncontrollable result; they are not used with imperative, request, or invitation type expressions. It is a pattern that appears frequently at N2 level and is commonly heard in everyday conversations.

mono-no.intro_tr: 〜ものの is a formal and somewhat literary concessive conjunction in Japanese that means "even though..." or "despite...". The speaker first accepts a situation that has occurred or been settled, and then expresses an unexpected, contrary, or disappointing result from that situation. It is close in meaning to 〜のに but contains less emotional complaint/surprise; compared to 〜けれども and 〜が, it is more formal and more common in written language. This pattern is only used for situations that have occurred or are known, so it is not suitable for hypothetical or future situations. This structure, frequently encountered at the N2 level, is attached to the plain form of verbs and adjectives.

〜ものの always expresses a situation that has occurred/been settled; it is not used in hypothetical (like もし〜ら) sentences.

wake-dewanai.title_tr: 〜わけではない / 〜わけがない — Not Like That / Cannot Be
wake-dewanai.intro_tr: Both 〜わけではない and 〜わけがない are two important patterns derived from the word わけ (reason, logic, meaning) but having different functions. 〜わけではない makes a PARTIAL negation by saying "this doesn't mean/that's not entirely the case" — in other words, the speaker doesn't completely deny the situation, but just softens the generalization. 〜わけがない, on the other hand, expresses a STRONG, definitive denial of possibility by saying "logically/presumably impossible, it cannot be." One must not confuse these two patterns with plain ない (simple negation) and 〜はずがない (impossibility based on expectations). Additionally, double negation patterns like 〜ないわけではない and 〜ないわけがない are also used very frequently and their meanings are quite different from each other.

koto-ka.intro_tr: The 〜ことか pattern is an exclamation structure used to express a strong emotion of the speaker such as surprise, admiration, sadness, or regret, and corresponds to the meaning of "How...!" in English. Although the sentence ends with か, this is not a real question; it is rhetorical, emotional emphasis. It is generally used together with intensifying adverbs like どんなに, なんと, どれほど, いくら, 何度[なんど], and can also be used without an adverb. It is attached to the plain form (plain, jisho/ta) of verbs and adjectives; it is frequently seen in written language, literary texts, and emotional narratives, and in everyday conversation it is generally replaced by expressions like 〜だろうね or 〜んだろう.

bakari-ni.title_tr: 〜ばかりに — Merely ...Because (Reason Pattern Indicating Negative Outcome)
bakari-ni.intro_tr: 〜ばかりに is an N2 grammar pattern meaning "simply/merely because ...-da/-di, precisely because of this" and ALWAYS indicates a negative, unfortunate, or unexpected bad result at the end. The reason is usually presented from the speaker's perspective as something small, insignificant, or unlucky, and the sentence carries a strong tone of regret, resentment, or helplessness. Unlike neutral causal conjunctions like から or ので, ばかりに carries an exaggerated feeling of "precisely because of this did this happen to me." It is NEVER used with positive or neutral results — this is the most important point distinguishing this pattern from seemingly similar patterns like だけに and ばかりか. It is typically used when describing a past event that has already occurred and cannot be changed.

ue-de.intro_tr: The pattern 〜うえで / 〜うえは comes from the noun 上[うえ], which has the literal meaning "top, over," and has two different but related functions. (1) Vた上で / Nの上で: meaning "…after, thereupon," it emphasizes that completing one action is a necessary prerequisite for another action — generally used in formal/business contexts. (2) Vる上で / Nの上で: meaning "…while, … in the process of, … regarding," it specifies what should be kept in mind when carrying out an important or abstract action. (3) 〜うえは (usually Vた上は, sometimes Vる上は): meaning "since…, given that…, then," it conveys a sense of determination, necessity, or recommendation as the natural consequence of an established situation; it is similar in meaning to からには but has a more written and formal tone. All three usages are patterns of somewhat formal-written language frequently encountered at the N2 level.

koto-nashi-ni.intro_tr: 〜ことなしに, a formal pattern used with the dictionary form (辞書形[じしょけい]) of a verb to express the meaning of "without doing" or "without…," specific to written language and quite formal. Its structure is こと (auxiliary noun that nominalizes verbs) + なしに (=without…), meaning first the verb is nominalized, then "without that thing" is expressed. In terms of meaning, it is almost the same as 〜ないで and 〜ずに used in everyday conversation, but ことなしに is much more formal and generally appears in newspapers, articles, formal speech, and written narratives; it is rarely used in casual conversation. The pattern is frequently used in combination with a negative predicate in the form 〜ことなしには…ない (=without… it is not possible), creating a strong, definitive emphasis such as "without X, Y is never possible." On this page, the structure of the pattern, its comparison with similar expressions, and frequently seen pattern structures are summarized in table form.

tables.caption_tr: Basic structure: Verb (dictionary form) + ことなしに
rows: 気付[きづ]かれることなしに
footnotes_tr: こと nominalizes the verb; なしに adds the meaning of 'without that noun.' For this reason, ことなしに is always attached to the dictionary (present, affirmative) form of the verb, not to the past form (〜た) or negative form (〜ない).
Since the negative meaning is already contained in なしに, the verb itself is kept affirmative: not ×見ないことなしに, but ○見ることなしに.

sai-ni.title_tr: 〜際に (さいに) — during, when, by occasion of
sai-ni.intro_tr: 〜際に(さいに), meaning "during, when, by occasion of", is the formal and written language equivalent of the 〜とき pattern. It is generally used when referring to important, one-time events, official announcements, guidelines, and business Japanese; in everyday conversation 〜とき is preferred. It combines with the dictionary form of a verb, the -た form, or noun+の, and is generally followed by an informative explanation or a polite request/instruction. It has variants such as 際に, 際は, 際には, この際, その際, and each carries a different emphasis.

ta-tokoro-de.title_tr: 〜たところで (…even if, to no avail)
ta-tokoro-de.intro_tr: 〜たところで, added to the past (た) form of a verb, gives the meaning of "…even if, the result doesn't change, …-ing is futile," and is an advanced-level (N2) pattern that typically ends with a negative or pessimistic conclusion. It expresses the speaker's firm conviction that carrying out the action in question will not bring the desired result. The sentence almost always ends with a negative or limiting predicate like 〜ない, 〜だけだ, 〜に過ぎない. It is frequently used together with adverbs like どうせ, いくら, たとえ, 今さら and adds a tone of disappointment, resignation, or irony specific to the speaker. It is similar in meaning to 〜ても and 〜たって in spoken language, but たところで carries a stronger emphasis on "futility."

mono-da.intro_tr: 〜ものだ is a multifunctional pattern in Japanese that carries multiple layers of meaning: (1) it expresses a truth that is considered valid and natural throughout society ("humans are such creatures"), (2) it adds a sense of nostalgia/longing by recalling habits frequently repeated in the past (especially 〜たものだ), (3) from a moral or social perspective, it conveys an indirect recommendation/obligation in the sense of "this should/should not be done," and (4) with the よく〜ものだ pattern, it expresses surprise or complaint. It is constructed as the dictionary form of the verb or -ta form + ものだ; its negation is 〜ものではない, and its past form is 〜ものだった. In spoken language, ものだ is usually shortened to もんだ. Since this pattern describes a general-universal rule or habit rather than a personal/singular event, attention should be paid to the context of use.

nagara-mo.intro_tr: 〜ながらも is a contrast/reinforcement pattern close to written language (somewhat literary) that expresses that despite the existence of a situation or quality, it does not produce the expected result. Basically, to prevent confusion with the "at the same time" meaning of 〜ながら, thanks to the も particle added at the end, it clearly pulls the meaning towards "…despite, …in contrast to". It is generally used with state-expressing verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives and nouns; it is not frequently seen with action verbs. Compared to のに or にもかかわらず, it has a more written, somewhat more formal and literary style; it is limited in use in spoken language. A contrast or surprising harmony is emphasized between the situation in the first half of the sentence and the result in the second half.

nari-nari.intro_tr: 〜なり is a particle with two completely different functions encountered at the N2 level. When attached on its own to the dictionary form (辞書形) of a verb, it gives the meaning of "…-er …-mez, without any waiting, immediately," and generally describes an unexpected or quick action (e.g., 帰[かえ]るなり寝[ね]る = "as soon as one comes home, one sleeps"). In the second and more frequently seen usage, it is repeated in the form 〜なり〜なり and attached to nouns or verbs, and is used in suggestion/advice sentences with the meaning of "either…or…, like for example you do either … or … or something like that," suggesting one option from several choices. Both usages are close to the written language and have somewhat literary tone; in daily conversation, 〜たとたん or 〜とか〜とか are more preferred. On this page, you will learn to clearly distinguish the two usages from each other and avoid confusing them with similar patterns.

koto-tote.title_tr: 〜こととて (…because it is, literary excuse)
koto-tote.intro_tr: 〜こととて, meaning "…because it is/because it must be," is a very formal and literary (書[か]き言葉[ことば]) conjunction that expresses reason and excuse. It is typically used to justify a fault, mistake, delay, or lack of knowledge, and is usually followed by an apology, request, or appeal for forgiveness (〜ください, 〜いただきたく, お許[ゆる]しください, etc.). It is almost never used in everyday conversation; it appears in formal letters, congratulatory/apology writings, literary texts, and classically-tinged expressions. Semantically it resembles ので/から, but it carries the nuance of "unfortunately due to a reason beyond my control" and places the speaker in a humble/apologetic position. Although it is considered N2 level, its structure can be easily recognized if memorized as fixed phrases.

uchi-ni.intro_tr: 〜うちに is a pattern that expresses the need to do/be something within a limited time period while a situation or state is continuing; it is generally translated into English as "…-ken" or "…-before". The basic logic of the pattern is as follows: the current situation will not last forever, so action must be taken before that situation changes/ends. The negative form 〜ないうちに means "not yet …, …before" and is semantically close to 〜前に but carries more of a nuance of "before an unwanted change occurs". When 〜ているうちに is used, it often describes a result that emerges over time, unconsciously to the person, while doing an action. This pattern appears frequently in both spoken and written language and is an important temporal conjunction at the JLPT N2 level.

うちに often carries the meaning of 'if you don't do it now, you'll miss the opportunity'; 前に does not carry this nuance.

sae-ba.intro_tr: 〜さえ〜ば is a pattern that emphasizes in a sentence that the minimum/sole condition is sufficient and corresponds to the Turkish expression 'yeter ki …-sa'. The structure expresses that the element marked with ~さえ alone is sufficient, and everything else remains in the background; it usually works together with the conditional suffix 〜ば (matches with ba-conditional form). さえ replaces and drops basic particles like は/が/を, but when used together with particles like に/で/と, these particles are preserved (like にさえ, でさえ). This pattern has different connection methods with nouns, verbs, い-adjectives, and な-adjectives, and generally carries a strong 'single condition is enough' emphasis. It is a practical pattern frequently encountered at N2 level, used in both everyday conversation and written language.

ka-to-omottara.title_tr: 〜かと思うと / 〜かと思ったら (just as…-ed)
ka-to-omottara.intro_tr: 〜かと思うと and 〜かと思ったら are N2 level grammar patterns that describe how immediately after realizing/noticing that one event has occurred (sometimes "just as one thinks something has occurred"), an unexpected, usually opposite or surprising second event takes place. It corresponds to the Turkish expressions "…-ed just as…-ed" or "I thought…, but it turned out…-ed". The pattern is attached to a verb/noun in past tense form (〜た/〜だった) and emphasizes that the time interval between the two events is extremely short. It only expresses objective observation and surprise; it cannot be used to describe the speaker's own intentional actions or commands/requests in the second clause. 〜かと思ったら is more common in spoken language, while 〜かと思うと can be used in both written and spoken language.

wo-towazu.title_tr: 〜を問わず / 〜にかかわらず (without paying attention to …)
wo-towazu.intro_tr: 〜を問[と]わず and 〜にかかわらず are N2-level patterns corresponding to the Turkish phrases "without considering/paying attention to", "regardless of". Both are used to indicate that a condition (age, gender, weather, experience, etc.) does not affect the result in any way. 〜を問わず appears more often in formal announcements, registration conditions, and written language with the meaning "without considering category/class distinction"; 〜にかかわらず can be used in both written and spoken language and can also be connected with adjective/verb positive-negative pairs. Both patterns end with the negative -zu (〜ず) suffix (問う→問わず, かかわる→かかわらず) and come after nouns or "A か B か" type opposite pairs. Note: 〜にもかかわらず ("despite/in spite of") has a completely different meaning and is a separate pattern and should not be confused.

wo-megutte.title_tr: 〜をめぐって — around/concerning ... (postpositional particle pattern indicating dispute, discussion)
wo-megutte.intro_tr: 〜をめぐって comes from the verb 巡[めぐ]る (to turn around, circulate), and is used with the meaning "around ..., concerning ...". The difference from expressions like について or に関して is that it is generally followed by a predicate expressing a dispute, argument, lawsuit, or difference of opinion (争う, 対立する, 議論する, 裁判になる, etc.); in other words, the topic is not a neutral "about", but rather "a matter over which disagreement/dispute exists". It appears very frequently in formal speech and especially in news/newspaper Japanese, but is rare in everyday conversation. It can also be used as a noun phrase in the form 〜をめぐる + noun; 〜をめぐり is a more literary variant in written language. It is frequently encountered at N2 level and is a critical pattern for news Japanese.

ni-sotte.title_tr: 〜に沿って — in accordance with ..., along ...
ni-sotte.intro_tr: 〜に沿って (そって), actually a particle-form grammar pattern derived from the te-form of the verb "沿う" (to follow a line, to go parallel), frequently encountered at the N2 level. It has two fundamental meanings: (1) in a concrete/spatial sense 'along something (river, road, border, coast), parallel to it' and (2) in an abstract sense 'IN ACCORDANCE WITH a plan, rule, expectation, or demand, adhering to it' to act. It comes directly after a noun: N + に沿って. When modifying a noun, the form 〜に沿った + noun is used (e.g. 方針[ほうしん]に沿った行動[こうどう] = conduct in accordance with policy). Frequently seen in formal speech, business correspondence, and instruction/guide texts; used less in everyday conversation, where simple expressions like もとに or -う are preferred instead.

ni-oite-okeru.title_tr: 〜において / 〜における (…-de, …in the area — formal place/context expression)
ni-oite-okeru.intro_tr: 〜において and 〜における are the formal, written-language equivalents of the particles で and に used in everyday conversation, and mean "…-de, …-da, …in the area/context". Their origin lies in the classical Japanese にありて expression; for this reason, they frequently appear in academic texts, news, formal speeches, and business Japanese. When において modifies a sentence or verb (…において + verb/sentence), における directly modifies a noun (…における + noun), that is, it serves the function of the の contextual particle. Using these patterns in everyday conversation comes across as contrived; instead で and に are preferred. Although they may appear at the N2 level, the basic logic is simple: it indicates "place/time/area" and adds formality.

ni-motozuite.intro_tr: 〜に基[もと]づいて, when added to a noun, gives the meaning of "based on this noun", "using this as a foundation" and is derived from the te-form of the verb 基[もと]づく. It is used when specifying a concrete and objective "foundation/source" such as law, rule, data, experience, or facts; it does not convey personal feelings or assumptions. It appears mainly in formal, written, news, and academic language; when modifying a noun, 〜に基[もと]づく or 〜に基[もと]づいた are used, and in more formal written language, the form 〜に基[もと]づき is preferred. This pattern, frequently encountered at N2 level, can easily be confused with similar patterns like によって, を踏[ふ]まえて, に沿[そ]って, so the nuance differences should be clearly distinguished.

bakari-ka.title_tr: 〜ばかりか / 〜ばかりでなく — Not Just …, But Also …
bakari-ka.intro_tr: 「〜ばかりか」and「〜ばかりでなく」are patterns belonging to written language and formal speech that convey the meaning of "not just A, but also B"; they serve the same function as 「〜だけでなく」in daily conversation but have a harsher and more literary style. Generally, they are used to add a situation that is further, more surprising, or worse than the speaker expected; therefore, emphasis particles such as 「も」「さえ」「まで」frequently appear in the second sentence. 「〜ばかりか」especially emphasizes an unexpected/surprising additional situation, while 「〜ばかりでなく」carries a more neutral meaning of "not just …". Both patterns can be attached to the plain (jisho/plain) form of nouns, na-adjectives, i-adjectives, and verbs; with nouns and na-adjectives, they are generally used together with 「である」. It is a structure frequently encountered in news articles, articles, formal speeches, and N2-N1 reading passages.

This structure can be used in both affirmative and negative sentences.

dake-ni.title_tr: 〜だけに / 〜だけあって（because of it / as expected）
dake-ni.intro_tr: 〜だけに and 〜だけあって are patterns that indicate when a reason is given (usually a notable characteristic, effort, position, or experience), the resulting outcome is "expected/normal in light of that reason" — they correspond to Turkish expressions like "haliyle" (naturally), "…elbette" (because...of course), and "tam da …-dığı için" (precisely because...). 〜だけあって is usually used with POSITIVE results that show appreciation and admiration, and carries an air of "さすが" (indeed, as expected); it is rarely used with negative results. 〜だけに, on the other hand, can be used with both positive and negative results, and is especially preferred to convey emphatic statements, sometimes unexpected or contrary results, like "precisely because of that much effort/expectation, the result was even larger/heavier than normal." Both are associated with written/formal and somewhat literary style rather than colloquial speech, and appear at the N2 level.
