shidai.title_tr: 〜次第 / 〜次第で / 〜次第だ (depends on …; as soon as …, immediately …)
shidai.intro_tr: The 〜次第[しだい] pattern has two distinct fundamental uses, and it is important not to confuse them. (1) When attached to the ます-root of a verb, it carries the meaning "as soon as X happens, immediately Y" (e.g., 届[とど]き次第[しだい] = as soon as it arrives). (2) When attached to a noun, 次第で(は) means "depending on X, it varies according to X", while 次第だ becomes a predicate at the end of the sentence meaning "depends on …". This second usage is semantically close to the いかんで and によって patterns, but is more neutral and appears very frequently in everyday-business language. In particular, the form 〜次第です stands out as an official closing expression in business letters and emails.

footnotes_tr: The 次第 with the meaning 'as soon as…, immediately…' comes after the ます-root of a verb and generally expresses an event that was not completed in the past and will occur in the future; it is used with the ます-root, not with the ta-form.
The 次第 with the meaning 'depends on …' is attached only to nouns, not to verbs.

wo-tsujite.intro_tr: 〜を通じて (~wo tsuujite) and 〜を通して (~wo tooshite) are important N2-level patterns that come after a noun and convey the meaning of "…through, …by way of, …throughout." They have two primary uses: (1) indicating the transfer of information/communication through a person, institution, or tool (means/agency sense) and (2) covering an entire time period or domain (continuity/scope sense). Both forms are largely interchangeable; however, 〜を通じて is slightly more preferred when expressing abstract/indirect means and possibility, while 〜を通して is somewhat more preferred when emphasizing concrete process and continuity. It is frequently encountered in written language and formal speech and can also be used in everyday conversation. Since it derives from the te-form, it is not as complex as verb conjugation; it is simply a fixed pattern of noun + を通じて/を通して.

mono-o.intro_tr: 〜ものを is a literary-toned pattern expressing regret, sadness, and especially reproach felt toward a behavior that was possible in the past but was not done (or was done when it shouldn't have been). It means '...if only (but it didn't happen)', '...would have been enough (but it wasn't like that)' and generally carries a mix of sadness and anger toward the other party on the speaker's part, as in 'I wish you had done it that way so you wouldn't have ended up in this situation'. Structurally, it is very similar to 〜のに, but 〜ものを is more emotional, more literary, and by leaving the sentence unfinished (ending with ものを) can add a more emphatic tone of reproach. It is usually used together with the pattern 〜ば+いい/よかった+ものを. It appears in emotional, reproachful expressions in spoken language but is more frequently seen in formal/written language.

ni-atatte.title_tr: 〜にあたって / 〜にあたり (…starting, by occasion of)
ni-atatte.intro_tr: 〜にあたって is a formal pattern used at the beginning of an important, special, or significant milestone event, or by occasion of its occurrence. It is typically translated into English as '…on the occasion of', '…at the start of', or '…at the eve of'. The dictionary form of a verb or a noun connects directly with にあたって/にあたり; にあたり is the variant more commonly seen in written language and formal speeches. It is not used for everyday or trivial actions; it is preferred for serious and usually one-time events such as weddings, graduations, starting a job, opening a meeting, or launching a product. It is typically followed by a sentence expressing preparation, advice, thanks, or determination.

tables.caption_tr: 〜にあたって Attachment Forms

footnotes_tr: にあたって is not a conjunction derived from the て-form; it is an idiomatic structure and is not used with the past tense (た).
A verb always remains in its dictionary (る) form: する → するにあたって, not した にあたって.

kagiri.title_tr: 〜かぎり / 〜ないかぎり (as long as…)
kagiri.intro_tr: The word 〜かぎり (限り) literally means "limit, bound"; as a grammar pattern, it functions as a conditional conjunction in the meaning of "as long as this situation/condition continues." When attached to the dictionary form of a verb, it means "as long as…", and when attached to the ない form, it carries the meaning "as long as… does not, unless…". かぎり is also frequently used with patterns like 知る限り, 見る限り to indicate limited personal knowledge in the form of "as far as I know/can see." This structure generally emphasizes that a result will remain valid as long as the current situation does not change; in this respect, unlike the 〜間 structure that only indicates a time interval, it carries the quality of a true condition. It is frequently encountered in both written and spoken language and is an important pattern at the N2 level.

to-ieba.title_tr: 〜といえば / 〜というと (Speaking of …, When you say …)
to-ieba.intro_tr: 〜といえば and 〜というと are used to take up a topic that appeared in a previous conversation with the meaning of 'speaking of that', 'what comes to mind when you say that', and continue with that. Based on a name, person, or event mentioned by the other person, you add your own associations, examples, or opinions. 〜といえば is a more common and natural conversational connector; 〜というと generally carries a nuance of confirming or expressing surprise by repeating what the other person said, and gives a slightly more formal/careful atmosphere. Both can be attached to nouns and plain (plain) verb/adjective phrases; they are used while presenting the most typical, most readily recalled association with the target topic. This pattern generally serves as a bridge for changing the subject or expanding the topic within dialogue.

ippou-de.title_tr: 〜一方(で) — One Hand… On the Other Hand… (N2)
ippou-de.intro_tr: 〜一方(で) (いっぽう(で)), is an N2-level conjunction used to link two different aspects of a subject or two situations occurring simultaneously. It corresponds to the Turkish expressions "one hand… on the other hand…" or "…while also". It has two basic uses: (1) comparing two contrasting/opposite situations in the same subject or topic, (2) indicating two different actions performed by one subject simultaneously or two characteristics of a subject. The で particle is optional and does not greatly change the meaning; furthermore, 一方 can also be used alone at the beginning of an independent sentence separated by a comma with the meaning "on the other hand". This structure appears frequently especially in written and formal language, in news texts, and in academic discourse.

Whether the で particle is added or not, the meaning is almost the same; adding で adds a slight pause/emphasis to the sentence.

you-ni-purpose.intro_tr: 〜ように is a multi-functional grammar structure added to a verb or negative verb that conveys four main meanings: (1) indicates an action taken to achieve a goal ("so that…, in order to…"), (2) shows the manner or form of an action ("just as…"), (3) expresses a wish, hope, or prayer ("I hope that…"), and (4) is used in indirect commands/requests (〜ように言う/伝える/頼む etc.). When used with the meaning of purpose, the verb is usually in the involuntary (spontaneous), potential (capability), or negative form; to express purpose with volitional verbs, 〜ために is used instead. This structure is extremely common in both spoken and written language, and while it appears from N4-N3 level, all the subtleties of its usage are fully reinforced at N2 level.

ni-tomonatte.title_tr: 〜に伴って / 〜につれて / 〜にしたがって (…as, …along with)
ni-tomonatte.intro_tr: The patterns "〜に伴って", "〜につれて", and "〜にしたがって" express that as one situation changes or develops, another situation also changes in parallel; they correspond to Turkish structures such as "…-dikçe" or "…ile birlikte". Although all three convey the basic meaning "as A changes/develops, B also changes", they differ in formality level, whether the change is natural or rule-based, and whether imperative/volitional expressions can be used in the second clause. につれて expresses the most natural and gradual change, while にしたがって can express both natural change and compliance with rules/instructions; に伴って, meanwhile, is preferred in more formal written language to describe large-scale factual changes. On this page, the connection patterns, semantic nuances, grammatical restrictions, and frequently confused points of the three patterns are summarized in table format.

tables.caption_tr: General comparison of the three patterns
rows: "…dikçe" — tamamen doğal, kademeli, kendiliğinden gelişen değişim
Doğa olayları, zamanla oluşan doğal gelişmeler (örn. yaşlanma, mevsim değişimi)

"…ile birlikte" — bir olguya eşlik eden, ona bağlı olarak ortaya çıkan değişim/durum

Büyük ölçekli, toplumsal, ekonomik veya sistemsel değişimler

tsutsu.intro_tr: 〜つつ is a conjunctive form that is attached to the ます-stem of verbs and is preferred in written language and formal/literary speech. It has two basic meanings: (1) to indicate that two actions are performed by the same subject simultaneously (...while, ...when; the formal equivalent of 〜ながら in everyday speech), (2) to indicate that something is done despite a known situation (...despite, ...although; similar to 〜のに). The pattern 〜つつある is a separate structure that expresses that a change or process is currently ongoing and gradually occurring (gradually ...is happening, ...is occurring). These structures are not used in everyday conversation; they appear in news, articles, formal speeches, and literary texts. Note that both actions must belong to the same subject and the verb must always be used with the ます-stem.

footnotes_tr: つつ is always attached to the ます-stem of the verb; it is never attached to the dictionary form or the た-form.
つつある is naturally used only with verbs expressing change/process (such as 増える, 減る, 進む, 変化する[へんかする]); it is not used with one-time/instantaneous actions.

ni-saishite.title_tr: 〜に際して (...during, on the occasion of)
ni-saishite.intro_tr: 〜に際して is a very formal expression meaning "...when, ...on the occasion of"; it is used to indicate an action performed at the beginning of or in connection with a special or important event such as a ceremony, conference, business meeting, opening speech, etc. It is almost never used in everyday conversation; it frequently appears in written formal texts, announcements, opening speeches, and in business Japanese. It is used only with important, one-time, milestone-type events—it is not suitable for ordinary daily actions. It is very similar in meaning to 〜にあたって, but 〜に際して is somewhat more formal and specific to written language. In written language, the usage without て as 〜に際し is also common and adds a more formal tone.

wa-betsu-toshite.intro_tr: 〜は別[べつ]として is an N2-level pattern that conveys the meaning of setting aside, temporarily, a topic, person, or matter from evaluation and saying 'setting that aside, let's move to what's really important.' It is attached directly to nouns, and to interrogative expressions as 〜かは別として or 〜かどうかは別として. With this pattern, the speaker generally says: 'This topic is debatable/a different matter, but I won't talk about it now, what comes next in the sentence is more important.' It is a neutral-formal expression that can be used in both written and spoken language; in meaning it is very close to 〜はさておき but has a slightly more written and formal style. It is often encountered with set phrases like 'joking aside', 'price aside', 'aside from liking or disliking' and similar.

ni-shiro-ni-shiro.title_tr: 〜にしても / 〜にしろ〜にしろ — even if; whether...or... (N2)
ni-shiro-ni-shiro.intro_tr: 〜にしても and 〜にしろ〜にしろ (also 〜にせよ〜にせよ), is an N2-level pattern that conveys the meaning of "no matter what, even if". While 〜にしても accepts a single situation and indicates a result despite it ("even if..."), 〜にしろ〜にしろ / 〜にせよ〜にせよ lists two opposite or alternative options side by side, giving the meaning "whether...or...", "either...or..." and emphasizes that the result won't change regardless of which one occurs. While にしろ is closer to conversational language, にせよ is more formal/specific to written language. These patterns can be attached to nouns, adjectives, verbs, and question words (だれ, なに, どちら) and typically end with a sentence expressing criticism, advice, or a natural consequence.

wo-komete.intro_tr: 〜を込めて is a pattern that expresses putting a specific feeling, intention, or power into an action you are performing; it is generally translated into Turkish as '…-i katarak', 'sincerely', 'with all …'. In terms of structure, the を particle comes after a noun expressing feeling/power, then the て-form (込めて) of the verb 込める is used, and the sentence continues with a verb. It is generally used in contexts where sincere feelings are important, such as giving gifts, cooking food, writing letters, and praying. If noun modification is to be done, 込めた is used instead of 込めて (〜を込めた + Noun). This pattern is at N2 level and has a wide range of use from everyday conversation to formal writing.

to-tomo-ni.intro_tr: 〜とともに[〜とともに], Japanese basically means 'together with', a versatile, written-language construction that expresses both accompaniment and simultaneous change. When attached directly to nouns, it gives the simple meaning of accompaniment as 'X together with', while when used with the dictionary form of verbs, it carries meanings of simultaneous or proportional change such as 'Y also happens when X happens' or 'as X increases, Y also increases'. In everyday speech と一緒に[といっしょに] is preferred more, while とともに frequently appears in formal speech, news texts, articles, and written narratives. Although it overlaps in meaning with 〜につれて[につれて] and 〜にしたがって[にしたがって], とともに is the only construction that also retains the pure meaning of accompaniment. Additionally, with the pattern 〜であるとともに[であるとともに], it is also used to express two qualities simultaneously in the meaning of 'both… and'.

tsutsumo.intro_tr: 〜つつも is a conjunction that describes a person's contrary behavior despite knowing or feeling that something is correct/bad/dangerous, and it is somewhat literary and close to written language. It corresponds to the Turkish expressions "…-mesine rağmen", "…bildiği halde" and generally emphasizes a person's internal contradiction (not being able to do despite knowing, doing despite not wanting). In structure, it is very similar to 〜ながらも and 〜ものの but has a more formal/literary tone and is rarely used in spoken language. The addition of も strengthens the meaning of contrast/contradiction; without も, the simple 〜つつ more often means "doing two things at the same time" (like ながら). It commonly appears in fixed expressions with knowledge/thinking verbs such as 知る, 思う, 分かる, 言う.

mono-to-shite.intro_tr: 〜ものとして is an N2-level formal pattern that expresses the action of processing something "as if it were true" or "counting it as such" regardless of whether it is actually true in reality. It is attached to a clause in the form of a verb, い-adjective, な-adjective(である), or noun(である), and is typically followed by a sentence expressing a result. It is frequently encountered in formal/written contexts such as contracts, regulations, examination rules, and business correspondence; it is rarely used in everyday conversation. While として alone expresses an identity or role ("...as"), ものとして emphasizes a hypothetical acceptance or formal "counting" process. The regulation-specific variant of this pattern, 〜ものとする ("...is counted"), is also an integral part of this topic.

nashi-dewa.intro_tr: 〜なしでは and 〜ぬきで, both meaning "…without" but used with different nuances and contexts, are N2-level patterns. 〜なしでは (and its literary form 〜なしに), is generally used with abstract concepts (water, love, effort, permission, etc.) in the sense of "a result is impossible / does not happen without this thing," used with a negative judgment. 〜ぬきで, on the other hand, comes from the verb 抜[ぬ]く (to pull out, to remove) and describes an action done "by leaving something out, by excluding it" (coffee without sugar, speaking without elaborating, etc.). Both come after nouns and can be used in different functions depending on verb conjugation: なしでは/なしに/なしの and ぬきで/ぬきに/ぬきの. In the tables below, the connection methods, nuance differences, and frequently used pattern expressions are shown comparatively.

nuku-kiru.title_tr: 〜ぬく / 〜きる (To do to the end, To do completely)
nuku-kiru.intro_tr: 〜ぬく and 〜きる are auxiliary verbs that, when attached to the ます-stem of verbs, add the meaning of "doing something to the end, doing something completely, doing something without omission." 〜ぬく (抜く) generally emphasizes that a task is carried through to completion while overcoming difficulty, hardship, or resistance (carrying a struggling nuance); 〜きる (切る) expresses that an action is completed entirely, physically or in quantity, without leaving anything remaining. 〜きる is also frequently used in potential forms like 〜きれる (being able to, being able to finish everything) and 〜きれない (not being able to do everything). Both structures are quite common at the N2 level in both spoken and written language.

tables.caption_tr: Attachment form: ます-stem + ぬく / きる
footnotes_tr: ぬく and きる, regardless of what main verb they attach to, are always conjugated according to godan conjugation (ぬく: く-godan; きる: る-godan exception group, like 切[き]る).

uru-enai.intro_tr: 「〜得る」(える/うる) verb, when added to the ます-root, conveys the meaning of "…-can, …-possible, may occur" and is a common pattern encountered at the N2 level, primarily in written language and formal speech. It expresses not a concrete physical ability, but logically/theoretically the possibility of something occurring — in this sense, it differs in meaning from the 〜られる capability (potential) form. The negative form 〜得ない conveys the meaning of "…-cannot, impossible" and there is an important reading rule to note: in the negative, えない is always read, うない is never used. The most commonly encountered pattern in daily language is あり得る (possible) and especially あり得ない (impossible, unbelievable!).

causative-keigo.intro_tr: 〜させていただく is one of the most polite Japanese expression patterns and falls into the "kenjōgo" (humble language) category. Its structure consists of adding いただく (the kenjōgo form of もらう, meaning "receive/ask for") to the causative (使役[しえき]) form of a verb; thus it conveys the meaning "with the other party's permission/favor I am..., please allow me to...". The speaker shows great humility and respect by presenting the action they are doing as if they are doing it with the other party's permission or favor. Especially in business Japanese (ビジネス日本語[にほんご]), in emails, in official announcements, and when facing customers, it is used very frequently. However, in daily conversation, excessive unnecessary use (especially in situations where it doesn't make sense to ask for permission) is criticized as unnatural, a so-called incorrect usage called "バイト敬語[けいご]"; therefore it is important to know when it is appropriate.

you-ga-nai.title_tr: 〜ようがない — "...no way to do it, impossible"
you-ga-nai.intro_tr: 〜ようがない is formed by adding 〜よう (wish/volitional root) + がない to the ます-stem (連用形) of a verb, and means "there is no way/method to do this, impossible." It emphasizes that an action cannot be performed due to physical impossibility, lack of means/method, or lack of available information; it carries the nuance not just "I cannot do it" but "there is no way to do it at all." しようがない (from する verb) has become fixed in everyday speech to mean "I cannot help it, I am helpless," and from this the form しょうがない has emerged. A more emphatic/literary variant, 〜ようもない, is used in the same structure. It is a practical pattern frequently encountered at N2 level, used in both written and spoken Japanese.

darake.intro_tr: 〜だらけ is a pattern attached to a noun that gives the meaning of 'full of it, covered with, completely soaked.' It is generally used to express a dense and scattered abundance of unwanted and negatively perceived things like dust, mud, blood, mistakes, or debt. だらけ is directly attached to the root of a noun and conjugates like な-adjectives: だらけの + noun (modification), だらけだ (predicate), だらけで (conjunction). It is frequently encountered in spoken language and is quite a useful pattern in everyday Japanese. Since it can be confused with similar expressions 〜まみれ, っぽい, and がち, it is necessary to pay attention to the nuance differences between them.

zuni-wa-irarenai.title_tr: 〜ずにはいられない (cannot help but…)
zuni-wa-irarenai.intro_tr: 〜ずにはいられない expresses that an emotion or urge is so strong that a person cannot restrain themselves and is "forced" to perform an action, whether they want to or not; the closest English equivalent is "cannot help but…", "cannot but…". The structure actually consists of double negation: from the negative (ない) root of the verb, ない is dropped and replaced with ず (classical negation suffix) + には + いられない ("cannot, am unable to"), meaning literally "cannot be without doing/I am unable not to do". This pattern is frequently used especially with emotional reactions like laughing, crying, being surprised, being amazed, and irresistible urges (eating, buying, saying); it emphasizes the speaker's instinctive, unconscious reaction. Should not be confused with 〜ざるを得[え]ない (necessity due to external circumstances) and 〜ずにはすまない (inevitability due to social/moral norms) — ずにはいられない is entirely a reaction stemming from a person's own inner world, their emotional urge. The past form of the pattern is 〜ずにはいられなかった and there is no other conjugation; this is a fixed, idiomatic form.

footnotes_tr: Rule: The ない in the ない-form is dropped, and ずにはいられない is added in its place.
The する verb is an exception: not しない, but the classical negative root せ is used → せずにはいられない.

to-shite-mo.intro_tr: 〜としても is a conjunction meaning "...even if / let's say ...is, still" and appears at JLPT N2 level. Structurally, it consists of a combination of the quotative particle と + the て-form して of the verb する + the particle も meaning "even"; therefore the underlying logic is shaped like "...even if we accept/assume..." Compared to 〜ても, it marks a more abstract and hypothetical premise, generally putting forward a claim or hypothesis and then emphasizing that its result won't change. When used together with adverbs like たとえ, 万一, 仮に, the emphasis becomes even stronger. When used with nouns and な-adjectives, だ must be added, and this is where students often make mistakes.

zaru-wo-enai.title_tr: 〜ざるを得ない - …must do (forced to do)
zaru-wo-enai.intro_tr: 〜ざるを得[え]ない is a formal and literary pattern that expresses being forced to do an action not by one's own will, but by external circumstances. Its structure consists of the combination of: the negative root of the verb + the classical negation suffix ざる + を + 得[え]ない (cannot obtain/cannot avoid); when two negations come together, it transforms into the meaning "I cannot avoid not doing" or in other words "I inevitably do it". Its most important exception is the verb する: しざる is NOT used, instead せざるを得[え]ない is used — this is the only major irregularity that needs to be memorized. The pattern is predominantly seen in written language, news articles, and formal speeches; in daily conversation, simpler expressions like 〜しかない or 〜なきゃ are generally preferred. It adds a tone of reluctance, helplessness, or compulsion to the sentence; it emphasizes that the person did the action not by their own choice, but because of circumstances.

nai-koto-niwa.title_tr: 〜ないことには (unless not; if not, [something] is impossible)
nai-koto-niwa.intro_tr: 〜ないことには is an N2-level conditional pattern added to the negative (ない) form of a verb, adjective, or noun, meaning "if...not/unless..., (something) is impossible." The structure almost always ends with a negative second clause (わからない, できない, 始まらない, etc.), thus emphasizing the point that "without X being done, Y definitely cannot occur" — in other words, X is an indispensable prerequisite for Y. Semantically it is similar to 〜なければ〜ない but has a more written and formal tone; it is rarely used in everyday conversation, being preferred more in written texts, explanations, and serious discussions. When used with nouns and な-adjectives, it takes the form でないことには. If a negative predicate is not used in the second half of the pattern, the sentence becomes unnatural, which is why the pair "negative + ことには + negative result" is the basic skeleton of this grammar.

zu-ni.intro_tr: 〜ずに and 〜ないで are two basic grammatical structures that correspond to the meaning of "...-without" in Turkish; they express doing one action without performing (or instead of) another action. While 〜ないで is very frequently used in everyday speech and writing, 〜ずに is more formal, specific to written language, and has a somewhat literary tone. Both structures are derived from the ない form of the verb: ない is removed and ず is added in its place; the only irregularity occurs with the する verb, because せずに is used, not しずに. Additionally, 〜ないで is also used in negative request sentences with 〜ないでください meaning 'please don't...' in a similar way to the 〜てください pattern — this usage cannot be done with 〜ずに. These two structures should not be confused with the 〜なくて structure, which is completely different in meaning and expresses cause/reason.

mamire.intro_tr: 〜まみれ is an adjective-forming suffix attached to nouns that expresses the idea that the surface of something or someone is completely covered or soiled by an unwanted, polluting substance. It is generally used with concrete and usually unpleasant substances such as mud, blood, sweat, dust, oil, and tears; metaphorically it can also be used in the sense of "immersed in abstract things like debt or mistakes" (as in 借金まみれ), but this usage is limited. It conjugates like な-adjectives (まみれだ / まみれの / まみれで). It is frequently confused with 〜だらけ, which has a similar meaning; the differences and usage limitations between them are summarized in the tables below.

keigo-humble-special.title_tr: Kenjōgo Special Verbs (伺[うかが]う / 申[もう]す / いたす...)
keigo-humble-special.intro_tr: Kenjōgo (謙譲語[けんじょうご]) is the language of humility in which the speaker lowers their OWN actions to indirectly show respect to the other party. Unlike sonkeigo, here the subject is ALWAYS "I/we" or someone from one's own group — never the listener or a third person. Some verbs have completely different, must-be-memorized "special kenjōgo verbs" instead of the normal -masu form (伺う[うかがう], 申す[もうす], いたす, etc.). This page contains the complete list of these special verbs that you will frequently encounter in business Japanese and formal speech, their conjugations, and usage differences. It is critical not to confuse the same verb with its sonkeigo (elevating the other party) form.

gimi.intro_tr: The 〜気味[ぎみ] suffix, when attached to the ます-root of a noun or verb, adds the meaning "somewhat ...-ish, inclined to ..., slightly ... like". It is generally used to express a physical or mental condition of a person (fatigue, illness, weight gain, tension) or a numerical trend (increase, decrease, delay), most often conveying a negative or neutral-slight impression. It carries the sense of "not exactly like that, but there is a tendency in that direction". Since it is used as a noun, it can be connected to the sentence in different forms such as 〜気味です/〜気味だ, 〜気味の+noun and 〜気味に+verb. It should not be confused with similarly meaning 〜がち and 〜っぽい; the subtle nuances between them are shown in the tables below.

tables.caption_tr: Attachment Rules (How to Use?)
footnotes_tr: 気味[ぎみ] is actually a noun, so it is connected with 〜です/〜だ, takes 〜の when modifying nouns, and takes 〜に when modifying verbs.

proverbs-yoji.title_tr: Four-Character Idioms 四字熟語[よじじゅくご] and ことわざ (Proverbs) — Introduction
proverbs-yoji.intro_tr: 四字熟語[よじじゅくご] are fixed idioms consisting of four kanji characters, typically derived from Chinese classics or historical narratives; they carry deep meaning or wisdom on their own. ことわざ (proverbs), on the other hand, are short words of wisdom passed down from generation to generation among people, usually structured as a single sentence. Both are frequently used in daily conversation, written texts, and news; not knowing them can make understanding the text difficult. Although this topic will be covered at a more advanced level at N2 proficiency, the aim here is to recognize the most common and basic examples, notice structural patterns, and see how they are used in everyday sentences. These expressions are generally memorized as they are; trying to break them down piece by piece is often misleading.

keigo-business.title_tr: Business Japanese Patterns (敬語[けいご] Practice) — Office, Telephone, Email and Meeting Language
keigo-business.intro_tr: Business Japanese (ビジネス日本語[びじねすにほんご]), which combines the elements of 尊敬語[そんけいご] (respectful language), 謙譲語[けんじょうご] (humble language) and 丁寧語[ていねいご] (polite language) in real office environments — telephone, email, meetings and everyday office dialogue — is formed. Here, more than grammar rules, memorizing "which phrase is automatically used in which situation" is important. This page compiles telephone opening-closing, email opening-closing, everyday office expressions, keigo equivalents of business verbs, request-apology patterns and meeting language in tables. Every phrase is repeated constantly in real business life; therefore, rather than knowing its meaning, the goal should be to use it reflexively at the right moment. At the N2 level, recognition and correct completion of these phrases are also frequently required in exams.

keigo-full-system.title_tr: Keigo General System: 3 Axes (尊敬語[そんけいご]・謙譲語[けんじょうご]・丁寧語[ていねいご])
keigo-full-system.intro_tr: Keigo[けいご] (敬語[けいご]), in Japanese is a comprehensive language system that expresses politeness and hierarchical relationships and consists of three fundamental axes: 尊敬語[そんけいご] (sonkeigo - honors and shows respect by elevating the actions of the other party or a third person), 謙譲語[けんじょうご] (kenjougo - shows respect indirectly by lowering the speaker's own actions) and 丁寧語[ていねいご] (teineigo - general, status-neutral polite language like です/ます). The most critical rule of these three axes is this: 尊敬語 is used ONLY for the other party's/third person's actions, 謙譲語 is used ONLY for your own actions or your group's actions — mixing these two (for example, applying sonkeigo to your own actions) is the most common and most serious keigo mistake. Moreover, according to the "uchi-soto[うちそと]" (in-group / out-group) logic, even when referring from someone in your own company/family to someone outside, 謙譲語 is used for that person, because your own group is considered "yourself". This page gathers the definitions of the three axes, formation rules, special verb conjugations, and the most frequently made errors in a single reference table.

ni-kuwaete.intro_tr: 〜に加[くわ]えて, meaning "…in addition to...", is a conjunctive expression frequently used in formal speech and especially in written language (news, articles, business correspondence). It indicates that a new element is being added to an already existing situation, characteristic, or event; in other words, it carries the logic of "not only A, but B in addition to A as well". Generally, the two added elements move in the same direction (both positive or both negative) and are presented in a neutral, objective style. It is semantically close to だけでなく or のみならず, but にくわえて is preferred more in statistics, cause-effect relationships, and formal narratives. It appears at the N2 level; in daily conversation, "〜だけじゃなくて" is preferred more.

to-iu-yori.intro_tr: 〜というより is used to present an alternative expression that is deemed more suitable or more accurate, instead of completely rejecting the initial expression; it corresponds to the meaning in Turkish of "rather than …, much more than …, it would actually be more correct to say …". The first statement is not completely wrong, but the speaker emphasizes that the second expression is closer to reality or to what they feel. It is generally used with the pattern "AというよりB(だ)" and A and B do not need to be from the same grammatical category (noun, adjective, verb); what matters is the semantic comparison. Using it together with the adverb むしろ (on the contrary, even more) is very common and strengthens the emphasis. It is an important comparison pattern frequently encountered at the N2 level in both spoken and written language.

te-aru.title_tr: 〜てある — Prepared State / Result State with Transitive Verbs
te-aru.intro_tr: 〜てある is formed by adding ある to the て-form of a TRANSITIVE (他動詞[たどうし]) verb, and describes a STATE that has EMERGED as a result of someone's conscious action and is STILL CONTINUING. The focus is not on who performed the action, but on the prepared/completed result that the action left behind; therefore, most of the time it is unclear or unimportant who the agent is. In this pattern, the object is usually marked with が instead of を, because now a STATE rather than an action is being described. The difference from 〜ている is that 〜ている can only show an ongoing action or (with intransitive verbs) a natural state, whereas 〜てある necessarily implies someone's intentional preparation/intervention. It should not be confused with 〜ておく: 〜ておく focuses on the PREPARATORY ACTION done beforehand for the future, whereas 〜てある focuses on the current state that is the RESULT of that preparation.

tables.caption_tr: Formation of the 〜てある Form (て形 + ある)
footnotes_tr: 〜てある is used only with TRANSITIVE (他動詞) verbs; this structure cannot be formed with intransitive (自動詞) verbs — instead, 〜ている is used.

ppoi.intro_tr: 〜っぽい, when added to a noun, verb root, or i-adjective root, is a suffix-adjective (接尾語[せつびご]) that conveys the meaning "...-ish, ...resembling, ...inclined, having that quality". Grammatically, it conjugates like a regular い-adjective (っぽい → っぽく、っぽかった、っぽくない, etc.). There are three main areas of use: (1) with nouns, meaning "resembling that thing/conveying that feeling" (子供[こども]っぽい, 嘘[うそ]っぽい), (2) with verb ます-root, meaning "frequently showing that tendency, having that habit" (忘[わす]れっぽい, 怒[おこ]りっぽい), (3) with i-adjective root, particularly in color and texture descriptions (白[しろ]っぽい, 安[やす]っぽい). っぽい often carries a slightly negative, superficial, or "not exactly that way but appears to be" nuance; therefore it should not be confused with みたい, らしい, and 気味[ぎみ]. At N2 level, learners are especially expected to distinguish the meaning differences among these three patterns.

footnotes_tr: When describing colors (白っぽい, 黒っぽい, 青[あお]っぽい, etc.), っぽい is used very commonly and neutrally, carrying no negative connotation.
In patterns describing personality/habits (忘れっぽい, 飽きっぽい, 怒りっぽい), there is generally 'a tendency to frequently or easily be/become that way', and it carries a neutral-to-slightly-negative tone.
In patterns like 嘘っぽい, 安っぽい, there is a strong negative/skeptical nuance; they should be used carefully.

examples.note_tr: っぽく + なる: expression of change meaning 'to become/appear that way'.

set-phrases-formal.title_tr: Official Set Phrases (よろしく / 恐[おそ]れ入[い]りますが...)
set-phrases-formal.intro_tr: In Japanese, there are set phrases that are especially used in business environments, formal correspondence, and situations requiring politeness. These expressions are not individual grammar rules; they function like "ready-made phrases" (定型表現[ていけいひょうげん]) that are commonly accepted by society; their meanings cannot be translated word for word, they should be memorized directly as set phrases. While よろしくお願[ねが]いします is an expression of a request or mutual goodwill, expressions like 恐[おそ]れ入[い]りますが function as "cushion words" (クッション言葉[ことば]) used before making a request without bothering the other person. On this page you will find the most frequently used formal phrases, their usage contexts, and levels of politeness in table format. The goal is to appear natural and fluent in business Japanese and formal correspondence at the N2 level."

hanmen.title_tr: 〜反面[はんめん] (…despite, on the other hand)
hanmen.intro_tr: The 〜反面[はんめん] pattern is used to indicate two opposite or contradictory characteristics about the same topic or person in the same sentence; it is translated to English as "…despite" or "…while on the other hand." The word consists of the kanji 反[はん] (opposite/contrary) and 面[めん] (direction, side), literally meaning "opposite side" — it is used to show the flip side of an issue. Generally a positive aspect is compared with a negative one (or vice versa); it is not natural for two entirely positive or two entirely negative characteristics. It is an N2-level conjunction frequently seen in written language, news articles, and formal/semi-formal speech. It is similar in meaning to the pattern 一方[いっぽう]で, but 反面 carries a more pronounced emphasis of contrast/opposition.

beku.title_tr: 〜べく / 〜べからず (…in order to; prohibition, literary)
beku.intro_tr: 〜べく and 〜べからず are two derivatives of the auxiliary verb 「べし」from classical Japanese (文語[ぶんご]) that still survive in modern written language and on official signs. 〜べく is used as the adverbial form (連用形[れんようけい]) of the verb and expresses a conscious intention meaning '…in order to, …for the purpose of'; it is a more literary/formal equivalent of modern 〜ために. 〜べからず, on the other hand, is the form where the classical negative suffix 「ず」is added to 「べし」, and it conveys a strict, firm prohibition meaning '…must not, …is forbidden'; it typically appears on official warning signs and in proverbs. Both structures are directly attached to the dictionary form (終止形[しゅうしけい]) of the verb; only the verb する takes the classical form すべく/すべからず. These structures are not used in everyday conversation; they appear in formal writing, literature, signs, and idioms.

tables.caption_tr: Attachment Rules (接続[せつぞく])

footnotes_tr: Both structures are directly attached to the dictionary form (終止形[しゅうしけい]) of the verb; the ます-stem or て-form are not used.
The classical rule for the verb する is based on the 為[す] root; therefore すべく/すべからず is considered the more 'correct' classical form, but するべく/するべからず also appears frequently in modern texts.

mono-nara.intro_tr: 「〜ものなら」At the JLPT N2 level, it is an emotionally charged pattern used in two fundamentally different but interrelated meanings. When used with the potential form (可能形[かのうけい]) of the verb, it expresses a challenge as in "if you can do it, go ahead" or an impossible wish as in "I wish I could do it." When used with the volitional form (意向形[いこうけい], 〜よう/〜おう) of the verb, it carries a serious warning in the sense of "if I/you dare to do something this risky/dangerous, a bad consequence will result." This structure is commonly seen in conversational language and narratives; unlike neutral conditional structures 〜たら/〜ば/〜と, it carries strong emotion (challenge, threat, regret, longing). It is not used with negative verb roots and almost always leads to a serious/negative conclusion.

tokoro-wo.intro_tr: The 〜ところを pattern is a formal pattern used for the purpose of apologizing or thanking because we disturb the person in front of us or take their time, while being aware of the situation/state they are currently in (being busy, resting, sleeping, etc.). It usually begins with a prefix お or ご politeness like お忙[いそが]しいところを, お休[やす]みのところを, and is followed by expressions such as すみません, 申[もう]し訳[わけ]ございません, ありがとうございます. This pattern frequently appears in business Japanese, formal correspondence, telephone conversations, and conversation openings. The fundamental difference from other 〜ところ patterns is that instead of emphasizing the "moment" when an action takes place, it expresses politeness by emphasizing the "state/condition" that the person is in. It is an important pattern that needs to be learned at the N2 level, especially in the context of keigo (respectful language).

おいそがしいところを
な形容詞 + な/の + ところを
お元気[げんき]なところを
動詞（ている形）+ ところを

名詞 + の + ところを
食事中[しょくじちゅう]のところを
しょくじちゅうのところを
footnotes_tr: The pattern almost always begins with an adjective/noun that takes a お or ご politeness prefix; this is important for maintaining the level of formality.
〜ところを attaches to the main verb of the sentence (すみません, ありがとうございます, etc.) and conveys the meaning of 'for disturbing you/taking your time while you are in this state'.

gachi.intro_tr: 〜がち is a pattern that is attached to the ます-stem of a verb or to a noun and conveys the meaning of "showing a tendency for something to frequently happen that way", "generally having a tendency towards…" It generally describes an undesired, negative, or unexpected situation that occurs repeatedly (illness, lateness, forgetfulness, bad weather, etc.). Grammatically, がち behaves like a な-adjective; it qualifies nouns ({がちな + noun}), becomes a predicate ({がちだ/です}), and can take past/negative conjugations. It carries the speaker's subjective emphasis that "this tends to happen frequently, it's a noticeable tendency" — not just statistical frequency, but has the nuance of "deviation from what should/is desired to happen". At N2 level, it is frequently encountered in both everyday conversation and written language.

nai-mademo.intro_tr: 〜ないまでも, which means "...even if not at least...", is an advanced (N1) pattern generally used in written language. It indicates that something did not reach its highest/ideal level, but that a lower, acceptable level at least was or is expected to be realized. It is very similar to the Turkish structures "...-mesek bile", "...even if not at least...". Generally, in the second half of the sentence, it is used together with expressions like せめて (at least), 少[すく]なくとも (at least), ある程度[ていど] (to a certain extent). It is rare in spoken language, and appears frequently in formal speech and written texts.

nagara-ni.title_tr: 〜ながらに (in a state of, from birth)
nagara-ni.intro_tr: 〜ながらに, which expresses the continuation of a state, condition, or characteristic indicated by a noun (or certain verb roots), and that something occurs "within that state"; it is a highly literary structure of N1 level, generally used in written language and fixed (idiomatic) expressions. Unlike the well-known simultaneity/contrast conjunction 〜ながら in daily conversation, 〜ながらに cannot be freely attached to every noun; it appears in a limited number of fixed expressions such as 生[う]まれながらに (from birth), 涙[なみだ]ながらに (with tears), 昔[むかし]ながらの (as in the old days). It has three main uses in meaning: (1) to indicate a state that has continued from birth/the beginning, (2) to describe the physical/emotional state at that moment, (3) to create an unexpected contrast ("despite being..."). The 〜ながらにして variant emphasizes the meaning "without moving from one's place/condition", while 〜ながらの comes before a noun and functions as an adjective. This structure is a closed group of expressions that frequently appears in advanced reading texts and literary/formal narratives, and needs to be memorized.

to-aimatte.intro_tr: 〜と相[あい]まって is a fairly formal and written-language-specific N1 pattern that describes how two or more factors (elements) come together and strengthen each other to produce a particular result. The word "相[あい]まって" is the te-form of the verb "相[あい]まる" (to mix together, to combine) and the structure "AとBが相まって" means "when A and B combine / when they complement each other" in Turkish. It generally appears in newspaper articles, academic texts, official reports, and literary narratives; it is almost never used in everyday conversation. Although the result clause usually conveys a neutral or positive situation, depending on the context, it can also be used for negative results. This pattern attaches directly to nouns (N); it is not added to adjectives or verbs.

yue-ni.intro_tr: 〜ゆえに and 〜がゆえに are very formal and literary reason-result patterns that mean '...because of, ...because it is.' In fact, it is the inflected form of the 故[ゆえ] 'reason, cause' noun that comes from classical Japanese (文語), and it is hardly used in spoken language today; it appears in written literature, official documents, legal texts, academic writings, and news language. Compared to から or ので, it has a much heavier, more serious, and distant style; it is generally preferred when explaining the reason for a negative or serious result (pain, loss, difficulty). Adding が (がゆえに) does not change the meaning, only adds a more literary/emphatic tone and is especially common after adjectives and verbs. The 〜ゆえの form, on the other hand, directly qualifies a noun and gives the meaning '...resulting from, ...caused by.'

ni-suginai.title_tr: 〜にすぎない (is nothing but..., is merely..., is no more than...)
ni-suginai.intro_tr: 〜にすぎない emphasizes that something is much less significant, smaller, or more limited than one might think, expect, or what should be the case — an advanced (N1) grammar pattern. It is typically translated into English as 'is nothing but...', 'merely...', 'is only...', or 'is no more than...'. It is used in contexts where the speaker belittles, minimizes, or finds something to be inadequate or insignificant, contrary to expectations; it is not a neutral limitation but rather a diminishing-disparaging tone. It is attached to the 普通形 (plain/standard form) of nouns, verbs, い-adjectives, and な-adjectives, and is often reinforced with emphasizing words like 単に, ただ, ほんの, たかが. In written and formal texts, the conjunctive (renyōkei) form 〜に過ぎず is also frequently encountered.

sura.intro_tr: 〜すら, meaning "…even", is a highly literary and formal pattern; it is rarely used in spoken language, appearing more in written language, formal address, and emphatic expressions. Functionally, it is the same as さえ: it presents a noun or situation as "the most extreme, the minimum example" to convey the message "if even this simple/small thing is the case, imagine the rest." It is most often used with negative predicates (すら〜ない) and carries a sense of surprise, disappointment, or emphasis. すら has a more rigid/classical tone than さえ; in everyday conversation, さえ or でも is preferred. This page provides the structure of すら, its usage contexts, and a table comparing it with similar particles (さえ, でも, だに).

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure: 〜すら
rows: O bile — çıplak isim + すら, en yalın kullanım.
Biraz daha yazılı/nazik ton; ですら, すら'ya göre az daha yumuşak ve açıklayıcı.
に edatının işaret ettiği hedef/yer anlamı korunur, üzerine すら vurgusu eklenir.
Klasik/edebî metinlerde görülür; modern Japoncada nadir, genelde すら doğrudan isme eklenir.
En sık görülen kalıp: 'bile' + olumsuzluk, aşırı vurgu için kullanılır.
footnotes_tr: すら always presents an 'extreme/minimum example'; the rest of the sentence implies that more 'normal/easy' situations also apply from this example.

koto-naku.intro_tr: 〜ことなく is an N1-level pattern used in written language and formal speech that expresses either that an action did not occur even once or that a process continues without interruption. It is directly attached to the dictionary (basic/辞書形) form of the verb and means "never...", "without...", "without failing to...". It is semantically very similar to the patterns 〜ずに and 〜ないで, but it is more literary and formal; it is rarely used in everyday conversation and appears more often in written texts, news, literature, and formal speech. It is often used together with adverbs like 一度も, 何一つ, 終始, 常に to strengthen the emphasis of "not even once / never". It does not combine with the negative (ない) form of the verb — it only attaches to the affirmative dictionary form; in this way it is also structurally different from ずに/ないで.

It is used in written language and formal speech; in everyday conversation, 〜ないで/〜ずに is preferred.

taru-mono.intro_tr: 〜たるもの is a very formal and literary pattern that expresses a moral expectation or responsibility based on a person's status, role, or position (teacher, leader, parent, doctor, etc.), meaning "a person in this position should behave like this/should be like this." Its structure is simple: a noun + たるもの (or たる者[もの]は), followed usually by necessity expressions like 〜べきだ, 〜なければならない. たる is the attributive form (連体形[れんたいけい]) of the auxiliary verb たり, which indicates definiteness/definition (だんてい) in classical Japanese, and has a root close to modern である; therefore it is rarely used in everyday conversation and appears more often in written texts, speeches, newspaper editorials, and formal speeches. Although encountered at N1 level, the pattern is actually fixed and easy to memorize: "status + たるもの + necessity expression".

wo-mono-tomo-sezu.intro_tr: 〜をものともせず is a very formal and literary N1 pattern that describes accomplishing something without minding or being bothered by a difficulty, obstacle, danger, or negative situation, as if defying it. It means 'without minding, disregarding, braving' and is generally used in biographies, news articles, and heroic stories to describe how a person achieves their goal with determination despite hardships. Structurally, it is only constructed with nouns and is a frozen expression that does not conjugate. It is almost never used in spoken language; the main clause generally contains a deliberate and positive/successful action.

This pattern is a frozen expression from the old structure 'ものとも+せず (negation of せぬ)'; it does not conjugate like a modern verb.

made-mo-nai.title_tr: 〜までもない / 〜までのことだ (no need to …)
made-mo-nai.intro_tr: 〜までもない, an N1-level formal/written-language-style pattern that emphasizes an action is unnecessary — because the result is already quite clear, simple, or trivial — and means "no need to …, no need to …" It is directly attached to the dictionary (present) form of the verb; it most frequently appears in fossilized expressions like 言[い]うまでもない (no need to even say). 〜までのことだ, though appearing similar, carries a different function: usually appearing at the end of a conditional sentence, it adds a tone of determination or indifference, saying "if not/if so, I'll only do X, it's that simple." This page clarifies the fundamental semantic difference between the two patterns and their attachment rules side by side. Additionally, comparison with the adverbial form 〜までもなく and other N1 patterns of similar meaning (〜べくもない, 〜に足りない) is also provided.

to-itte-mo-kagon-dewanai.title_tr: 〜と言[い]っても過言[かごん]ではない — "…it is not an exaggeration to say"
to-itte-mo-kagon-dewanai.intro_tr: 〜と言[い]っても過言[かごん]ではない, corresponding to the Turkish "…it is not an exaggeration to say / …it would be apt to say" phrase, is an N1 level formal and written-emphasis pattern. The speaker expresses what might normally seem like a very strong/exaggerated claim, and then emphasizes that this claim actually reflects reality and should not be considered an exaggeration. It is generally used to express praise, admiration, or a very strong observation, and appears in written language rather than spoken language, in presentations, articles, and formal narratives. Structurally it is formed by adding (と) 言[い]っても過言[かごん]ではない to the quoted form of a sentence; the word 過言[かごん] means "exaggerated speech, excessive speech", and ではない is its negation (that is, "it is not exaggerated speech").

footnotes_tr: With nouns and な-adjectives, the である form can also be used: 〜であると言っても過言ではない (more formal).
Verbs are generally used with past tense (〜た) because they evaluate a result/completed state; however, simple present tense (〜る) is also possible.

ni-katakunai.title_tr: 〜に難くない (not difficult to ..., can easily ...)
ni-katakunai.intro_tr: 〜に難[かた]くない, when translated directly means '…-ing is not difficult', but it actually carries the meaning of '…-ing is easy, …-ing is not difficult at all' through double negation, and it is a very formal (書[か]き言葉[ことば]) N1 pattern. It is only used with a limited number of 'mental comprehension' verbs/nouns such as 想像[そうぞう]する (imagine), 理解[りかい]する (understand), 察[さっ]する (perceive), 推測[すいそく]する (guess) — it is almost never used in everyday conversation. Generally, with the pattern '〜は/が + [noun]に難くない', it is used in newspapers, articles, and formal texts to indicate that someone's emotion, thoughts, or the background of an event can 'easily be guessed/understood'. In polite/formal writing, the negative form is '〜に難くありません', and '〜に難くないです' is not much preferred.

footnotes_tr: '難くない' is literally the negation of the adjective '難[かた]い (difficult)'; therefore, the meaning is 'it is easy/not difficult', it does NOT carry a negative meaning.

to-omoikiya.intro_tr: 〜と思[おも]いきや, which means "...I thought, but..." or "...I assumed, but in an unexpected way..." is a pattern unique to N1 level literary/written language. It is used when the speaker's previously established prediction or expectation is met with the exact opposite or a completely unexpected result; it carries strong emphasis on surprise and contrast. Etymologically, it derives from 「思[おも]うや」, a prediction/interrogative suffix in classical Japanese, which is why it is used in both written texts (news, essays, literature) and spoken language to add dramatic/ironic emphasis. Compared to expressions like のに or ところが, it is more literary and the tone of surprise is more prominent. Generally, the first half of the sentence expresses a "supposition/assumption", and the second half expresses the "actual" result that is the exact opposite of this supposition.

nari-ni.title_tr: 〜なりに / 〜なりの — Unique to …-, in one's own way
nari-ni.intro_tr: 〜なりに and 〜なりの is a pattern that expresses how a person, group, or object acts, thinks, or achieves a result in a manner befitting the limited ability, knowledge, position, or characteristic they possess. It carries the nuance of "Although not perfect, they did their best according to their own level/situation" and is usually translated into English as "in one's own way," "personally," "unique to …-". While なりに functions as a verb or adjective (like an adverb), なりの modifies the noun that follows it (like an adjective). In particular, the pattern それなりに/それなりの is a semi-conventionalized expression frequently used in everyday language meaning "fairly, to an acceptable degree, adequate for that." This structure, encountered at N1 level, appears frequently in both written and spoken language and is used to express humility or relative evaluation.

ni-hokanaranai.title_tr: 〜にほかならない (nothing but …; not other than …)
ni-hokanaranai.intro_tr: 〜にほかならない is an N1 pattern used to define a name or situation in a definite and strong manner, which is quite formal and specific to written language. Etymologically, it comes from the combination of "他[ほか] (other) + ならない (cannot be)"; that is, it means "this cannot be anything other than X / it is definitely X". Most frequently, it is used in the pattern 「〜のは、〜からにほかならない」 ("the reason for this is solely …") to emphasize the true cause of an event or situation. It is almost never used in spoken language; it is frequently found in articles, essays, formal speeches, and written analysis texts. In terms of meaning, it carries the opposite emphasis to 〜にすぎない (only/merely …, disparaging): にほかならない is a strong affirmation, while にすぎない is a limiting/diminishing affirmation.

koso-sure.title_tr: 〜こそすれ (…I will do it, but never…-not)
koso-sure.intro_tr: 〜こそすれ, used in literary and formal written language, is an advanced N1-level pattern. The emphasis particle こそ combines with すれ, the classical 'occurred/certain' conditional form of the verb する, creating the meaning 'it is definitely A'; the following clause must contain a negative expression (〜ない, 〜はしない, 〜まい, etc.). The structure thus creates a sharp contrast like 'A definitely happens/is true, but B definitely does not happen'—it is generally translated into Turkish as '…-I do/will, but never…-not' or '…at most X happens, never Y happens'. It is usually attached to Sino-Japanese nouns that conjugate with する, such as 感謝[かんしゃ], 尊敬[そんけい], 同情[どうじょう], or to the ます-stem of verbs; it is almost never used in daily conversation, but appears in articles, speeches, and formal writings.

beku-mo-nai.intro_tr: 「〜べくもない」is a quite literary and formal N1 pattern formed by the combination of 「〜べく」, which is the adverbial form of the classical auxiliary verb 「べし」, and 「もない」which expresses negation. Its meaning is "...ing is absolutely impossible", "it is futile to hope/wait/imagine ...-ing"; in other words, it does not merely mean "cannot be done" but emphasizes that the possibility of that thing occurring was not even in question from the beginning. It is attached directly to the dictionary (jisho) form of a verb; however, the verb する transforms to its classical root 「す」and takes the form 「すべくもない」(in modern usage 「するべくもない」is also seen). It generally appears in written/literary texts, news, and formal speeches that describe how unreachable or unexpected a situation is, typically used together with verbs like 望[のぞ]む・知[し]る・比[くら]べる・想像[そうぞう]する. It is almost never used in everyday spoken language; instead, more natural patterns like 「〜わけがない」or 「〜はずがない」are preferred.

べくもない is always attached to the AFFIRMATIVE dictionary (jisho) form of a verb; it is not attached to negative forms or inflected forms like the ta-form.

ba-koso.intro_tr: 〜ばこそ is a literary/written language pattern used to express a reason in an extremely strong, certain, and emphatic way; it carries the meaning "precisely because …, for no other reason whatsoever" and is almost always used together with a positive, commendable result. It is very close in meaning to からこそ, but ばこそ is more formal, literary, and has a somewhat old/classical flavor; it rarely appears in everyday conversation, but much more often in written texts, speeches, or emotional/serious narratives. The structure is formed by adding the こそ particle to the ば (conditional) form of verbs and adjectives, and the sentence typically ends with 〜のだ/〜のです or ends directly. It is a pattern inherited from classical Japanese that frequently appears on N1 level exams.

ni-hikikae.title_tr: 〜にひきかえ (as opposed to..., in contrast to...)
ni-hikikae.intro_tr: 〜にひきかえ is an N1 level expression preferred in written language and formal speech for presenting two situations/people/phenomena as COMPLETE OPPOSITES of each other. It means "as opposed to..., in contrast to..., the opposite of..." in English, and generally carries a subjective contrast reflecting the speaker's personal evaluation (one good, the other bad). Since it derives from the verb 引[ひ]き替[か]える (to exchange), it creates a sharp sense of contrast as if two things were "exchanged" — in this way it differs from に対[たい]して, which expresses neutral contrast. It is also frequently used as a conjunction at the beginning of a sentence in the form それにひきかえ. In spoken language, のに, 反面[はんめん], 一方[いっぽう]で are more commonly preferred; 〜にひきかえ, on the other hand, is seen in written/literary contexts such as articles, essays, and formal speech.

wo-yoginakusareru.title_tr: 〜を余儀[よぎ]なくされる — To be forced to..., To be compelled to do...
wo-yoginakusareru.intro_tr: 〜を余儀[よぎ]なくされる, which means "forcing someone to do something without leaving any other option," is a very formal, specialized N1 pattern used in written language (news, business correspondence, academic texts). Structurally, it is constructed as a noun (usually the nominal form of a スル verb: 中止, 変更, 閉鎖, etc.) + を余儀なくされる, and the subject, against their own will and due to an external condition, is forced to do that action — in other words, it carries a passive meaning. The corresponding active (causative) form is 〜を余儀[よぎ]なくさせる: here the subject is the cause that forces something/someone into that situation. This pattern is almost never used in spoken language; in everyday language, the same meaning is expressed through phrases like 〜ざるを得[え]ない or 〜しかない. Because it carries the nuance of "compelled by circumstances beyond one's control," it is not used for actions that a person does of their own choice.

Instead of a noun, the nominal form of a スル verb is used: 中止[ちゅうし]する → 中止[ちゅうし]を余儀[よぎ]なくされる.

examples.translation_tr: Due to management difficulties, that factory was forced to close.
examples.note_tr: A formal pattern very frequently seen in news/business language.

examples.target: 大雪[おおゆき]が交通[こうつう]の混乱[こんらん]を余儀[よぎ]なくさせた。

examples.translation_tr: Heavy snow made chaos in transportation unavoidable (forced transportation into chaos).
examples.note_tr: Here the causative 〜させる form is used: the subject (大雪[おおゆき]) forces something else (交通[こうつう]の混乱[こんらん]).

examples.target: その会社[かいしゃ]は資金[しきん]不足[ぶそく]で事業[じぎょう]の縮小[しゅくしょう]を余儀[よぎ]なくされた。

examples.target: 地震[じしん]の影響[えいきょう]で、多く[おおく]の住民[じゅうみん]が避難[ひなん]を余儀[よぎ]なくされた。

examples.translation_tr: Due to the earthquake, many residents were forced to evacuate.

examples.target: 政府[せいふ]の政策[せいさく]変更[へんこう]は、国民[こくみん]に生活[せいかつ]様式[ようしき]の変化[へんか]を余儀[よぎ]なくさせた。
examples.reading: せいふのせいさくへんこうは、こくみんにせいかつようしきのへんかをよぎなくさせた。
examples.translation_tr: The government's policy change forced the people to change their lifestyle.
examples.note_tr: Two-sided structure: 政府[せいふ]の政策[せいさく]変更[へんこう]は (subject, the one forcing) + 国民[こくみん]に (to whom) + 変化[へんか]を余儀[よぎ]なくさせた (forced to what).

wo-motte.intro_tr: 〜をもって is a versatile N1 pattern used in formal speech and written language, and can be considered the formal/literary equivalent of the particle で in everyday language. Basically it has three main meanings: to indicate an instrument/means ("...with, ...by way of"), to indicate a time limit or a starting/ending point ("...as of"), and in some fixed expressions to carry an emphatic meaning like "in person, with all sincerity." Structurally it always comes after a noun: N + をもって. When wanting to increase formality even more, the form 〜をもちまして is used; this form is frequently heard especially in ceremony opening/closing speeches and in formal announcements. It is almost never used in everyday conversation; it appears in business correspondence, formal announcements, ceremonies, and literary/classical-sounding texts.

wo-fumaete.title_tr: 〜を踏まえて — Taking …-i into Consideration, Taking into Account
wo-fumaete.intro_tr: 〜を踏[ふ]まえて comes from the verb 踏[ふ]まえる, which literally means "stepping on/placing one's foot firmly"; in a figurative sense, it expresses "carrying out the next action by taking information, facts, or opinions as a basis, keeping them in mind." Usually a previous research result, data, opinion, or situation is mentioned first, and then an evaluation, decision, or explanation based on this foundation follows. It is an extremely formal expression; it is frequently encountered in business reports, academic writings, news articles, and meetings, and is almost never used in daily conversation. It is always constructed as a noun (or nominalized phrase) + を踏まえて and is not attached directly to verbs. Although it is close in meaning to 〜に基[もと]づいて (based on …) and 〜を考慮[こうりょ]して (taking … into account), there are nuance differences.

to-iu-mono-da.title_tr: 〜というものだ / 〜というものではない (That's What It Is / That's Not The Case)
to-iu-mono-da.intro_tr: 〜というものだ is used to express the essence of something, its true nature, or a definitive judgment such as 'that's exactly what it is'; the speaker presents a situation as a general truth or natural consequence. 〜というものではない (or 〜というものでもない), conversely, does the opposite—it rejects a common assumption or generalization, meaning 'it's not always that way / it's not that simple.' These two patterns are frequently encountered at N1 level, appearing in written and formal spoken language, and express personal evaluation/commentary. In particular, the pattern 〜ば/たら/さえ + いい + というものではない is very common and means 'merely ...is not sufficient.' In everyday conversation, it is used more often when stating opinions, giving advice, or correcting a generalization.

to-bakari-ni.intro_tr: 〜とばかりに expresses a thought or attitude that someone does not state explicitly in words but makes clear through their behavior; it is an advanced pattern used primarily in written/literary language. It corresponds to the Turkish expressions "…-cesine", "…dercesine", "as if …-ed". It typically follows a short, quotation-like phrase, exclamation, or imperative expression, and describes this "unspoken word" together with an action. It is rare in everyday conversation; it appears frequently in novels, newspaper articles, and narrative texts. It also has formulaic uses such as ここぞとばかりに, and these should be memorized as separate idioms.

to-ittara-nai.title_tr: 〜ったらない / 〜といったらない (extremely …, beyond description …)
to-ittara-nai.intro_tr: 〜ったらない / 〜といったらない, a pattern used to emphasize that an adjective or condition is extraordinarily indescribable, is a N1-level expression close to spoken language. The origin of the word lies in the idea of 〜と言[い]ったらない (=even if you say so, it still falls short) that is, it carries the meaning of "too much/extreme to express in words." It is generally used with strong personal emotions — complaint, admiration, surprise, anger — and can come with both positive and negative adjectives. It appears much more in everyday conversation than in formal writing, especially in emotionally emphasized expressions. It is semantically close to other "extremely" expressions like 〜極[きわ]まりない and 〜かぎりだ, but differs in register and tone.

no-itari.title_tr: 〜の至り[いたり] / 〜の極み[きわみ] — "...The Peak of, Extremely..."
no-itari.intro_tr: 〜の至り[いたり] and 〜の極み[きわみ] are highly formal and literary (書[か]き言葉[ことば]) N1 patterns that express reaching "the extreme point, the peak of" a situation or feeling; they are almost never used in everyday conversation. Both are connected in the form "noun + の + 至り/極み" and are generally limited to abstract nouns of Chinese origin (漢語[かんご]), appearing with only a few fixed phrases. 〜の至り is used more in formal speech and expressions of gratitude/apology to humbly emphasize the speaker's own feelings (honor, shame, gratitude, etc.), while 〜の極み is used with a wider range of nouns (fatigue, luxury, regret, sorrow, etc.) to describe "the extreme state that something can reach" in both speech and writing (somewhat more flexible). Both end as a predicate on their own with "〜です/である" and generally express positive or intensely negative feelings in an exaggerated manner. In meaning, they are closely related to 〜極まる/〜極まりない; in fact の極み is derived from the same root (極める).

tables.caption_tr: 〜の至り[いたり] and 〜の極み[きわみ] General Comparison
rows: Soyut isim (漢語[かんご]) + の + 至り
Resmî konuşma, teşekkür/özür/tebrik ifadeleri; genellikle konuşmacının kendi duygusu hakkında alçakgönüllülükle
Genellikle olumlu (onur, minnet) veya kendini küçültme (utanç, mahcubiyet)
Soyut isim (漢語[かんご]) + の + 極み
Yazılı dil, edebiyat, resmî anlatım; hem olumlu hem olumsuz durumları betimlemek için
Olumlu veya olumsuz olabilir (lüks, yorgunluk, pişmanlık, keder)
〜極まる[きわまる]/〜極まりない[きわまりない]
な-sıfat kökü + 極まる/極まりない
Konuşmada ve yazıda daha yaygın; sıfatlarla kullanılır (isim değil)
Genellikle olumsuz/eleştirel (失礼[しつれい]極まりない gibi)
footnotes_tr: Although 〜極まる is based on the same root (極[きわ]める), it is a different pattern: it takes な-adjective stems rather than nouns and is a separate grammar topic (〜極まる/〜極まりない).

gotoki-gotoku.intro_tr: 〜ごとし(如し) is an auxiliary verb that comes from classical Japanese and is used in modern Japanese especially in written, literary or formal style; in meaning it is almost the same as 〜のようだ (…is like). According to classical grammar conjugation, it has three basic forms: 〜ごとし ending at the end of a sentence, 〜ごとく in adverbial function (=〜のように) and 〜ごとき in adjective function before nouns (=〜のような). Besides this, 〜ごとき has a special usage that is alive in everyday language: when attached directly to a noun (without の) it expresses contempt or self-deprecation in the meaning of "…insignificant/worthless person/thing" (e.g. 私ごとき, 子供ごとき). This structure is encountered at N1 level and is a pattern seen nowadays mostly in literature, ceremonial speeches, proverbs and official/classical quotations.

wa-sate-oki.intro_tr: 〜はさておき is a pattern used to temporarily set aside a topic, person, or matter and proceed to the subject one intends to explain, meaning "setting aside …" or "let's move on from the topic of … for now". It is generally used during conversation to bypass a matter that will not be discussed at that moment or is considered unimportant before drawing attention to the main important point. In meaning, it is very similar to 〜は別[べつ]として, but 〜はさておき is more natural and has a tone that frequently appears in spoken language. Its idiomatic usages like それはさておき and 冗談[じょうだん]はさておき frequently appear in daily conversation and business settings. Although it is evaluated at N1 level, thanks to these fixed expressions, it can be heard in daily conversation from early levels onwards.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure and Usage Forms
rows: 仕事[しごと]はさておき
冗談[じょうだん]はさておいて
Şakayı bir yana bırakırsak (aynı anlam, biraz daha konuşma dili)
それ/その話 + はさておき
Onu bir yana bırakalım / Sadede gelelim
疑問詞 + か + はさておき
誰[だれ]が悪[わる]いかはさておき
İsim + かどうか + はさておき
本当[ほんとう]かどうかはさておき
footnotes_tr: はさておき generally marks a change of topic by being separated with a comma in the sentence.
In spoken language, it can also be used in the shorter form さておき, but the form with は is the standard.

nashi-ni-wa.title_tr: 〜なしに(は) / 〜なくして(は) — "...Cannot Be Done Without"
nashi-ni-wa.intro_tr: 〜なしに(は) and 〜なくして(は), meaning "...without, ...cannot happen / is not possible," is a very formal and literary (書き言葉[かきことば]) N1 grammar pattern. It emphasizes that for something to occur, another thing is absolutely necessary, that is, without it the result is impossible. While 〜なしに attaches directly to nouns, 〜なくして is generally used with abstract and positive concepts (愛[あい], 努力[どりょく], 協力[きょうりょく], etc.) and は can be added to the end to further strengthen the meaning. Both patterns typically end in a predicate that expresses negation or impossibility (〜ない, 〜得[え]ない, 〜できない) at the end of the sentence. In everyday conversation, these patterns are replaced by much simpler expressions like 〜なしでは or 〜がなければ.

ni-shite.intro_tr: 〜にして is a multifunctional pattern encountered at N1 level, frequently seen in literary and formal expressions. When attached to nouns or numerical/temporal expressions, it can carry four different meanings: (1) emphasizing a specific stage or moment ('...at, ...while'), (2) expressing contrast/admiration by unexpectedly emphasizing 'even' ('...despite being, ...even'), (3) indicating that the same subject carries two qualities simultaneously ('both...and...'), (4) emphasizing change that occurs in a very short period of time ('suddenly, in an instant'). It is rarely used in daily conversation; it generally appears in written language, news articles, biographical narratives, and literary style. On this page, we examine all four meanings with structures and examples, comparing them with similar expressions.

tari-tomo.intro_tr: 〜たりとも, meaning "not even a single ... (even) ... not/won't," is an extremely formal and literary N1 pattern. It is typically used together with a number or counter (like 一瞬たりとも, 一日たりとも) or with indefinite pronouns like 誰一人・何人 and is always completed with a negative predicate. In terms of meaning, it is similar to 〜さえ and 〜すら, but it has a much stricter, more definitive, and formal tone; it is rarely used in everyday conversation. It frequently appears in oaths, legal texts, formal speeches, news, and literary works. It is preferred to emphasize the message "not a single exception is acceptable."

to-mo-naku.title_tr: 〜ともなく / 〜ともなしに (Without Realizing, Aimlessly)
to-mo-naku.intro_tr: 〜ともなく / 〜ともなしに is a literary (written language-oriented) N1 pattern that expresses an action occurring without a specific purpose, consciousness, or intention, meaning "without realizing," "spontaneously," or "absentmindedly." The most common usage is the structure "V(dictionary form) + ともなく + V" where the same verb is repeated twice: the first verb indicates the action "was not done for a real purpose," while the second verb indicates "yet that action still occurred" (e.g., 見[み]るともなく見[み]る = to look without trying to look). The second common usage combines with question words like 誰[だれ]・どこ・いつ・どこへ to give the meaning "whose/where/when is uncertain" (e.g., どこからともなく = from an uncertain direction). 〜ともなしに is used in nearly the same meaning as 〜ともなく and can generally be substituted for each other; only 〜ともなしに has a somewhat more literary/classical tone. This pattern is rarely used in daily conversation; it appears more in written expression, novels, and literary texts.

to-kitara.title_tr: 〜ときたら / 〜とくると (when it comes to …, complaint)
to-kitara.intro_tr: 〜ときたら and 〜とくると (〜とくれば) are advanced-level (N1) conversational patterns that introduce a topic of conversation by saying "when it comes to …" or "when the matter involves …". 〜ときたら is generally used to express a complaint, resentment, or disappointment about a person, animal, or thing close to the speaker, and carries a strong negative emotion. 〜とくると / 〜とくれば, on the other hand, is more neutral; it indicates a result or association that naturally comes to mind when a topic is mentioned, and does not necessarily have to be negative. Both patterns are used in everyday and intimate conversation, not in formal writing. On this page, the structure of the two patterns, tone differences, and usage restrictions are summarized in tables.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Connection Form

とくると and とくれば are almost synonymous; とくれば has a somewhat more written/literary tone.

n-ga-tame.intro_tr: 〜んがため(に) is composed of the literary form of negation auxiliary verb 'ず/ん' in classical Japanese (actually an old form of む) combined with 'がため' (literary form of 'ため' expressing purpose), making it a very formal and literary way of expressing purpose. In meaning, it is the same as modern 〜ために, but it has a much heavier, more dramatic, and writing-specific tone; it is almost never used in everyday conversation. It is formed by taking the negative (ない) root of a verb and adding 'んがため(に)' in place of 'ない'; the verb する exceptionally takes the form 'せんがため(に)'. It typically appears in novels, poetry, formal speeches, or historical/literary texts with a strong emphasis on determination, resolve, or sacrifice; for this reason, it is important for understanding reading passages correctly at the N1 level.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Table: How 〜んがため(に) is formed
footnotes_tr: Although the normal negative root of the する verb is 'し', when combined with 〜んがため(に), it reverts to the classical 'せ' root: しんがため(✗) → せんがため(に)(◯).
The classical negative root of the ある verb is 'あら'; this is a very rarely seen usage.

to-areba.title_tr: 〜とあれば (If / Since ..., Such Being The Case)
to-areba.intro_tr: 〜とあれば, meaning "if / since... / if such-and-such is the case," is quite a formal N1 grammar pattern that leans toward written language. Rather than a simple condition, it emphasizes that when the indicated situation occurs, the speaker (or subject) will engage in a resolute, extraordinary, or even selfless action no matter what. It is generally used together with expressions carrying the meaning "no matter what," such as どんな〜でも, 何[なに/なん]でも, いくら〜でも. It scarcely appears in conversational language; it appears in formal speech, written texts, and sentences expressing determination or commitment. It should not be confused with 〜とあって: while とあって explains a causal result (it naturally came to be that way), とあれば explains a hypothetical condition and a strong response/decision tied to that condition.

wo-kagiri-ni.intro_tr: 〜を限りに, taking a point in time or an event as a boundary and conveying the meaning 'from now on it will not happen again, I am doing this for the last time and finishing', is a pattern specific to N1 level formal and written language. It appears most frequently in store/business closure announcements, retirement/resignation statements, and expressions of decisively stopping a habit. The basic structure is [time/event noun] + を限りに + [action that will no longer occur] and the sentence usually ends with verbs meaning 'finishing, stopping, ending'. Additionally, in set phrases like 声を限りに and 力の限り(に), it is also used with the meaning 'to one's limit/end, with all one's might'; this is a completely different nuance and should not be confused. It is almost never used in spoken language; it is preferred in formal announcements, newspaper texts, literary narratives, and formal speeches.

The following sentence almost always ends with a verb meaning 'finishing, stopping, ending' (やめる, 引退する, 閉店する, 終わる, etc.).

ikan.title_tr: 〜いかんで / 〜いかんによらず (dependent on ...; regardless of ...)
ikan.intro_tr: The pattern 〜いかんで(は) is based on the word 如何[いかん] (how, in what manner) from classical Japanese and carries the meaning "depending on how something is, according to ...". Conversely, 〜いかんによらず、〜いかんにかかわらず、〜いかんを問わず means "no matter what, regardless of ...". This structure is extremely formal and literary written language expression; it appears frequently in official announcements, news, business correspondence, and legal/institutional texts, but is almost never used in everyday conversation. It connects directly to nouns or with の: N（の）いかんで. Semantically it is close to the pattern 〜次第[しだい]で, but いかん is used with more abstract and formal nouns (such as 結果、内容、事情、天候) and has a higher register.

to-wa-ie.intro_tr: 〜とはいえ is a conjunction frequently used in written language and formal speech that shows the speaker first accepts a fact ("yes, but..."), and then indicates a result that contradicts this fact or is unexpected ("nevertheless..."). It is very similar to the structure "although ...so, nevertheless..." in Turkish. It is similar in meaning to 〜ものの, but とはいえ more emphasizes "I accept... but..." and is generally used to soften the speaker's own evaluation. At the N1 level, it appears mostly in articles, news texts, business correspondence, and formal speech; in daily conversation, simpler patterns like けど or のに take its place. In the second sentence, there is usually a warning, limitation, or negative/neutral evaluation contrary to what is expected.

tables.caption_tr: とはいえ Attachment Forms (According to Word Type)
rows: Fiil (sözlük/olumsuz/geçmiş - 普通形[ふつうけい])
動詞普通形[どうしふつうけい] + とはいえ

te-kara-to-iu-mono.title_tr: 〜てからというもの — "…ever since, always" (N1)
te-kara-to-iu-mono.intro_tr: 〜てからというもの is a literary and formal N1 pattern used to emphasize a major change or situation that emerges after an event and continues WITHOUT INTERRUPTION from that moment onward. It means "…ever since / from that day onward continuously…" and typically carries the speaker's emotional emphasis (surprise, regret, satisfaction, etc.). The difference from simple 〜てから is that it describes not just a time sequence, but a DISTINCT CHANGE or CONTINUITY that has persisted from that moment onward. It generally appears in written language, narratives, and formal speech; it is rarely used in everyday conversation. The second half of the sentence typically ends with expressions indicating continuity such as ずっと, いつも, すっかり, or with a negative/unusual situation.

footnotes_tr: It is attached only to the て-form of verbs; it does not directly connect to nouns or adjectives.
It is generally used with verbs that describe a past event, a one-time and distinct turning point or incident.

footnotes_tr: 〜てからというもの carries the strongest emotional/literary emphasis; in everyday conversation, 〜てから or 〜てからずっと are preferred.
