te-mae.title_tr: 〜てまえ / 〜手前[てまえ] (because of …, being forced to remain consistent in front of others)
te-mae.intro_tr: 〜手前[てまえ] (~temae), originally a noun meaning "front, this side," carries the grammatical meaning "because …, (looking at that situation/statement/relationship) I/we must behave this way/must not behave otherwise." It expresses that because of a statement the speaker previously made, a task they undertook, or a social relationship/position they are in (for example, being "in front of" a superior, one's child, or a customer), they cannot act differently in order to "save face" or appear consistent. The sentence typically ends with a negative obligation/restriction expression like 〜わけにはいかない, 〜なければならない, or 〜できない. It is a formal and somewhat literary N1 pattern, closely related in everyday speech to expressions like だけに or 立場上.

ga-gotoshi.intro_tr: 〜がごとし is a classical Japanese-origin literary comparison pattern meaning "…is like, …as if"; it is the classical/literary equivalent of 〜のようだ in modern language. The word 如[ごと]し is a classical adjectival verb (形容詞型助動詞) that, depending on its conjugation, is used at the end of a sentence (〜がごとし), as an adverb (〜がごとく), or as a noun modifier (〜がごとき). It is generally formed by attaching が to the dictionary form of a verb or by attaching の to nouns; it frequently appears in proverbs, official writing, literature, and discourse. It is closely related to 〜ごとき/〜ごとく, but がごとし is more commonly seen as a complete predicate (sentence-final comparison), particularly with verb phrases. At N1 level, recognition is expected in reading passages, idioms, and four-character compounds (四字熟語); it is rarely used in everyday conversation.

gatera.intro_tr: 〜しな and 〜がてら are patterns frequently encountered in both spoken and written Japanese that express the idea of doing a second thing during or as part of a movement or action. 〜しな is used primarily with a limited number of motion verbs like 'go/return/pass', is quite colloquial, and carries a short '...while, at that very moment' meaning as a suffix. 〜がてら, on the other hand, works on the logic of 'killing two birds with one stone', expressing the meaning of doing a second task as an opportunity along with the main purpose, and can be used with a much broader range of verbs and nouns in both written and spoken language. Both are natural Japanese patterns that appear at N1 level and can be heard in daily life; although they resemble each other, they differ in formality level and scope of use.

tables.caption_tr: 〜しな — Connection form and common uses
footnotes_tr: 〜しな is naturally used only with a specific, limited group of verbs; it cannot be freely added to every verb.
It is generally also seen together with 'に' in the form '〜しなに': 通りしなに。

tables.caption_tr: 〜がてら — Connection form
rows: 出張[しゅっちょう]がてら
footnotes_tr: がてら can be used with both nouns and the ます-stem; this provides a much broader scope of use compared to 〜しな.
Generally, the main purpose is the action that comes before がてら, while the secondary/opportunistic action is in the following clause.

tote.intro_tr: 〜とて is a literary and somewhat old-fashioned phrase; it fundamentally means 〜としても or 〜と言っても and conveys the idea of '...even though, ...even if, ...despite'. It is almost never used in spoken language; it appears in novels, essays, formal writing, and texts with classical nuance. In a second usage, it reinforces strong negation with patterns like だれとて (anyone), 何[なに]一つ[ひとつ]とて (not a single thing). It is expected to be recognized in N1-level reading passages and literary texts; production in daily conversation is not required.

zu-ni-wa-sumanai.title_tr: 〜ずにはすまない / 〜ないではすまない (cannot help but …; there is no way without …)
zu-ni-wa-sumanai.intro_tr: 〜ずにはすまない and its synonym 〜ないではすまない is an N1-level pattern meaning '...cannot complete the matter without doing / ...there is no way without doing / ...I must do it, because otherwise it won't be accepted'. The verb 済[す]む means 'to be completed, to be settled, to be concluded'; when the pattern is used in its negative form, it conveys that 'this matter cannot be concluded without the relevant action being taken'. It typically emphasizes that an action is unavoidable due to social norms, moral responsibility, conscience pressure, or the gravity of the situation—regardless of personal preference, carrying the sense that 'society/conscience compels me to do this'. It frequently appears in written language and formal/serious discourse, but is rare in everyday conversation.

wa-oroka.intro_tr: 〜はおろか is a N1-level pattern unique to formal and written language. With the structure "A はおろか、B も/さえ/すら〜", it emphasizes that A is already something unexpected, difficult, or impossible, and that even B—which is much easier/simpler/smaller than A—does not occur or does not exist. It corresponds to the Turkish pattern "A şöyle dursun, B bile..." and is used almost always with a negative predicate (〜ない, 〜できない, 〜なかった, etc.). In meaning it is very close to 〜どころか, but 〜はおろか carries a more literary, written, and serious tone; in everyday conversation 〜どころか is preferred. In the second part, particles も、さえ, or すら are typically found; は is not used again.

footnotes_tr: In the second part, は is not used again; one of the particles も、さえ、すら comes.
The predicate is almost always negative; affirmative usage is very rare and limited to special contexts.

While もさることながら can be used comfortably in affirmative contexts, はおろか is almost always negative.

wo-kawakiri-ni.title_tr: 〜を皮切りに (starting with …, from … onwards one after another …)
wo-kawakiri-ni.intro_tr: 〜を皮切[かわき]りに is a formal and written pattern that shows an event or time as the starting point and explains how similar events develop and become widespread consecutively after that point (N1 level). The word meaning comes from "first cut, first slice"; it refers to the first piece cut in leather tanning, from which it has expanded to mean "first step, beginning." Its most important feature is that after the pattern there must ALWAYS be discussion of events that develop, expand, or occur consecutively in plural/serial form — it cannot be used for a single event. It typically appears in contexts such as concert tours, work/career beginnings, company expansions, or consecutively occurring negative events (criticism, scandal, disaster). It is almost never used in spoken language; it is frequently seen in newspaper articles, official reports, business correspondence, and literary texts.

ni-tarinai.intro_tr: 〜に足[た]りない is an N1 grammar pattern formed from 足[た]る (to be sufficient, to merit, to be worthy), a classical Japanese verb, with its negative form 足[た]りない, predominantly encountered in written language and formal/literary speech. When added to the dictionary form of a verb, it conveys the meaning "this does not merit..., is insignificant, need not be heeded"; in other words, it expresses a strong value judgment emphasizing the insignificance or insufficiency of something. The most frequently encountered form is 取[と]るに足[た]りない (insignificant, not worth considering), and it is frequently used in set expressions such as 恐[おそ]れるに足[た]りない (does not merit fear), 驚[おどろ]くに足[た]りない (does not merit surprise). Learning it together with its positive counterpart 〜に足[た]る "worthy of..., sufficient, deserving" strengthens its meaning. It is rarely heard in daily conversation; it appears more often in articles, critical essays, and formal evaluation sentences.

made-da.title_tr: 〜まで(のこと)だ — I'll only…, that's all
made-da.intro_tr: 〜まで(のこと)だ is an N1-level pattern with a fairly formal/literary tone that emphasizes the speaker's determination or that there is no special reason behind an action. When used with a future action, it expresses determination or indifference in the sense of "if it doesn't work/if there's no other way, I'll only…, that's all, no big deal." When used with a past action, it diminishes or limits the reason for the simple action performed by saying "I just did…, I had no other purpose/intention." It is generally seen together with conditional expressions (〜ば, 〜たら, 〜なら) or causal conjunctions like 〜から/〜ので. Instead of まで, the more emphatic までのこと can also be used; the meaning is the same, only adding のこと increases the formality somewhat.

iza-shirazu.intro_tr: 〜いざ知[し]らず, meaning "…the status of... is unknown / it may be like that, but…"—a rather literary and formal (N1 level, mostly in written language) expression used to compare and contrast two situations against each other. The structure works on the logic of "If X (perhaps) is so, I don't know, but Y is definitely different/more serious/more certain"; it is usually translated into Turkish as "…one side", "…if so I don't know but", "…beyond". Generally used to put forward a lighter/more excusable situation (X) first, and then present the situation that is meant to be emphasized and is more serious/certain (Y)—that is, it carries a kind of "let alone" / "not to mention" nuance. It is attached to nouns with は or なら; it also appears in question expressions as 〜かはいざ知らず. It is almost never used in spoken language; we encounter it in records such as formal writing, essays, and newspaper articles.

bekarazaru.intro_tr: 〜べからざる is the 連体形[れんたいけい] (attributive form) of べからず, the negative form of the classical auxiliary verb べし; in other words, it functions as an adjective preceding a noun with the meaning "…-(e)mez, …-(il)memesi/olmaması gereken" (must not ..., should not ...). Structure: 動詞[どうし]辞書形[じしょけい] + べからざる + 名詞[めいし]; the only irregularity occurs with the する verb, taking the forms すべからざる (classical) or するべからざる. It is a very literary, formal, and classical (文語[ぶんご]) pattern; in modern Japanese it appears most frequently in set phrases like 許[ゆる]すべからざる行為[こうい] (inexcusable behavior), 欠[か]くべからざる存在[そんざい] (indispensable existence), 侵[おか]すべからざる権利[けんり] (inviolable right). Unlike べからず when used at the end of a sentence, べからざる always directly modifies a noun and cannot end a sentence on its own. At the N1 level, it is an important pattern that must be recognized, especially in formal writing, legal texts, newspaper headlines, and literary narration.

narade-wa.title_tr: 〜ならではの — Unique to …, Only (Found in…) (Rare Quality)
narade-wa.intro_tr: 〜ならではの is a pattern considered literary at N1 level, used to emphasize a positive quality unique to a particular name or person, that can only be found in that person/place/thing and is not encountered anywhere else. It is generally translated as "unique to …", "but only happens in …", or "made possible precisely because of …" and almost always carries an overtone of praise/appreciation. The structure is formally composed of the conditional suffix なら ("if...then") and the particle では ("in.../as if..."), and originates from the classical negative pattern 〜ならでは…ない ("unless N, it is not possible"); in modern usage, this negation is dropped and の is added instead, yielding a positive-laudatory nominal phrase. It most frequently appears as a nominal phrase (N+ならではの+noun) or as a predicate at the end of a sentence (N+ならでは+だ/です); in both cases, it is attached only to nouns (or words functioning as nouns), and is not directly connected to verbs or adjectives.

de-are-de-are.intro_tr: 〜であれ〜であれ is a quite formal and literary N1 pattern that lines up two (or more) different options side by side and conveys the meaning "whichever it may be, the result or judgment does not change." It is formed by the repetition of "あれ", which is the old imperative/conditional form of the copula だ/である, and is generally seen in written language, newspaper articles, formal speeches, or sentences stating rules; it is rarely used in everyday conversation. It corresponds to the Turkish structure "whether … or …", "… or … (either way)." The pattern is generally attached to nouns and na-adjective roots; in the second half, there is an unchanging conclusion, a general rule, advice, or prohibition. In meaning it is nearly identical to 〜にしろ〜にしろ and 〜にせよ〜にせよ, but it carries a more formal and literary style than these.

footnotes_tr: This pattern is not used directly with い-adjectives and verbs; instead 〜であろうと or 〜にしろ/〜にせよ is preferred.
The second part of the sentence generally contains an unchanging judgment, rule, or advice (such as べきだ, 〜なければならない, 〜てはいけない).

nominalization-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Nominalization: こと / の / ところ / 次第 Comparison
nominalization-advanced.intro_tr: In Japanese, to use a verb or clause as a noun, there are several different structures: こと, の, ところ, and 次第. Although all of them perform "nominalization," their meanings and applicable contexts differ considerably from one another. While こと nominalizes an abstract, general, conceptual matter; の nominalizes a concrete, immediately perceived or experienced event (especially mandatory with perception verbs). ところ, meanwhile, is a "moment/point" nominalization that shows at exactly which stage an action stands (about to begin, in progress, just finished). 次第, on the other hand, carries both the meaning of "…-dependent on" (dependency) and "…-as soon as" (instantaneous sequence), and is a more formal structure generally seen in business and written language. This page clarifies which of these four structures should be used in which situation by placing them side by side for comparison.

mo-sarukoto-nagara.title_tr: 〜もさることながら (…aside, …also) — N1 Grammar Guide
mo-sarukoto-nagara.intro_tr: 「〜もさることながら」 is an N1-level expression commonly used in formal and written language that conveys the acknowledgment that something (X) is already important/impressive/positive, while the main emphasis and attention are drawn to a second thing (Y). It is generally translated to Turkish as "X is already so (clear/indisputable), Y is also so/or even more" or "X aside, Y also...". Note: this pattern never belittles or rejects X — on the contrary, it acknowledges the truth/value of X, only emphasizing that Y is also at least as (sometimes even more) striking. It is generally used in positive, laudatory contexts (product, person, work evaluation) and rarely appears in spoken language; it is common in written/formal records such as articles, reviews, formal speeches. It is generally attached to nouns or nominalized verb/adjective phrases and is not used with negative sentences.

nu-zu-negation.title_tr: 〜ぬ / 〜ず — Classical Negation Suffixes and Modern Remnants
nu-zu-negation.intro_tr: 〜ぬ and 〜ず are negation suffixes that have survived from classical Japanese (文語[ぶんご]) to the present day; they are the ancestors of modern 〜ない. 〜ぬ is used as a sentence-ending negative verb suffix (like modern 〜ない) or as an adjective before a noun, and still survives in formal speech, proverbs, literature, and some regional dialects (especially Kansai). 〜ず, on the other hand, is a conjunctive form meaning 〜ないで/〜ずに and carries the meaning 'without, without doing'; it also frequently appears in frozen adverbial patterns like 相変[あいか]わらず and 知[し]らず知[し]らず. Both suffixes are attached to the -a stem of the verb (未然形[みぜんけい]), and today they are fundamental remnant structures that must be recognized to read news articles, formal correspondence, and literary works at the N1 level. This page summarizes formation rules, usage patterns, and the most common frozen expressions in tabular format.

The negation of ある verb is formed with ない directly, not with ぬ/ず; あらぬ/あらず appears only in literary texts.

kanbun-kakikudashi.title_tr: 漢文訓読[かんぶんくんどく] Remnants: In Official Text 〜べく / 〜ざる
kanbun-kakikudashi.intro_tr: 漢文訓読[かんぶんくんどく] (kanbun-kundoku) is a method developed to read classical Chinese texts according to Japanese grammar rules; auxiliary verbs like 〜べし and 〜ず from this tradition have been passed down to modern Japanese. Today, these suffixes, which are almost never used in spoken language, still appear in official correspondence, legal texts, signs, newspaper headlines, and literary style. This page particularly addresses 〜べく (the renyōkei/te-form-like form of classical べし; indicates purpose or necessity) and 〜ざる (the rentaikei/adjective form of the classical negation suffix ず; the literary equivalent of modern 〜ない). These forms are no longer freely attached to every verb; they are generally found frozen in set (idiom) expressions, which is why the most effective way to understand them is to first memorize the classical conjugation table, then memorize the frequently used patterns.

written-vs-spoken.title_tr: Written Language vs Spoken Language: である体 / だ・である/です Comparison
written-vs-spoken.intro_tr: In Japanese, the same meaning is expressed in three different 'copulas' (だ・である・です) depending on the context of use, and a series of word/particle changes associated with it. です・ます体 is used in everyday polite speech and informal written communication; だ体 (普通体) in intimate conversation, everyday and novel dialogues; である体, on the other hand, is used in 'written language' (書[か]き言葉[ことば]) such as newspaper articles, academic papers, encyclopedia entries, and formal reports. The most important characteristic of である体 is that it carries a completely objective and distant tone, avoiding emotional expressions in the first/second person. The key point at the N1 level regarding this topic is not to mix だ/です and である in a text (文体[ぶんたい]の統一[とういつ]) and that abbreviations/words specific to spoken language (てる, じゃない, だから etc.) should not be used in written language. The tables below comprehensively show both inflection differences and changes at the word/conjunction level.

wo-hete.intro_tr: 〜を経て[へて] is a formal N1 pattern that, coming after a noun, expresses reaching a conclusion after passing through a specific process, stage, time period, or place. The pattern is derived from the て-form of the verb 経る[へる] (to pass, to go through) and generally implies a long process, multiple stages, or difficulty. It is used both in concrete place/time transitions (passing through Tokyo) and in abstract processes (going through discussions, exams, experiences). It is rarely seen in spoken language; it frequently appears in news articles, official reports, and written narratives. It is not used at the end of a sentence, but as a connector between two events/stages, and generally the result sentence that follows 経て is the natural/expected outcome of the previous process.

shimatsu-da.intro_tr: 〜しまつだ (始末だ) is used to emphasize the BAD, DISAPPOINTING RESULT reached after a series of negative events or behaviors have been described; it is similar to Turkish expressions like "finally ...it turned out", "the matter ended up ...". It generally also conveys the speaker's surprise, anger, or helplessness — it is not a neutral "result" expression. It is used with the dictionary form of a verb or the progressive form (〜ている) and is most commonly seen together with time/result adverbs like あげくの果てに, とうとう, 結局. It is a very formal/literary N1 pattern, rarely heard in casual speech; it appears in written criticism, complaint narratives, and formal discourse. It can also be used in the form この/その/あの始末だ to give the meaning "that's how it turned out."

ki-keri-tari.title_tr: Classical Past Suffixes: 〜き / 〜けり / 〜たり (For Reading)
ki-keri-tari.intro_tr: These suffixes are classical Japanese (文語[ぶんご]) past tense auxiliary verbs; they are not used in modern spoken language but appear in classical literature, waka[わか]/haiku[はいく] poems, proverbs, religious/legal texts, and some fixed modern expressions (especially in written, literary style). 「き」expresses a past that the speaker directly witnessed/experienced, while 「けり」expresses a past heard or narrated by someone else (especially in narrative contexts with the tone of "once upon a time"). 「たり」, derived from 「て+あり」, describes the completion of an action or a state where its result persists — it is similar to modern 〜ている/〜てある. These three suffixes are learned at N1 level mainly for reading (読解[どっかい]) skill; their production in speech is not expected. Additionally, since the kakari-musubi (係[かか]り結[むす]び) rule can change the form at the end of these suffixes, recognizing this interaction is important when reading classical texts.

nomi-narazu.intro_tr: 〜のみならず, meaning "not only … (but also …)," is a quite formal and literary conjunction. It carries the same basic meaning as だけでなく or ばかりでなく, but is preferred in written language (articles, news, formal speech, academic texts); it is rarely used in everyday conversation. In the second clause, there is usually an emphatic particle such as も, さえ, or まで, reinforcing the meaning of "moreover/even." It attaches to nouns, な-adjectives, い-adjectives, and verbs in different ways; therefore, it is necessary to study the connection patterns well.

wo-yoso-ni.intro_tr: 〜をよそに is a pattern that describes when a person performs an action without heeding others' concerns, warnings, expectations, or opposition, and is frequently found in formal and written language. It is constructed with the structure Noun + をよそに + sentence and is generally used with abstract nouns that express emotions/attitudes such as 心配[しんぱい], 反対[はんたい], 批判[ひはん], 期待[きたい], 不安[ふあん]. The pattern often emphasizes, with a critical or surprised tone, that the person remains indifferent to the emotions and reactions of those around them; therefore, it is not used for the speaker's own feelings. It is frequently encountered at the N1 level in news texts, newspaper headlines, and literary works; it is almost never used in everyday spoken language.

hazumi-hyoushi.title_tr: 〜はずみに / 〜拍子に (at the moment of..., at that instant — due to the effect of a movement/event)
hazumi-hyoushi.intro_tr: 〜はずみに and 〜拍子に[ひょうしに] are advanced-level patterns at the N1 level and mean "at that exact moment, due to the effect of that movement/sound, in an unexpected manner." They express how a physical movement (falling, hitting, standing up, etc.) or a sudden sound (sneezing, noise) occurs at the exact same time as another result, usually negative and dependent on chance. In terms of meaning, it is similar to 〜たとたん (at that moment), but 〜はずみに/拍子に carries the particular nuance of "momentum, coincidence, the impulse given by a sudden movement" and the resulting sentence is almost always an accident, misfortune, or unwanted situation. 〜はずみに comes more from the idea of physical "bouncing/impulse" (弾む[はずむ]), while 〜拍子に comes from the idea of "rhythm/moment harmony" (拍子[ひょうし]); in everyday speech, 拍子に is slightly more common and flexible in usage. This pattern generally appears not in spoken language, but in somewhat more written/literary and factual narrative styles.

ku-shite.intro_tr: 〜くして is a conjunctive structure attached to the ren'you (〜く) form of i-adjectives, specific to written language and literary narration; it can be considered the formal/classical equivalent of the 〜くて (te-form) structure in modern spoken language. It has two main functions: (1) In patterns such as 若[わか]くして, 幼[おさな]くして, it indicates a condition ("...while, ...as, while still...") and generally conveys an unexpected, striking, or prematurely occurring result; (2) In the pattern 〜くして(は)〜ない, when used together with a negative predicate, it carries the meaning "Y is not possible without X, does not occur inevitably." This second usage is directly related to the structures なくして/なしに; because なくして is nothing other than the くして form of the ない adjective (ない → なく + して). 〜くして frequently appears in novels, essays, news texts, formal speech, and literary narration; it is almost never used in everyday conversation and is important for understanding N1 level reading/listening texts.

te-shikarubeki.title_tr: 〜てしかるべき — It is appropriate/natural that …; it is expected to be so (N1)
te-shikarubeki.intro_tr: 〜てしかるべき derives from the word 然[しか]るべき and is a remnant of the combination of the verb 然[しか]り (to be so) and the auxiliary verb べし (necessity) in classical Japanese. It means "it is natural that …, it is appropriate, and it is expected to be so as a matter of logic or justice." It is very similar to べきだ but more literary and formal; it is most commonly used to convey criticism or disappointment by implying that something should normally or justly be a certain way, but in REALITY it is not. It is an N1-level pattern frequently seen in written language, newspaper articles, formal speeches, and discussion texts. When used with the past tense (〜て然るべきだった), it generally carries regret or criticism: "…should have been (but was not)."

mono-ka.intro_tr: 〜ものか (whose casual/shortened form in everyday conversation is 〜もんか) is an N1-level pattern used to express with strong emotional reaction that one will absolutely not do something or that a proposition is never true. In form it resembles a question sentence, but it is actually not a question; on the contrary, it is a strong, rhetorical negation meaning "As if ...will happen! Absolutely never ...!" It is attached directly to the plain (indicative) form of verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives, or nouns, and generally carries a sense of anger, stubbornness, pride, defiance, or firm determination. Unlike patterns like 〜わけがない which express logical/objective impossibility, 〜ものか highlights the speaker's subjective, emotional, and determined attitude. In women's speech and more polite contexts 〜ものですか is preferred, while in masculine/casual speech 〜もんか form is preferred.

de-aru-tai.title_tr: 〜である体 (である Register) — Article and Thesis Writing Language
de-aru-tai.intro_tr: 〜である体 is a conjugation system unique to the most formal written Japanese; it is used in academic articles, newspaper reports, encyclopedia entries, and official reports. It replaces だ (だ体) and です (です体) in spoken language, but unlike です/ます, it does not show politeness to the person in front of you — its purpose is not politeness, but to create an objective and distanced writing style. The dictionary/negative form of verbs and い-adjectives remains unchanged; the most noticeable difference is in noun (名詞[めいし]) and な-adjective (な形容詞[なけいようし]) predicates: だ → である, です → である. If である体 is chosen in a text, it must be used consistently from start to finish and not mixed with です/ます — this is a consistency rule frequently asked at the N1 level. Additionally, である体 is used together with its own formal conjunctions (しかしながら, ゆえに, したがって, etc.) and patterns (〜のである, 〜と考えられる).

denai.title_tr: 〜でなくてなんだろう — "If it's not this... what is it!" (Rhetorical Emphasis Pattern)
denai.intro_tr: 〜でなくてなんだろう is an N1 pattern corresponding to the Turkish rhetorical question "if it's not this... what is it?", and is highly literary and emotional. Although the structure contains negation (でなくて), its meaning is the opposite—a strong AFFIRMATION: the speaker emphasizes that the thing in question cannot be called by any other name, that it is precisely what is being mentioned. It generally appears in sentences starting with demonstrative pronouns like これ/それ, in literary and emotional narratives such as novels, poetry, essays, and news commentary; it is almost never used in everyday conversation. The structure is [Noun]+でなくて+何[なん]だろう(か) and is generally used to summarize a situation described in the previous sentence and say "this is it!"

kagiri-da.intro_tr: 〜かぎりだ (限りだ), a formal and literary N1-level pattern that emphasizes the emotion felt by the speaker at that moment in the sense of "extremely, very much, at the peak of -", is used only with adjectives expressing subjective emotions such as joy, sadness, jealousy, shame, confidence, anxiety; it cannot be used directly with objective facts or about a third person's emotions. It is generally found in written language, formal speeches, thank-you/congratulatory speeches, and literary texts. It can be thought of as a more formal/literary equivalent of everyday expressions like 〜てたまらない or 〜てしょうがない. It is closely related in meaning to 〜極まりない and 〜ったらない but differs in usage domain and nuance.

ga-hayai-ka.intro_tr: 〜が早いか, a N1 pattern specific to literary and written language that expresses that a second action occurs immediately after a first action occurs. It corresponds to the Turkish structure "…-ir …-mez" and is generally used in narrative/novel sentences that describe past, unexpected, or rapidly developing events. It is attached to the dictionary (present/dictionary) form of the verb, and generally both verbs are actions of the same subject or of events that occur consecutively, close together. The second clause indicates an involuntary, suddenly developing result; therefore it cannot be used together with expressions indicating request, command, or personal will (〜てください, 〜ましょう etc.). It is rare in spoken language; it appears more in written narratives, newspaper articles, and literary texts.

conj-ichidan-full.title_tr: Verb Conjugation Table: Ichidan (一段動詞) — All Forms
conj-ichidan-full.intro_tr: Ichidan verbs (一段動詞[いちだんどうご]) are one of the two regular verb groups in Japanese and are also commonly referred to as "る-verbs". The greatest advantage of this group is that its conjugations are very simple: the verb root never changes, only the final る is dropped and replaced with the appropriate suffix. To understand whether a verb is Ichidan or not, one checks if the syllable before る has an i-sound or e-sound (i-dan/e-dan) — for example, 見る[みる] (mi+ru) and 食べる[たべる] (be+ru) are typical Ichidan verbs. However, note: some verbs ending in る (帰る[かえる], 入る[はいる] and the like) are actually in the Godan group despite their appearance; these are listed separately in a table below. This page compiles ALL basic and advanced conjugation forms of the Ichidan group using the 食べる[たべる] verb in one place.

Bazı る ile biten fiiller aslında Godan'dır (帰る[かえる], 入る[はいる] vb.) — Tablo 5'e bakınız.

nakereba-narimasen.title_tr: 〜なければなりません — Obligation Expression (must…, have to…)
nakereba-narimasen.intro_tr: 〜なければなりません is a very common obligation pattern frequently encountered at the N4 level that conveys the meaning of Turkish "…-meli / …-mek zorunda". The structure is derived from the negative (ない) form of the verb: first the ない form is created, then the final い is removed and ければ is added, and finally なりません (or the more informal ならない in casual speech) is placed at the end. The literal meaning is actually "if [you] don't…, it won't do" (based on double negation logic), which is why it is translated into Turkish as "…-meli, …-mek zorunda, …-mesi gerekir". For い-adjectives, な-adjectives, and nouns there is also a similar obligation structure. In everyday conversation なければ is often shortened to なきゃ and なりません is sometimes completely omitted.

conj-godan-full.title_tr: Verb Conjugation Table: Godan (五段動詞) — All Forms
conj-godan-full.intro_tr: Godan verbs (五段動詞[ごだんどうし]) are the largest and most regular verb group in Japanese; their dictionary forms end with a syllable bearing the u-sound: う, く, ぐ, す, つ, ぬ, ぶ, む, る. The name "Godan" (five-step) comes from the fact that during conjugation, the final syllable of the verb stem can change across all five rows of the あ・い・う・え・お chart — unlike ichidan verbs, here all vowel rows come into play. When forming て形 and た形, sound softening rules called 音便[おんびん] also apply (changes of っ, ん, い). This page summarizes all godan conjugation forms, sound change rules, and frequently confused exceptions (行く[いく], ある, verbs ending in "る" that appear ichidan-like) in table format.

ni-yotte-yoru.intro_tr: 〜によって (and its attributive form 〜による) is a highly versatile particle pattern: (1) in passive voice, it indicates the agent performing the action ("by"), (2) it expresses the cause/reason for an event ("because of, due to"), (3) it indicates the means/method of an action ("via, through"), (4) it expresses on what basis a situation changes ("according to, depending on"). It is composed from に + よって (the て-form of the verb よる); による is the attributive form appearing before nouns (~による + 名詞[めいし]). In written/formal language, により is an abbreviated form; in conversational/news language, によると・によれば is used with the meaning "according to, based on the source". At the N3 level, the most frequently encountered meanings are "variability/dependence" (人[ひと]によって, 場合[ばあい]によって, etc.) and "by" in passive sentences.

rows: 受身[うけみ]動詞[どうし] + によって
この絵[え]はピカソによって描[か]かれた。 (Bu resim Picasso tarafından çizildi.)
名詞[めいし] + によって
地震[じしん]によって多[おお]くの家[いえ]が壊[こわ]れた。 (Deprem yüzünden birçok ev yıkıldı.)
名詞[めいし] + によって
努力[どりょく]によって成功[せいこう]した。 (Çaba sayesinde başarılı oldu.)
名詞[めいし] + によって(は)
国[くに]によって法律[ほうりつ]が違[ちが]う。 (Ülkeye göre kanunlar farklıdır.)
footnotes_tr: Note: In a passive sentence, the agent can generally be marked with に as well (例[れい]: 先生[せんせい]に褒[ほ]められた), but によって is more commonly used with passive verbs that denote a work/result (書[か]かれる, 作[つく]られる, 発見[はっけん]される, etc.).

ni-tsuite-kanshite.title_tr: について / に関[かん]して (…about)
ni-tsuite-kanshite.intro_tr: について and に関[かん]して, meaning "...about, ...related to" are two particle patterns used to indicate a topic of conversation/writing. Both carry the same basic meaning, but について is more neutral and is used comfortably in everyday language, while に関して is more formal, written, and academic in tone. When one wants to directly modify a noun, についての is used instead of について, and に関する is used instead of に関して. To emphasize or compare the topic, the forms については / に関しては are preferred. This structure, with the same meaning but different nuances, should not be confused with patterns like に対して (...toward/against) and をめぐって (...around, topic of discussion).

hajimeru-dasu-owaru-tsuzukeru.title_tr: 〜始める / 〜出す / 〜終わる / 〜続ける (Aspect Verbs)
hajimeru-dasu-owaru-tsuzukeru.intro_tr: 〜始める、〜出す、〜終わる、〜続ける are auxiliary verbs added to verbs to indicate at what "phase" (beginning, sudden beginning, ending, continuation) an action occurs. They are all added to the ます形の語幹 (masu-stem) of the verb and are conjugated normally according to their own verb group (ichidan/godan). Although both 〜始める and 〜出す mean "to begin," 〜出す emphasizes a sudden, unexpected, or emotional beginning; 〜始める, on the other hand, expresses a neutral, general beginning. 〜終わる indicates the completion of an action, while 〜続ける indicates the uninterrupted continuation of an action. These structures appear very frequently at the N3 level and are also widely used in everyday conversation.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Rule: ます形の語幹 (masu-stem) + 始める/出す/終わる/続ける
footnotes_tr: Some combinations like 降り終わる are not often used because they are not semantically natural; it is important to learn from examples which verbs combine naturally with which suffixes.

kanenai-kaneru.title_tr: 〜かねない / 〜かねる（…might happen negatively; …cannot, …struggle to do）
kanenai-kaneru.intro_tr: 〜かねない and 〜かねる actually come from the same 兼[か]ねる verb but represent completely different usage patterns. 〜かねない is attached to the ます-root and carries the meaning "it is possible for something negative/bad to happen, such a thing might occur" — it is generally used in sentences conveying danger, risk, or anxiety. 〜かねる (or its polite form 〜かねます) on the other hand means "I struggle to..., I cannot..., my situation/position does not allow for this", and is mostly used in business Japanese to express a polite refusal or reservation. Both are frequently encountered patterns at the N2 level, patterns close to formal/written language; in daily conversation できない or にくい are preferred more. かねる itself is an ichidan verb, therefore it follows normal ichidan conjugation rules.

tables.caption_tr: Formation Rules: ます-root + かねない / かねる

mai.intro_tr: 〜まい is an auxiliary verb suffix with classical/literary origins and appears in modern Japanese, especially in written language, formal speech, literature, and somewhat old/heavy style. It has two basic meanings: (1) the speaker's firm and strong negative will — "definitely I won't..." (similar to 〜ないつもりだ / 〜ないぞ), and (2) negative prediction — "probably won't / probably will not" (similar to 〜ないだろう). The first meaning is generally used with the first person, while the second meaning is used with third person or situations. The way it attaches to verbs varies by verb group, and some verbs (especially する and 来[く]る) have more than one acceptable form. In everyday speech, it has generally given its place to more modern patterns like 〜ないだろう or 〜ないつもりだ.

tokoro-ka-emphatic.title_tr: 〜たところが / 〜たところ (…-when it turned out)
tokoro-ka-emphatic.intro_tr: 〜たところが and 〜たところ are N1-level patterns used to describe encountering an unexpected, often surprising result following a past action. In Turkish, they can be translated as "…-when it turned out", "…-but it turned out", "…-but it was", etc. Both are attached to the た-form (past) of the verb; however, ところが carries a stronger sense of contrast and surprise, while ところ creates a more neutral "…-when, and then" connection and is especially common in written/formal narratives (reports, newspapers, novels). This structure typically conveys situations where the speaker's expectations were dashed or plans went awry, and the following sentence always states a fact that occurred in the past and cannot be changed (in other words, an imperative, request, or future tense does not follow 〜たところが/ところ).

to-shite-nai.title_tr: 〜として〜ない — Not a single … …-es (Absolute Negation)
to-shite-nai.intro_tr: 〜として〜ない is a strong negation pattern frequently encountered in N1 level, very formal written language. With the structure "Bir[数量詞]として" a counter (一つ, 一人, 一度, 一日 etc.) is taken and then a negative predicate follows; thus an absolute, unconditional negation emphasis like "not even a single one … is not / … does not exist" is made. It corresponds to "none", "not a single …" in Turkish and is generally much more literary and emphatic in tone than だけ or しか. It is typically used only with the number "one" (一); it is almost never used with numbers like two, three because the purpose is to say "not even the smallest unit". Formulaic variants like 何一つとして (nothing at all) and 誰一人として (not a single person) are very common.

koto-to-natte-iru.title_tr: 〜こととなっている (according to the rule/by rule …is)
koto-to-natte-iru.intro_tr: 〜こととなっている is a very formal pattern specific to written language that indicates that something is the case as required by a rule, law, regulation, or social/institutional tradition. It means "…by rule …is / …is stipulated" and generally, without specifying who made the decision, the rule is presented in an objective and impersonal manner. It is semantically almost identical to 〜ことになっている, but 〜こととなっている is more formal and is preferred in legal texts, official documents, regulations, and institutional announcements. It is constructed as: verb dictionary form or ない form + こととなっている; 〜こととなる (without いる) emphasizes a decision made at a specific moment or a resulting outcome. At N1 level, it is particularly important for the skill of reading formal/legal texts.

arisama.title_tr: 〜ありさま / 〜てい (…state, condition — usually negative)
arisama.intro_tr: The 〜ありさま (有様) and 〜てい (体) patterns are N1-level literary expressions used to emphasize that a person, place, or event is in a pitiable, bad, embarrassing, or unexpected state. ありさま is originally a noun meaning "state, condition"; but unlike the everyday words "様子[ようす]" or "状態[じょうたい]", it is almost always used to describe a negative, disappointing scene. 体(てい), on the other hand, means "appearance, outward bearing" and sometimes carries the meaning that the actual situation is hidden and it only appears that way from the outside. The harshest and most critical relative of these patterns, 体[てい]たらく, means "shameful state, pitiful condition" and generally contains strong censure. Both expressions are rarely used in everyday conversation; they frequently appear in written language, critical texts, news, and literary narratives.

dani.intro_tr: 〜だに, classical (文語[ぶんご]) in origin, is an emphatic particle that appears rarely in N1 level written/literary language and in fixed expressions. Its basic meaning is "…even, …even doing X is enough": it expresses that a small, single action (usually mental verbs such as imagining, thinking, remembering) produces a big result. In the second usage, with the pattern 〜だに〜ない, it expresses strong negation meaning "not even… …-ed" (一言[ひとこと]だに言[い]わなかった = "didn't say a single word"). It is almost never used in modern conversational language; it appears mainly in literature, newspaper articles, formal/classical style and in fixed expressions (夢[ゆめ]にだに, 想像[そうぞう]するだに, 微動[びどう]だにせず like). Although semantically close to さえ and すら, だに is older and has a more rigid/literary tone.

The second usage is a modern remnant of the classical 〜だに〜ず structure.

kiwamaru.intro_tr: 〜極[きわ]まる and 〜極[きわ]まりない are a fairly literary and formal N1 pattern that expresses that a quality indicated by a な-adjective has reached an extremely high degree. 極[きわ]まる actually means "to reach the limit, to attain the peak," and is a 五段[ごだん] verb; 極[きわ]まりない, on the other hand, is composed of a combination of the noun 極[きわ]まり (limit, extreme point) and ない, but its meaning is not negation; rather the opposite—it means "limitless, extremely." It is generally used in conjunction with な-adjectives that express negative or critical judgments such as 失礼[しつれい]、危険[きけん]、残念[ざんねん]. It is almost never used in everyday spoken language; it appears in newspaper articles, official critical texts, and literary writings. The two forms are almost identical in meaning, but 極[きわ]まりない is used much more frequently in modern Japanese.

transitive-intransitive.title_tr: Transitive / Intransitive Verb Pairs (自動詞[じどうし]・他動詞[たどうし])
transitive-intransitive.intro_tr: In Japanese, many verbs appear in pairs—transitive (他動詞[たどうし]) and intransitive (自動詞[じどうし])—to describe the same event from two different perspectives. Intransitive verbs express that something happens spontaneously and take が with the subject (e.g., ドアが開[あ]く — the door opens); transitive verbs express that a conscious subject affects an object and take を with the object (e.g., ドアを開[あ]ける — to open the door). This distinction resembles voice differences in Turkish like "açılmak/açmak", "kırılmak/kırmak", but in Japanese each verb pair has its own unique suffix that often appears irregular; therefore these pairs must be memorized. At the N4 level, knowing approximately 20-25 of the most frequently used pairs and how they combine with 〜ている / 〜てある is a fundamental topic. This page brings together the pairs, morphological patterns, particle usage, and aspect differences in one place.

tables.caption_tr: Most Frequently Used Transitive / Intransitive Verb Pairs (Essential List for N4)
footnotes_tr: Some verbs' transitive and intransitive equivalents may have the same reading (直[なお]る/直[なお]す for example) or completely different words (見[み]る/見[み]える for example); each pair must be memorized separately.

you-to-suru.title_tr: 〜ようとする / 〜ようとしない (to try to do...)
you-to-suru.intro_tr: The 「〜ようとする」pattern is formed by adding 「とする」to the volitional form of the verb, called the istek/意向形[いこうけい] (volitional) form, and carries the meanings "to try to do something," "just about to do/on the verge of doing." The negative form 〜ようとしない, for animate subjects, means "stubbornly not do, refuse to do," and for inanimate subjects (car, motor, machine, etc.), means "won't work/won't function no matter what." This pattern generally describes an effort or attempt with uncertain or unsuccessful results; when combined with 〜ている it takes on the nuance of "currently trying / just about to ...". It is frequently encountered at the N2 level in both spoken and written Japanese and is a very practical structure in daily life.

tabi-ni.intro_tr: 〜たびに, meaning "every time … / each time", is a pattern that expresses that another thing regularly happens based on a repeated event or situation. The difference from とき is that たびに must emphasize a repeated, habitual situation — it is not used for one-time events. With verbs it is attached to the dictionary form, and with nouns it is used together with の (noun+のたびに). Generally it establishes a cause-effect or accompaniment relationship in the form of "every time X happens, Y also happens" and frequently appears in sentences describing a changing/increasing situation (like ますます, だんだん). It is a quite common N2 pattern that can be used comfortably in both spoken and written language.

tables.caption_tr: Connection Forms (How is たびに attached?)
rows: 動詞[どうし]辞書形[じしょけい] + たびに
名詞[めいし] + の + たびに
旅行[りょこう]のたびに
名詞[めいし] + の + たびに
食事[しょくじ]のたびに
動詞[どうし]辞書形[じしょけい] + たびに
footnotes_tr: たびに is always used with 動詞の辞書形 (dictionary form of verbs); it is not used with た-form or ない-form.
When used with nouns の is required: 名詞 + の + たびに.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of とき and たびに

Evet, mutlaka tekrarlanan/alışkanlık hâlini ifade eder

wake-da.intro_tr: ～わけだ is used to draw a logical conclusion in the form of "meaning, then, naturally so" based on a previously known reason or situation. It expresses the speaker's inference drawn from their own observations and knowledge; rather than providing new information, it reinterprets an already known fact from a different angle or explains it by saying "that's why." It generally comes after a reason clause (から/ので) or together with conjunctions like "それで/だから/道理[どうり]で". It should not be confused with sibling patterns like わけではない and わけがない — these are semantically related but functionally different negative forms of わけだ. It is a natural connective pattern that frequently appears at N2 level and is widely used in both spoken and written language.

tables.caption_tr: Attachment Rules: After Which Forms Does わけだ Come?
rows: Sözlük formu / た形 / ない形 + わけだ
行[い]くわけだ ／ 行[い]ったわけだ ／ 行[い]かないわけだ
高[たか]いわけだ ／ 高[たか]くなかったわけだ
語幹 + な + わけだ
静[しず]かなわけだ ／ 静[しず]かだったわけだ（geçmişte な düşer）
学生[がくせい]なわけだ ／ 学生[がくせい]だったわけだ
footnotes_tr: In な-adjectives and nouns in the past tense, な drops, and only だった/でなかった + わけだ is used.
In colloquial speech, だ can generally be dropped: 高いわけ (with questioning intonation)。

tables.caption_tr: Three Main Usage Types of わけだ
rows: Verilen bir sebepten (から/ので) doğal biçimde ulaşılan sonucu belirtir.
毎日[まいにち]3時間[さんじかん]勉強[べんきょう]しているから、上手[じょうず]になるわけだ。
Aynı fikri başka kelimelerle özetler veya netleştirir; sıkça つまり/要[よう]するに ile birlikte.
つまり、彼[かれ]は来[こ]られないというわけだ。
Önce şaşıran konuşmacının, sebebi öğrendikten sonra 'ha demek ki bu yüzdenmiş' diyerek aydınlanması.
道理[どうり]で寒[さむ]いわけだ、雪[ゆき]が降[ふ]っている。
footnotes_tr: These three usages are not separated by clear lines from each other; they can overlap depending on context.

tables.caption_tr: わけ Family: Comparison of Confusing Patterns
rows: 忙[いそが]しいわけだ。（işte bu yüzden meşgulmüş）
…olduğu anlamına gelmez, tam olarak öyle değil
嫌[きら]いなわけではない。（sevmiyor değilim）
彼[かれ]がうそをつくわけがない。
今日[きょう]は休[やす]むわけにはいかない。

tables.caption_tr: わけだ vs Similar Patterns (はず・ので・ということだ)
rows: Bilinen bir sebepten çıkan mantıksal, kaçınılmaz sonuç
Konuşmacı zaten sebebi biliyor; sonucu 'işte bu yüzden' diye açıklar
Kesin bilgi olmayabilir; 'olması gerekir' anlamında öngörü
Sadece sebebi bildirir; わけだ gibi 'demek ki' vurgusu/sonuç çıkarımı yoktur
Başkasından öğrenilen bilgiyi nakleder, kişisel çıkarım değildir
footnotes_tr: わけだ emphasizes the speaker's own reasoning; ということだ, on the other hand, emphasizes conveying information from outside.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は10年[じゅうねん]もアメリカに住[す]んでいた。道理[どうり]で英語[えいご]が上手[じょうず]なわけだ。

yara-yara.title_tr: 〜やら〜やら (...and so on, this and that)
yara-yara.intro_tr: 〜やら〜やら is a construction used when listing multiple things, situations, or feelings with the meaning of "and so on, both ... and ..."; it generally expresses chaos, disorder, confusion, or an intense/mixed emotional state. Similar to other listing constructions like と か or だの, but やら carries more of a nuance of "it's not exactly clear what it is, there's confusion." Two or more elements are arranged in sequence with やら, and the sentence generally continues with 〜で (because/for this reason) to indicate the result. Additionally, when やら is used by itself, it also carries a meaning of "uncertainty" equivalent to か (like 何[なに]やら, どこへ行[い]くやら). This construction can be used in both spoken and written language, giving it a somewhat literary/stylistic feel.

wo-hajime.intro_tr: 〜をはじめ (and formal variants 〜をはじめとして / 〜をはじめとする), by highlighting the most representative, most typical, or most important example from a group, means "...starting with, ... like (including many more things/people)". It is used more in written language than in spoken language, in formal speeches, news, and promotional texts. It comes directly after a noun and typically in the continuation of the sentence, a list or scope is indicated with expressions like "など、様々な〜、〜も". れい caution: this pattern is not only for listing concrete examples, but is used to emphasize that the given example is the most representative/leading member of the group — that's why it is semantically different from random counting patterns like "とか" or "や".

ta-totan.title_tr: 〜たとたん(に) — at the moment of …, as soon as … (N2)
ta-totan.intro_tr: 〜たとたん(に) (途端[とたん]), a pattern expressing the immediate aftermath of the completion of an action, usually describing the occurrence of a second event that is generally unexpected or surprising; it is translated to Turkish as "…-diği anda" (at the moment of …), "…-er …-mez" (as soon as …). It is used only with the past tense (た形) form of a verb, and in the second sentence it generally describes a situation that develops beyond the subject's control, sudden, unexpected, or negative. For this reason, a volitional (意志的[いしてき]) action, command, request, or offer cannot generally be used in the second sentence — this is the biggest difference from the similar pattern 〜たら. とたん also comes from the noun 途端[とたん] (=moment, that moment), so it is sometimes also written in kanji as 〜た途端. At the N2 level, the nuance differences with frequently confused patterns such as かと思うと, や否や, が早いか, なり are compared in the tables below.

tables.caption_tr: Form Rule: Verb-た + とたん(に)
footnotes_tr: とたん is always attached to the た形 (past tense) form of a verb; it is not attached to the dictionary form or the て形.
The に particle is optional and frequently drops in spoken language: 〜たとたん = 〜たとたんに.
The pattern is essentially used with verbs; usage of adjective/noun + とたん is very rare and unnatural.

dano-dano.title_tr: 〜とか〜とか / 〜だの〜だの (Enumeration, Exemplifying Counting)
dano-dano.intro_tr: 〜とか〜とか and 〜だの〜だの are used to list two or more examples in a non-definitive, exemplifying manner like "things like this, things like that"; it is generally implied that there may be other things beyond the list. とか is a neutral and very common pattern in everyday speech and can also be used on its own (N1とか). だの has the same structure but almost always carries a nuance of complaint, dissatisfaction, or negative attitude, and is not used as frequently as とか in modern times—it gives a somewhat archaic or literary tone. Both patterns combine directly with the dictionary/inflected form of nouns, verbs, i-adjectives, and na-adjectives. This page shows the structure, nuance differences, and usage details according to word types in detailed tables.

examples.note_tr: だの with い-adjectives: strengthens the tone of complaint.

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんとか鈴木[すずき]さんとかに聞[き]いてみたら？

examples.translation_tr: Why not ask people like Tanaka-san, Suzuki-san, and such?
examples.note_tr: With nouns/personal names とか — a non-definitive suggestion.

examples.target: あの店[みせ]は高[たか]いだの、まずいだの、評判[ひょうばん]が悪[わる]い。
examples.reading: あの みせ は たかい だの、まずい だの、ひょうばん が わるい。

examples.note_tr: Transmission of gossip/complaints with だの, third-person criticism.

wari-ni.intro_tr: 〜わりに (漢字: 割[わり]に), taking a situation (X) as the basis, it expresses that the result (Y) comes out different from what is expected according to that situation — generally better or worse. Its closest equivalents in English are "according to..." or "despite being... (unexpectedly)" expressions. Here, the speaker points out the imbalance/inconsistency between normal expectation and actual result; in this respect, unlike 〜のに, it is not an emotional complaint, but rather carries a more neutral "disproportion" observation. The emphasis can be strengthened by adding は to form 〜わりには. There are different attachment patterns with verbs, い-adjectives, な-adjectives, and nouns; on this page you will find all attachment patterns, comparisons with similar structures, and plenty of examples.

tables.caption_tr: 〜わりに(は) Attachment Patterns (According to Word Type)
rows: Fiil (辞書形[じしょけい]) + わりに

Fiil (ない形[けい]) + わりに

初心者[しょしんしゃ]ではない
初心者[しょしんしゃ]ではないわりに
footnotes_tr: When used as 〜わりには by adding は, the emphasis of contrast/unexpected situation is strengthened.
The character 割[わり] means 'ratio, proportion'; the pattern originates from the basic meaning 'according to the ratio'.

gatai-zurai.title_tr: 〜がたい / 〜づらい (difficult to..., hard to...)
gatai-zurai.intro_tr: 〜がたい and 〜づらい are two suffixes that express the difficulty of accomplishing a verb, and both are attached to the ます-stem (連用形[れんようけい]) of the verb. 〜がたい is a more literary and formal expression; it generally expresses a degree of difficulty that is "nearly impossible, unacceptable" from an emotional, logical, or moral perspective, and is used in a fixed manner only with a limited number of verbs (such as 信[しん]じる, 理解[りかい]する, 許[ゆる]す, 忘[わす]れる). 〜づらい, on the other hand, frequently appears in everyday conversation and expresses subjective situations where the person performing the action feels physical or psychological discomfort, hesitation, or difficulty. These two suffixes should be studied together with 〜にくい (objective/natural difficulty) which is semantically close, and with 〜やすい (ease) which is opposite in meaning. Both suffixes conjugate like い-adjectives (〜がたかった, 〜づらくない, etc.).

tables.caption_tr: Formation Rule: がたい and づらい
rows: Fiil ます-kökü (連用形[れんようけい])
信[しん]じる → 信[しん]じます → 信[しん]じがたい
Fiil ます-kökü (連用形[れんようけい])
言[い]う → 言[い]います → 言[い]いづらい
footnotes_tr: Both suffixes, when attached with づらい/がたい, behave and conjugate like い-adjectives.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of 〜がたい / 〜づらい / 〜にくい / 〜やすい
rows: yazı dili, edebî, sınırlı fiil seti
理解[りかい]しがたい (anlaşılması güç)

hem yazı hem konuşma, geniş fiil kapsamı
読[よ]みにくい字[じ] (okunması zor yazı)
分[わ]かりやすい説明[せつめい] (anlaşılması kolay açıklama)
footnotes_tr: づらい and にくい can often substitute for each other; づらい emphasizes subjective discomfort, while にくい emphasizes more objective/general difficulty.
Unlike にくい/づらい, がたい is not natural with concrete physical difficulties (e.g. 開[あ]けにくい/×開[あ]けがたい); it is used more with abstract, conceptual verbs.

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used Fixed 〜がたい Expressions

te-miru.intro_tr: 〜てみる is formed by adding みる (to see) auxiliary verb to the て-form of a verb, and carries the meaning of 'trying something, attempting by doing.' The みる here no longer carries the real meaning of 'to see'; it has completely become a grammaticalized auxiliary verb; therefore it is usually written in hiragana as みる, not 見る. 〜てみる expresses doing an action with curiosity, with the intention of testing, or to see the result of something whose outcome is unknown—it corresponds to structures like '…-ip bakmak' or '…-meyi denemek' in Turkish. Since みる itself is an ichidan (2nd group / る-verb), the 〜てみる pattern is conjugated exactly like an ichidan verb. It is generally used in positive, curious, or neutral actions; for the meaning 'trying to accomplish' a difficult/dangerous task, 〜ようとする is preferred instead.

tables.caption_tr: Formation of て-Formu + みる According to Verb Groups
footnotes_tr: When みる is an auxiliary verb, its meaning becomes grammaticalized, so it is usually written in hiragana: not 食べて見る but 食べてみる.

conj-tense-aspect-map.title_tr: Tense-Aspect Map (〜る / 〜た / 〜ている / 〜てある / 〜ておく)
conj-tense-aspect-map.intro_tr: In Japanese, tense and aspect generally work like two separate systems: 〜る/〜た only distinguish 'now/future' from 'past', while 〜ている/〜てある/〜ておく indicate what stage the action is at (is it ongoing, is the result permanent, was it prepared beforehand). When these five forms are considered together, a much more nuanced aspect map emerges, different from the simple 'past/present/future tense' logic in English or Turkish. Particularly, the four different uses of 〜ている (progression, resultant state, habit, permanent characteristic) and the transitive/intransitive verb distinction between 〜てある and 〜ている are the most frequently confused points for Turkish speakers. This page clarifies which form to use in which situation by placing these five forms side by side.

te-iku-kuru.title_tr: 〜ていく / 〜てくる (Auxiliary Verbs Indicating Direction of Time and Space)
te-iku-kuru.intro_tr: 〜ていく (〜て行く) and 〜てくる (〜て来る) are auxiliary verbs that attach to the て-form and indicate DIRECTION according to the speaker (or a designated reference point). 〜ていく carries the meaning of "moving away / progressing from now toward the future," while 〜てくる carries the meaning of "approaching / coming from the past to the present." These two are used on three different levels: (1) SPATIAL — the direction of actual physical movement, (2) TEMPORAL — the time span during which an action lasts, (3) CHANGE — how a situation gradually develops or emerges. When used as an auxiliary verb, 行く and 来る are generally written in hiragana (ていく / てくる). Understanding the concept of direction correctly is the key to establishing the time line and perspective of the sentence correctly.

Konuşmacıya / referans noktasına doğru YAKLAŞARAK gelmek: 歩[ある]いてくる (yürüyerek yaklaşmak)

Geçmişten ŞİMDİYE kadar devam etmiş olmak: 今[いま]まで続[つづ]けてきた

conj-keigo-table.title_tr: Honorific Language Conjugation Table (尊敬語[そんけいご] / 謙譲語[けんじょうご] / 丁重語[ていちょうご] Side by Side)
conj-keigo-table.intro_tr: Honorific Language (敬語[けいご]) in Japanese consists of three main axes used to express politeness: 尊敬語[そんけいご] (sonkeigo) which elevates the other party, 謙譲語[けんじょうご] (kenjōgo) which shows respect to the other party by lowering one's own actions, and 丁重語[ていちょうご]/謙譲語[けんじょうご]II (teichōgo) which addresses the listener with general formality. Some common verbs have completely irregular special honorific forms (e.g., 行[い]く → いらっしゃる); other verbs are derived using general patterns (such as お＋ます語幹[ごかん]＋になる). This page compiles the conjugations of the most frequently used verbs across three politeness axes side by side and the general production rules for regular verbs in a single reference. It is very important not to confuse which form shows respect to whom (to the other party or to the listener), because incorrect usage can reverse the meaning (such as using sonkeigo to oneself or kenjōgo to the other party).

kanji-compounds.title_tr: Kanji Compounds (熟語[じゅくご]) and Reading Patterns
kanji-compounds.intro_tr: 熟語[じゅくご] is when two or more kanji come together to form a single word (such as 勉強[べんきょう], 学校[がっこう]). The reading of a compound depends on whether the kanji within it use on'yomi or kun'yomi, and it is divided into four main patterns: 音+音, 訓+訓, 重箱読み[じゅうばこよみ] (音+訓) and 湯桶読み[ゆとうよみ] (訓+音). Additionally, in some compounds the initial sound of the second kanji softens and changes; this is called 連濁[れんだく] (like 火[ひ]→び). Finally, some compounds have special readings that cannot be read separately by individual kanji, but must be memorized as a whole; these are called 熟字訓[じゅくじくん] (like 今日[きょう], 明日[あした]). This page summarizes compound reading patterns and structure types frequently encountered at N3 level in table form.

tables.caption_tr: 熟語の読み方パターン (Types of compound kanji readings)

footnotes_tr: The 音+音 pattern is the most frequently encountered type at N3 level; when encountering a new compound whose reading is unknown, this pattern should be tried first.
The 重箱読み and 湯桶読み patterns are considered exceptions; these are usually learned by memorization.

keigo-kenjougo.title_tr: Humble Language: 謙譲語[けんじょうご] (kenjōgo)
keigo-kenjougo.intro_tr: 謙譲語[けんじょうご] (kenjōgo) is a type of keigo in which the speaker lowers their OWN actions to indirectly show respect to the listener (or the third party in question). It is never used for the listener's actions—in that case 尊敬語[そんけいご] (sonkeigo) is needed; kenjōgo is used only for "I/we" or "my/our group" (my company, my family). There are two main production methods: (1) irregular special verbs (words like 申[もう]す, いたす, 伺[うかが]う that must be memorized) and (2) the regular お〜する / ご〜する pattern. In business Japanese, it is frequently used when introducing yourself and your company to a customer, a superior, or an outsider (soto). At the N3 level, it is necessary to memorize the most common special verbs and the お/ご pattern by heart.

te-oku.title_tr: 〜ておく (Making Advance Preparation / Leaving as is)
te-oku.intro_tr: 〜ておく is formed by adding the verb 置[お]く (to put) to the て-form of a verb. Its basic meaning is 'to do something in advance so it will be useful in the future, to prepare and leave it.' Its second important usage is to intentionally leave a current situation unchanged, to leave it as it is (e.g., leaving the door open). In spoken language, ておく is often shortened to とく, and でおく to どく. This structure can be used with all conjugations including past, negative, request (〜ておいて), and desire (〜ておこう), and it is a practical pattern frequently encountered at the N3 level.

toori-ni.title_tr: とおりに / どおり — like ...-ed, according to ...
toori-ni.intro_tr: とおり(に) and どおり(に) are constructions that express something happening exactly as specified, stated, shown, or expected; they correspond to Turkish expressions like "...-ed like", "according to ...", "in accordance with ...". Although 通り[とおり] on its own means "road, street", in this grammar pattern it takes on the meaning "manner, style, form". When used after verbs (dictionary form or た form) and after nouns connected with の, とおり(に) is used; when directly attached to nouns, it becomes どおり(に) with 連濁[れんだく] (sound change). In a sentence, とおり/どおり can be used alone without に, especially before だ/です or before a comma. It is a practical structure frequently encountered at the N3 level, and is widely used in both everyday conversation and business Japanese (with patterns like 予定[よてい]どおり, 時間[じかん]どおり).

examples.note_tr: Verb た form + とおりに: after one action is completed, it describes another action performed by exactly following that instruction/statement.

examples.translation_tr: According to the plan, the meeting started at nine o'clock.
examples.note_tr: Since 予定[よてい] is a noun, どおりに is attached directly; the possessive particle の is not used (not 予定のどおりに).

examples.target: マニュアルどおりに機械[きかい]を操作[そうさ]してください。
examples.reading: マニュアルどおりにきかいをそうさしてください。

examples.translation_tr: As I thought, the exam was very difficult.
examples.note_tr: If there is a pause in the middle of the sentence, に can be omitted; とおり alone is used with the meaning 'as expected/anticipated'.

examples.note_tr: いつもどおり is an idiomatic adverbial expression meaning 'as always, as usual'.

keigo-special-verbs.title_tr: Keigo Special Verbs: いらっしゃる・なさる・おっしゃる (Root-Changing Verbs in Honorific Speech)
keigo-special-verbs.intro_tr: In Japanese, certain basic verbs have a completely separate "尊敬語[そんけいご]" (honorific language) root used to show respect to the person in front of you (a teacher, customer, or higher-ranking person) — these are called "special honorific verbs". For example, いらっしゃる is used instead of 行[い]く/来[く]る/いる, なさる instead of する, and おっしゃる instead of 言[い]う. These verbs are used when describing the actions of that person; when describing your own actions, you use humility (謙譲語[けんじょうご]) verbs instead (such as 参[まい]る, いたす, 申[もう]す) — it is very important not to confuse the two. Also, verbs like いらっしゃる, なさる, おっしゃる, くださる have an irregular ます-form (いらっしゃいます instead of いらっしゃります). Adding an honorific suffix like られる to these verbs is considered a "二重敬語[にじゅうけいご]" (double honorific) error and is incorrect.

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used Special Sonkeigo Verbs (For the Other Party's Action)
rows: 行[い]く / 来[く]る / いる
お休[やす]みになります
お亡[な]くなりになります
footnotes_tr: These verbs are used only for the person in front of you or the high-ranking person in question; they are never used for your own actions.

tables.caption_tr: Irregular ます-Root Conjugation (いらっしゃる・なさる・おっしゃる・くださる)
footnotes_tr: These four verbs are apparently godan る-verbs, but when ます is added, 〜います occurs instead of the expected 〜ります. This is the same irregularity pattern as ございます.
The て-form also does not follow an exceptional pattern but rather follows the normal godan る rule to form 〜って (いらっしゃって, くださって, etc.) — only the ます and imperative forms are irregular.

tables.caption_tr: Sonkeigo (Other Party) vs Kenjōgo (Yourself) Comparison
rows: いらっしゃる / お越[こ]しになる
申[もう]す / 申[もう]し上[あ]げる
存[ぞん]じておる / 存[ぞん]じ上[あ]げる
footnotes_tr: 尊敬語 = exalts the action of the person in front of you or a third high-ranking person.
謙譲語 = shows respect to the other party indirectly by humbling your own actions. These two groups are NEVER used in place of each other.

rows: 先生[せんせい]がおっしゃられました。
先生[せんせい]がおっしゃいました。
おっしゃる zaten saygı formudur; üzerine 〜られる eklemek gereksiz çift saygıdır.
部長[ぶちょう]がいらっしゃられます。
部長[ぶちょう]がいらっしゃいます。
いらっしゃる zaten saygı formudur, 〜られる eklenmez.
お客様[きゃくさま]が召[め]し上[あ]がられます。
お客様[きゃくさま]が召[め]し上[あ]がります。
召し上がる zaten saygı formudur.

先生[せんせい]がご覧[らん]になる。
ご覧になる zaten お〜になる kalıbıyla saygılıdır, 〜られる fazladır.
footnotes_tr: Note: Some dictionaries exceptionally accept the form なさられる for the verb なさる, but it is not recommended in everyday usage; the most natural and accepted form is なさいます.

ka-question.intro_tr: か (ka) is the most basic and most frequently used particle in Japanese that transforms a sentence into a question sentence (助詞[じょし]). It is added to the very end of the sentence; there is no need for any change in verb conjugation, word order, or sentence structure — in this way it is much simpler than English/Turkish. か is used both to form "yes/no" questions and to create "wh-questions" together with question words like だれ・何・どこ. Additionally, か offers a choice between two options with the meaning "or/either...or" and with the pattern 疑問詞[ぎもんし]+か (like 何[なに]か, 誰[だれ]か) also gives the meaning "something/someone indefinite". In polite speech, か is added to the end of a sentence, but in everyday/informal speech, か is usually omitted and rising intonation is used instead.

tables.caption_tr: Basic usage of か: Forming yes/no questions
footnotes_tr: か is always added to the very end of the sentence without changing conjugation.
In writing, a question mark (？) is generally not used after か, but it can be added in casual correspondence (SNS, messages).

tables.caption_tr: 疑問詞[ぎもんし] (question words) + か for forming questions
rows: 何[なに]を食[た]べますか。
どうして遅[おく]れましたか。
調子[ちょうし]はどうですか。
footnotes_tr: In sentences containing question words, か is generally kept, but can be omitted in casual speech: 何[なに]食[た]べる？

tables.caption_tr: か vs も: The difference between 疑問詞+か (someone/something indefinite) and 疑問詞+も (no one/nothing)
rows: 何[なに]か食[た]べましたか。
何[なに]も食[た]べませんでした。
誰[だれ]か来[き]ましたか。
誰[だれ]も来[き]ませんでした。
どこか行[い]きたいです。
どこも行[い]きませんでした。
いつか日本[にほん]に行[い]きたいです。
footnotes_tr: In these patterns, か does not carry question meaning; it is an independent usage that adds 'indefiniteness' to the word.
The も form is almost always used with negative verbs.

tables.caption_tr: Other uses of か: offering options and indirect questions
rows: 紅茶[こうちゃ]かコーヒーを飲[の]みます。
電車[でんしゃ]ですかバスですか。
肉[にく]か魚[さかな]、それとも野菜[やさい]ですか。
Et mi balık mı, yoksa sebze mi?
行[い]くかどうかまだわかりません。
する か しないか 決[き]めてください。
何[なに]を買[か]うかわかりません。
footnotes_tr: In the 〜かどうか pattern, どうか is added after か to a sentence that does not carry yes/no meaning; this is not used in direct wh-questions other than yes/no.
In indirect questions, verbs like か + わかる/知[し]る generally come at the end of the sentence.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of forming questions according to politeness level
rows: Düz form + yükselen tonlama, か yok
行[い]くかい？ 元気[げんき]かい？
Genelde yaşlı erkekler veya eski üsluplarda
だ asla か'dan önce kalmaz
❌学生[がくせい]だか → ✅学生[がくせい]か / 学生[がくせい]ですか
footnotes_tr: The だ copula is not used together with the question particle か; だ drops (学生[がくせい]か, a casual/masculine usage meaning "is [he/she] a student?").
The same rule applies to な-adjectives: not 静[しず]かだか, but 静[しず]かか。

verb-groups.intro_tr: Japanese verbs are divided into three main groups according to their conjugation patterns: Godan (五段[ごだん]) verbs, Ichidan (一段[いちだん]) verbs, and Irregular (不規則[ふきそく]) verbs. This classification is one of the fundamental pillars of learning Japanese because it determines how all conjugations such as ます-stem, て-form, and negative form are formed. While Godan verb stems change with five different vowels (a/i/u/e/o), in Ichidan verbs only the final る character drops and the stem remains fixed. Irregular verbs are only する and 来る[くる], having their own unique, memorization-required conjugation. Moreover, there are also "false Ichidan" verbs that end in る but actually conjugate like Godan — distinguishing them is one of the most confused topics at the beginning level.

Sadece る düşer, kök sabit kalır
不規則[ふきそく]動詞[どうし] / 変格[へんかく]動詞[どうし] (Düzensiz)

rows: 上[かみ]一段[いちだん] (i-sesi öncesi)
下[しも]一段[いちだん] (e-sesi öncesi)

Godan (帰[かえ]ります, 帰[かえ]って)
い sesi + る → Ichidan gibi görünür

long-vowels-sokuon.title_tr: Long Vowels (長音) and Small っ (促音)
long-vowels-sokuon.intro_tr: In Japanese, vowel length and the small っ (sokuon) are two important spelling/pronunciation rules that can completely change word meaning, but are easily overlooked by Turkish speakers. Long vowels (長音[ちょうおん]) are shown in hiragana by repeating certain vowel characters, and in katakana with the ー line, and are pronounced at exactly twice the length of short vowels. The small っ (促音[そくおん]) creates a "pause" by doubling (lengthening) the consonant following it, and is distinguished in writing from the normal つ by its smaller size. Using these two elements correctly is vital for both correct pronunciation and correct spelling (especially in word pairs like ちいさい vs ちさい). This page systematically explains both rules with tables and examples.

arimasu-imasu.title_tr: あります / います — To Exist, To Be Located (N5)
arimasu-imasu.intro_tr: あります and います are two fundamental verbs in Japanese meaning 'to exist / to be located' and are similar to the 'there is/are' construction in English. The most important difference between them is whether the subject is ANIMATE or INANIMATE: for inanimate objects, plants, and abstract concepts, あります is used; for animate beings such as humans and animals, います is used. These verbs are used together with the particles は/が/に/で to form location sentences such as 'there is something/someone somewhere' or 'something is in a specific place'. あります is also used in additional meanings such as possession ('I have ~') and expressing events/happenings ('there is a meeting'). This distinction is one of the most fundamental and most common mistakes at the N5 level, so it must be well reinforced.

kara-node-reason.title_tr: から / ので (because, because of -) — Cause-Effect Conjunctions
kara-node-reason.intro_tr: から and ので are two fundamental conjunctions that correspond to the Turkish meanings "because / for / because of -" and establish a cause-effect relationship in a sentence. Both are added to the end of a clause expressing a cause, and then a result/action clause follows: [CAUSE] + から/ので、[RESULT]。 The most important difference between them is nuance: から emphasizes the speaker's own subjective reasoning, decision, or emotional emphasis, while ので expresses a more objective, natural, and logical cause-effect relationship and carries a more polite/formal tone. At the N5 level, both conjunctions frequently appear; for this reason, you need to clearly distinguish how they attach to which word types and in which situations one is preferred over the other. The following tables summarize the attachment rules, the usage differences between the two, and common mistakes.

te-iru.intro_tr: 〜ている in Japanese is a versatile structure that corresponds to both the "present tense" (-yor) in Turkish and the "state/result state" meanings. It is formed by attaching the auxiliary verb いる to the て-form of the verb, and it has four basic meanings: (1) an action in progress at that moment, (2) a permanent resultant state remaining from the completion of an action, (3) habit/repeated action, (4) "state verbs" (知る, 住む, 似る etc.) that by nature are used only in this form. Which meaning applies depends largely on whether the verb is transitive/intransitive and on the context in the sentence. Since いる itself is an ichidan verb, ている also inflects like an ichidan verb. In spoken language, the い often drops: 食[た]べてる, 見[み]てる etc.

na-adjectives.intro_tr: な-Adjectives (also known as 形容動詞[けいようどうし]), behave similarly to nouns in Japanese but take the な suffix when modifying nouns. Their dictionary forms end with だ (e.g., 静か[しずか]だ = is quiet) and unlike い-adjectives, their conjugations are almost entirely done through だ/です. When they come before a noun, they must take the な suffix (静か[しずか]な部屋[へや] = quiet room), and when forming adverbs, the 〜に suffix is used (静か[しずか]に = quietly). Note: some words like きれい (beautiful/clean) and 嫌い[きらい] (to dislike) end with い but are actually な-adjectives — this is a common pitfall. The tables below provide all conjugation forms, comparison with い-adjectives, frequently used words, and sentence-joining patterns all together.

kanji-basics.title_tr: Kanji Basics: 音読み[おんよみ] / 訓読み[くんよみ] Readings
kanji-basics.intro_tr: Each 漢字[かんじ] generally has at least two reading styles: 音読み[おんよみ] (Chinese-origin reading) and 訓読み[くんよみ] (Japanese native reading). 音読み[おんよみ] is usually used within 熟語[じゅくご] (compound words) where two or more kanji come together and is short, one or two syllables; 訓読み[くんよみ] is used when a kanji stands alone as the root of a word, followed by 送[おく]り仮名[がな] (hiragana suffixes). The same kanji can sometimes be read with 音読み[おんよみ] and sometimes with 訓読み[くんよみ] depending on context; which one is used is generally determined by surrounding kanji or hiragana. At N5 level, the most important thing is to memorize fixed patterns like day names (曜日[ようび]) and when you see a single kanji + okurigana, try the kun reading; when you see two kanji side by side (without okurigana), try the on reading. This page brings together basic rules, the most frequently confused examples, and exceptional reading patterns (重箱読み[じゅうばこよみ], 湯桶読み[ゆとうよみ]) in a single reference.

footnotes_tr: Okurigana is the hiragana portion that carries the conjugation suffixes of verbs and adjectives (〜る, 〜い, 〜む, etc.); the root of the kanji doesn't change, only the final hiragana changes according to conjugations (食[た]べる → 食[た]べます → 食[た]べない).

footnotes_tr: The 生 kanji is one of the kanji with the most readings in Japanese; such variety is exceptional, most N5 kanji have 1-2 on and 1-2 kun readings.
To choose the correct reading, one must always look at the context of the word and its okurigana; memorization alone is not sufficient, habit is gained through extensive reading.

nai-form.title_tr: ない Form and Its Derivatives (N5)
nai-form.intro_tr: The ない[ない] form is the fundamental structure that creates the negative form of verbs and is used instead of 〜ません in everyday spoken language (casual register). Depending on the verb group (Godan, Ichidan, irregular), it is derived differently, but once formed, ない is conjugated like an い-adjective (なかった, なくて, なければ, etc.). On this page, the formation of the ない form, its exceptions, and the most frequently used structures derived from it such as 〜ないで, 〜なくて, 〜なければならない, 〜なくてもいい are gathered together. At the N5 level, recognizing these patterns is necessary for understanding both everyday conversation and basic written language.

tables.caption_tr: Formation of the ない Form (According to Verb Groups)

The verb ある is an exception: the ない形i is not あらない, but simply becomes ない (あります → ありません / ない).

hiragana-chart.intro_tr: Hiragana is one of the two syllabic writing systems (kana) of Japanese and is taught using an orderly table called gojūon (五十音, "fifty sounds"); each character represents a single syllable (vowel or consonant+vowel) and does not carry meaning like kanji. The basic table contains 46 characters; by adding dakuten (゛) and handakuten (゜) marks to these, 25 more sounds are derived (が, ざ, だ, ば, ぱ rows). By combining with small ゃゅょ, an additional 33 compound syllables called yōon (拗音) are obtained. Hiragana is used for verb/adjective inflection suffixes, particles (with special readings like は・を・へ), native Japanese words, and kanji readings. The letters は, へ, and を are read differently from their normal pronunciation; when used solely in the particle (postposition) function, they are read as "wa", "e", and "o" respectively — this is the most frequently confused point at the N5 level.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Gojūon Table (清音 seion) — 46 basic hiragana
footnotes_tr: し is read as 'shi' not 'si', ち as 'chi' not 'ti', つ as 'tsu' not 'tu', ふ as 'fu' not 'hu' — these are irregular romanizations.
い and う (the empty cells in the や/わ rows) are the same as い and う in the あ行 row; they do not have separate characters.
を is used almost exclusively as the object particle (〜を) and is read as 'o'; it almost never appears within words.
ん is the only consonant that forms a syllable by itself and never appears at the beginning of a word.

tables.caption_tr: Sounds Derived with Dakuten (゛) and Handakuten (゜) (濁音・半濁音)
footnotes_tr: ぢ and づ are pronounced the same as じ and ず in modern standard Japanese; they are preserved only in the written form of certain words (such as つづく, ちぢむ, はなぢ).
Only the は行 row can take both dakuten (ば行) and handakuten (ぱ行); other rows take only dakuten.
Dakuten/handakuten marks are added to the top right corner of the character: は→ば (゛), は→ぱ (゜).

tables.caption_tr: Yōon (拗音) — Compound Syllables with Small ゃゅょ
footnotes_tr: Yōon always consists of a combination of a syllable from the い段 row (き・し・ち・に・ひ・み・り + dakuten/handakuten variants) with small ゃゅょ.
Small ゃゅょ is distinguished from normal-sized ya/yu/yo by character size; if written large, they become two separate syllables (for example きや = ki-ya, きゃ = kya).
じゃ/じゅ/じょ are pronounced the same as ぢゃ/ぢゅ/ぢょ, but in practice the じ-based spelling is preferred.

tables.caption_tr: Particles with Special Readings: は・へ・を
footnotes_tr: These three exceptions are the source of the most frequently made reading mistakes at the N5 level; one must pay attention to whether it is a word or a particle.
を practically appears almost exclusively as the 〜を object particle.
