aru-majiki.title_tr: 〜まじき (...is not fitting/appropriate, should not be)
aru-majiki.intro_tr: 〜まじき is the conjugated (連体形) form of the negative auxiliary verb 「まじ」 in classical Japanese and survives in modern Japanese only as a crystallized, literary/written expression. It is attached to the dictionary (る) form of a verb and always modifies a noun; it conveys the meaning "...will not/should not be (noun)". The most frequently seen patterns are 「あるまじき」 (should not be, is not fitting) and 「許[ゆる]すまじき」 (cannot be forgiven); it is generally used to strictly condemn behavior that does not accord with someone's profession, status, or identity. It almost never appears in everyday speech; we encounter it in news articles, official statements, and literary writings. It is important for understanding at the N1 level; it is not a productive pattern (to be used in speech).

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure and Usage
rows: 動詞[どうし]辞書形[じしょけい] + まじき + 名詞[めいし]
Cümleyi asla bitiremez; her zaman ardından bir isim gelir.
ある + まじき → あるまじき
En sık kullanılan kalıp; genellikle 〜にあるまじき〜 şeklinde
許[ゆる]す + まじき → 許[ゆる]すまじき
İkinci en yaygın kalıp; genellikle 〜まじき犯罪[はんざい]/行為[こうい] gibi kelimelerle
する → するまじき / すまじき
すまじき daha eski/edebî; するまじき modern metinlerde de görülür
言[い]う → 言[い]うまじき
footnotes_tr: 〜まじき only creates a noun phrase/modification and does not end a sentence as a predicate (in this respect, it is very similar to 〜べからざる).
This structure is not productive; it is used in crystallized form with a limited number of verbs (especially ある, 許す, する).

tables.caption_tr: Frequently Used Fixed Expressions
rows: 〜にあるまじき発言[はつげん]
〜にあるまじき言葉遣[ことばづか]い
〜にあるまじきことばづかい
許[ゆる]すまじき犯罪[はんざい]
ゆるすまじきはんざい
許[ゆる]すまじき行[おこな]い
ゆるすまじきおこない
footnotes_tr: A noun of position/identity used together with 「〜として」 or 「〜に」 specifies which role the behavior is not fitting for: 教師[きょうし]として / 教師[きょうし]に.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison with Similar Literary Structures
rows: Vる + まじき + 名詞
Vる + べからざる + 名詞
Vる + べきではない (cümle biter)
Vて + はならない (cümle biter)
footnotes_tr: Both 〜まじき and 〜べからざる are noun modifiers and cannot end a sentence; they are very close in meaning, but 〜まじき carries more moral/character criticism, while 〜べからざる emphasizes rules/prohibition more.

tables.caption_tr: Classical Source: 文語 助動詞「まじ」Conjugation Table
rows: まじ (終止形[しゅうしけい])
Cümle sonunda; modern dilde neredeyse kullanılmaz
まじき (連体形[れんたいけい])
Modern dilde tek yaşayan biçim: 〜まじき + 名詞
まじく (連用形[れんようけい])
Zarf işlevi; çok nadir, klasik metinlerde
まじけれ (已然形[いぜんけい])
Sadece klasik metinlerde, modern kullanımda yok
footnotes_tr: In modern Japanese, from the 「まじ」 family, only 連体形, which is 「まじき」, has survived in practice.

ni-taru.title_tr: 〜に足る / 〜に足りない (worth / not worth)
ni-taru.intro_tr: 〜に足[た]る and 〜に足[た]りない are fairly literary and formal (N1 level) patterns that express whether something has the quality of being "adequate/worthy" or "inadequate/unworthy" to a certain value, trust, or emotion. 足る[たる] is the classical (文語) form of the modern 足[た]りる verb and today exists almost exclusively in this frozen form within this pattern. While 〜に足る carries a positive meaning of "worthy of..., sufficient for...", 〜に足りない carries a negative meaning of "unworthy of..., insignificant, not worth considering." It is generally used in formal speech, newspapers, articles, and literary texts; when evaluating a person's qualities, the importance of an event, or whether a fear/suspicion is unfounded. In everyday speech, it is replaced by simpler expressions (for example 〜する価値[かち]がある).

wo-kinjienai.intro_tr: 〜を禁じ得ない (きんじえない), literally means "cannot forbid/prevent …, unable to prevent …"; in everyday usage it means "I cannot refrain from …", "I cannot suppress …". It typically comes after nouns expressing emotions such as 涙[なみだ], 怒[いか]り, 驚[おどろ]き, 同情[どうじょう] and expresses that the speaker cannot contain that emotion, that they express it outwardly. It is a highly formal and writing-specific pattern; it appears frequently in newspaper articles, official reports, essays and literary texts, but is hardly ever used in everyday conversation. The pattern itself already carries a negative meaning (禁[きん]じる = to forbid, 得[え]ない = cannot), so it does not take an additional negation suffix. It is one of the classic ways to express emotion in formal writing, frequently encountered at the N1 level.

tables.caption_tr: Structure and Basic Conjugations
rows: İsim + を + 禁[きん]じ得[え]ない
涙[なみだ]を禁[きん]じ得[え]ない
İsim + を + 禁[きん]じ得[え]なかった (geçmiş zaman)
怒[いか]りを禁[きん]じ得[え]なかった
İsim + を + 禁[きん]じ得[え]ぬ (edebî/klasik varyant)
驚[おどろ]きを禁[きん]じ得[え]ぬ

疑問[ぎもん]を禁[きん]じ得[え]ないでいる
footnotes_tr: The pattern is used only with nouns (especially emotion nouns); verbs in their root form cannot be directly attached to it.
禁[きん]じ得[え]る is actually the potential (ability) form of the verb 禁[きん]じる; in everyday language it is used almost only in its negative form (〜得[え]ない).

It can also be used with neutral or positive nouns (e.g., 喜[よろこ]び) but it emphasizes that the emotion is 'powerfully irrepressible'.

to-atte.intro_tr: 〜とあって is a formal conjunction that carries the meaning "because a special, striking, or extraordinary situation exists, naturally/as a result such an outcome occurred," used mainly in news articles and written narratives. First a striking situation/event is presented, then the natural, expected outcome brought about by this situation is described — it is an observed objective development, not the speaker's own wish, request, or command. It is similar in meaning to だけあって, but とあって carries more the nuance of "because of a special occasion / because a special situation exists" and is generally used with concrete events told in past or present tense. At the N1 level it frequently appears in news, newspaper, and official report language; it is rarely used in everyday conversation.

ni-mo-mashite.intro_tr: 〜にもまして is a formal and literary pattern that expresses a degree exceeding even the standard indicated by a noun, and an even greater extent beyond that; it is typically translated into Turkish as "…-den de fazla" (…more than), "…-den daha da çok" (even more). The verb まして comes from 増す[ます] (to increase, to multiply) and carries the nuance of 〜に加えてもっと (additionally even more). Structurally, にもまして is added directly after a noun or time expression; fixed expressions like İ何[なに]にもまして (more than anything) and いつにもまして (even more than usual) are particularly frequently used. At the N1 level, it mainly appears in written language, in news articles, in formal speeches, and in literary narration; in everyday conversation, it gives way to simpler structures like より or もっと. It is preferred to strongly emphasize the comparison point in the sentence and to convey that a situation has exceeded what was expected or customary.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure and Meaning
rows: Belirtilen ölçütün kendisinin bile aşıldığını, o dereceden daha ileri gidildiğini vurgular
her şeyden çok, her şeyden önce

Zaman içindeki bir artışı, değişimi vurgular
前回[ぜんかい]にもまして
footnotes_tr: にもまして is added directly to a noun or time expression; it does not attach directly to verbs or adjectives.
The structure functions like an adverbial phrase that intensifies the situation/emotional state described in the rest of the sentence.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は以前[いぜん]にもまして仕事[しごと]に熱心[ねっしん]になった。

examples.target: 台風[たいふう]の影響[えいきょう]で、平年[へいねん]にもまして雨[あめ]が多[おお]かった。
examples.reading: たいふうのえいきょうで、へいねんにもましてあめがおおかった。

examples.note_tr: A comparison is made with 平年[へいねん] (ordinary/average year) to emphasize an extraordinary situation.

examples.target: 今回[こんかい]の試験[しけん]は前回[ぜんかい]にもまして難[むずか]しかった。
examples.reading: こんかいのしけんは ぜんかいにもまして むずかしかった。
examples.translation_tr: This exam was harder than the previous one.
examples.note_tr: Taking 前回[ぜんかい] (the previous time) as a reference, it is expressed that this time surpasses even that.

ni-kaketewa.title_tr: 〜にかけては (…no one can surpass him/her in...)
ni-kaketewa.intro_tr: 〜にかけては is an N1-level advanced pattern used to emphasize that a person or thing is superior in a particular subject, field, or ability, and that no one can surpass them. It corresponds to Turkish expressions such as "he/she has no equal in…" or "no one can surpass him/her in…". The sentence always concludes with a positive judgment (一番[いちばん], 負[ま]けない, 自信[じしん]がある, etc.); it is not used with negative or unfavorable evaluations. Structurally, it is formed only as a noun (or nominalized verb) + にかけては, and the は particle within it, by emphasizing the topic, implicitly makes a comparison with other areas: "perhaps not in every subject, but definitely in THIS subject...". It is a vibrant pattern expressing praise and pride that can be used in both everyday conversation and written/formal language.

tables.caption_tr: Basic Structure and Connection Pattern
rows: 名詞[めいし] + にかけては
料理[りょうり]にかけては
動詞[どうし]辞書形[じしょけい] + ことにかけては
泳[およ]ぐことにかけては

de-are-darouto.title_tr: 〜(で)あれ / 〜であろうと (even if ..., whatever)
de-are-darouto.intro_tr: 〜(で)あれ and 〜であろうと, meaning "no matter what, even if...", is a very formal and literary (書[か]き言葉[ことば]) N1 pattern. Generally used with question words like 誰[だれ]・何[なに]・どこ・いつ or together with two contrasting options, it conveys the idea that "regardless of the condition, the result does not change". あれ is the imperative/hypothetical stem of the verb ある in classical Japanese (文語[ぶんご] remnant); であろう is the formal-literary form of だろう, and by adding と after it serves the same function. In everyday conversation, でも, にしても or にしろ are preferred instead; this pattern appears in written language, speeches, and formal texts.

mu-volitional.title_tr: 〜む → 〜ん (Classical Request/Conjecture Suffix and 〜んとする Pattern)
mu-volitional.intro_tr: In Classical Japanese, the auxiliary verb 「む」, attached to the 未然形[みぜんけい] (negative base) of the verb root, conveyed meanings of conjecture, request/intention, invitation, or polite expression — it is the ancestor of modern 〜だろう and 〜（よ）う. During the transition to spoken language, the sound 「む」 contracted to 「ん」 (this sound change is called 撥音便[はつおんびん]). This old 「ん」 has not completely disappeared today; it continues to survive especially in grammaticalized, literary/written expressions like 〜んとする (literally meaning "…in order to/…trying to do"). This construction is nearly identical in meaning to modern 〜ようとする but carries a more formal, classical, and literary tone; it frequently appears in narrative writing, proverbs, and journalistic/fixed expressions. Caution: another 「ん」 heard in modern spoken language (行かん, 知らん, etc.) comes from a different origin (the negation suffix ぬ) — it is important not to confuse these two 「ん」.

tables.caption_tr: 古典助動詞「む」の Principal Meanings (Classical Japanese)
rows: 明日[あす]は雨[あめ]降[ふ]らむ。

footnotes_tr: 「む」 is always attached to the 未然形[みぜんけい] of the verb. In Modern Japanese, this function is distributed among suffixes like 〜だろう, 〜（よ）う.

keigo-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Keigo: Double Politeness (二重敬語[にじゅうけいご]) Errors
keigo-advanced.intro_tr: 二重敬語[にじゅうけいご] is the excessive use, for the same verb or noun, of two politeness/honorific markers from the same category (尊敬語[そんけいご] or 謙譲語[けんじょうご]) layered on top of each other — for example, adding 〜られる to a verb that already has an honorific expression. In Japanese language rules, this is generally considered incorrect and unnecessary because the verb is already sufficiently polite on its own. However, some double structures (お伺いする, 拝見させていただく, お召し上がりになる, etc.) have become so widespread over time that in everyday business Japanese they are recognized as "慣用[かんよう]" (established usage). At the N1 level, it is important both to recognize errors and to know which double structures are accepted as exceptions. This page summarizes the most frequently made 二重敬語 errors, their correct equivalents, and exceptions in table format.

お伺[うかが]いいたす（誤／一部許容）

examples.target: 先生がお帰りになりました。
examples.reading: せんせいがおかえりになりました。
examples.translation_tr: The teacher returned home (respectfully).
examples.note_tr: The correct and singular 尊敬語[そんけいご] pattern: お～になる. Adding られる to this (お帰りになられました) is a common 二重敬語[にじゅうけいご] error.

examples.target: ✕ 先生がお帰りになられました。
examples.reading: せんせいがおかえりになられました。
examples.translation_tr: (Incorrect sentence) The teacher returned home.
examples.note_tr: 『お～になる』 is already 尊敬語 on its own; adding 'られる' additionally is a double politeness (二重敬語) error. The correct form is: お帰りになりました.

examples.target: 社長は明日9時[く じ]にいらっしゃいます。
examples.reading: しゃちょうはあしたくじにいらっしゃいます。
examples.translation_tr: The general manager will come at 9 o'clock tomorrow.
examples.note_tr: いらっしゃる is already a special honorific verb (replacing 来る/行く/いる). Saying いらっしゃられます is a double politeness error.

examples.target: お客様[きゃくさま]が何[なに]になさいますか。
examples.reading: おきゃくさまがなにになさいますか。
examples.translation_tr: What would the honored customer like?
examples.note_tr: なさる is already the special honorific form of する; saying なさられますか is an unnecessary and incorrect instance of double politeness.

examples.target: 資料[しりょう]を拝見[はいけん]しました。
examples.reading: しりょうをはいけんしました。
examples.translation_tr: I examined the document (humbly).
examples.note_tr: 拝見する is already the special 謙譲語[けんじょうご] form of 見る verb; saying ご拝見しました is an incorrect double politeness.

examples.target: お伺[うかが]いしてもよろしいでしょうか。
examples.reading: おうかがいしてもよろしいでしょうか。
examples.translation_tr: May I ask something?
examples.note_tr: According to strict rules, since 伺う is already 謙譲語, お伺いする is technically considered double politeness; however, in business Japanese this pattern is a widely used and accepted exception.

examples.target: 部長[ぶちょう]がお召[め]し上[あ]がりになりました。
examples.reading: ぶちょうがおめしあがりになりました。
examples.translation_tr: The manager ate the meal (respectfully).
examples.note_tr: 召し上がる is already the special honorific form of 食べる/飲む verbs; adding お～になる to this is theoretically double politeness, but it is a widely used and accepted exception in society.

examples.target: 田中様[たなかさま]でいらっしゃいますか。
examples.reading: たなかさまでいらっしゃいますか。
examples.translation_tr: Are you Mr./Ms. Tanaka?
examples.note_tr: The でいらっしゃる pattern is not double politeness; it is the polite form of the だ/である copula, a single-layered correct 尊敬語 structure.

imada-ni.title_tr: 〜いまだに / 〜ずじまい — Still; Ending without ...-ing
imada-ni.intro_tr: 〜いまだに and 〜ずじまい, though apparently different, are two N1 patterns that complement each other in meaning. 〜いまだに (未だに) means "still, even now" and generally emphasizes that an expected change has not occurred, that a situation persists stubbornly; it is most often used with negative verbs or disappointment-laden sentences. 〜ずじまい, on the other hand, is added to the negative -ず form of a verb to convey the meaning "ended up without ...-ing, finished without ...-ing"; it expresses regret or disappointment regarding an action that was planned but did not happen. Both appear in written and formal/literary narratives rather than everyday conversation, in emotionally emphasized sentences. The formation rules, exceptions, and frequently used patterns are given in detail in the tables below.

tables.caption_tr: 〜いまだに: Structure and Basic Usage
rows: いまだに + olumsuz fiil (〜ない)
いまだに分[わ]からない
いまだに続[つづ]けている
いまだに独身[どくしん]だ
それでも いまだに〜
それでもいまだに信[しん]じない
いまだかつて〜ない (edebî varyant)
いまだかつて経験[けいけん]したことがない
footnotes_tr: いまだに generally carries the speaker's surprise, disappointment, or criticism: it has the nuance of 'despite so much time passing, still...'
It can also be written as 今[いま]だに, but the standard spelling is 未[いま]だに; the kanji 未 comes from the 未[みだ] root meaning 'yet/not yet'.

footnotes_tr: Rule: the 'ない' in the ない form of the verb is removed, and ずじまい is added in its place (classical 〜ず negation suffix + じまい 'ending up').
The most important exception: the verb する becomes せずじまい, NOT しずじまい (the classical ず suffix uses the archaic 古語 root form せ instead of する).
The word じまい comes from the noun 仕舞[しま]い meaning 'ending, closure'; the meaning of the construction is precisely 'finished without ...-ing'.

volitional-form.title_tr: Request/Suggestion Form (〜よう / 〜ましょう) — Volitional Form
volitional-form.intro_tr: 〜よう (意向形[いこうけい], "request/volitional form") and 〜ましょう are conjugations in Japanese that mean "...-let us, ...-I will, let's ...-" and express the speaker's own desire, decision, or a suggestion. 〜ましょう is used in polite speech, while 〜よう is used in family/friend casual speech and when speaking to oneself (inner voice). This form also serves as the foundation for advanced patterns like 〜(よ)うと思[おも]う (expressing intent) and 〜(よ)うとする (trying to do). It is derived differently depending on the verb group (godan, ichidan, irregular); all rules and exceptions are summarized in the tables below.

tables.caption_tr: Godan Verbs: う-row → お-row Transformation Table (forming 意向形[いこうけい])
column_headers: 意向形[いこうけい] hali
footnotes_tr: Rule: the う-row sound in the final syllable of a godan verb is changed to the お-row, and う is added at the end.
The verb 行[い]く works regularly: 行[い]こう (ikou).

quotation-to-iu.intro_tr: The particle と is used in Japanese to convey (quote) something that someone else said, thought, or wrote. Combined with the verb 言う[いう] (to say), it forms the pattern と言う[という]; this pattern can be used for both direct quotation (exact conveyance of a sentence in quotation marks) and indirect quotation (summary of a sentence conveyed in 普通形[ふつうけい], or plain form). また, という is also frequently used to introduce or name something with the meaning "called, named, or said to be" (e.g., 桜[さくら]という花[はな] "a flower called sakura"). The same と + verb logic works with perception and thought verbs such as 思う[おもう] (to think), 聞く[きく] (to hear), 書く[かく] (to write). At the N4 level, the most commonly encountered uses in everyday conversation are conveying someone's words, naming something, and indicating heard or read information.

Dolaylı alıntı: söyleneni özetleyerek/plain formla aktarma

名詞[めいし] + という + 名詞[めいし]
寿司[すし]という料理[りょうり]を知[し]っていますか。
footnotes_tr: In indirect quotation, verbs/adjectives/nouns generally take the 普通形[ふつうけい] (dictionary/plain form); the polite です・ます形 is rarely used except in direct quotation.

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は「明日[あした]は忙[いそが]しい」と言[い]いました。
examples.reading: かれは「あしたはいそがしい」といいました。
examples.translation_tr: He/She said, "I'm busy tomorrow."
examples.note_tr: Direct quotation: the sentence within quotation marks is conveyed exactly as is, and the polite form can be preserved.

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんは来[こ]られないと言[い]いました。
examples.reading: たなかさんはこられないといいました。
examples.translation_tr: Tanaka-san said that he/she could not come.
examples.note_tr: Indirect quotation: the verb is used with 普通形[ふつうけい] (plain form), and there are no quotation marks.

examples.target: これは「桜[さくら]」という花[はな]です。
examples.reading: これは「さくら」というはなです。
examples.translation_tr: This is a flower called "sakura."
examples.note_tr: Noun + という + noun: a pattern for introducing/naming something.

examples.target: 明日[あした]の会議[かいぎ]は中止[ちゅうし]だということです。
examples.reading: あしたのかいぎはちゅうしだということです。
examples.translation_tr: It is said that tomorrow's meeting has been canceled (according to what I heard).
examples.note_tr: 〜ということだ: a pattern for conveying hearsay/information heard, giving the meaning 'it is said that.'

examples.target: 「頑張[がんば]って」と友達[ともだち]に言[い]われました。
examples.reading: 「がんばって」ととものだちにいわれました。
examples.translation_tr: My friend told me, "Do your best."
examples.note_tr: 言われる: the passive form of the verb と言う, meaning 'I was told/it was said to me.'

examples.target: 田中[たなか]さんという人[ひと]を知[し]っていますか。
examples.reading: たなかさんというひとをしっていますか。
examples.translation_tr: Do you know a person called Tanaka?
examples.note_tr: という is used here for introductory purposes with the meaning 'called, named, or said to be.'

examples.target: 母[はは]は明日[あした]早[はや]く起[お]きると言[い]っていました。
examples.reading: はははあしたはやくおきるといっていました。
examples.translation_tr: My mother was saying that she would wake up early tomorrow.
examples.note_tr: 〜と言っていた: conveying a statement made in the past that is still valid.

examples.target: どういう意味[いみ]ですか。
examples.reading: どういういみですか。
examples.translation_tr: What does this mean?
examples.note_tr: どういう: the interrogative form of という with the meaning 'what kind of' or 'how.'

dake-shika-bakari.title_tr: だけ / しか / ばかり (Only)
dake-shika-bakari.intro_tr: だけ, しか, and ばかり are all three often translated into English as "only," but their grammatical structures and emotional tones are quite different from each other. だけ expresses a neutral amount/scope limitation and is used in affirmative sentences. しか, on the other hand, must always come with a negative predicate and emphasizes scarcity, insufficiency, or disappointment (the logic of "nothing but/only"). ばかり is used both to mean "mostly/always" (expressing that something is done excessively frequently, generally in a tone with slight criticism) and in additional patterns such as 〜たばかり ("just...-ed") and 〜てばかりいる ("constantly...-ing"). Knowing the correct attachment rules and nuance differences of these three particles is the key to speaking natural Japanese.

tables.caption_tr: だけ・しか・ばかり General Comparison

passive-form.title_tr: Passive Voice (受身形[うけみけい]) ~られる / ~れる
passive-form.intro_tr: Passive voice (受身形[うけみけい]) expresses that an action is not performed by the subject, but rather the subject is affected by that action; it corresponds to Turkish suffixes "-il-, -in-, -ün-" (yazılmak, görülmek, sevilmek, etc.). However, Japanese passive voice has an important difference: it not only expresses the meaning of "being done by someone," but also carries the meaning of "迷惑受身[めいわくうけみ]" (nuisance/inconvenience passive) which indicates that the speaker is negatively affected by an event — this usage does not have a direct equivalent in Turkish and is usually translated as "happened to me, I was annoyed," etc. The conjugation form changes depending on the verb group: in Godan verbs, the う sound changes to あ sound and れる is added; in Ichidan verbs, る is dropped and られる is added; the する verb becomes される, and the 来る[くる] verb becomes 来られる[こられる]. In Ichidan verbs, the form of the passive voice and the potential voice are exactly the same (られる), so the meaning must be determined from context and particles in the sentence. In passive sentences, generally the object in the active sentence moves to the subject position, and the old subject is marked with に (sometimes によって).

conj-irregular-full.title_tr: Verb Conjugation Table: する / 来[く]る (Irregular Verbs, All Forms)
conj-irregular-full.intro_tr: する and 来[く]る are the only two completely irregular (outside the verb groups) verbs in Japanese; therefore, their conjugations do not follow godan and ichidan rules and must be memorized separately. During conjugation, する shows sound (stem) changes between し／す／せ／さ, while 来[く]る changes between こ／き／く. Additionally, する combines with hundreds of 漢語[かんご] or カタカナ nouns (like 勉強[べんきょう]する, 電話[でんわ]する) to form new verbs; in these compound verbs, only the する part is conjugated while the noun part remains fixed. The capability (可能形[かのうけい]) form of する is not しられる but rather the completely different word できる — this is the most frequently confused exception at the N4 level. In the tables below, all conjugation forms of both verbs, compound する verbs, and comparisons with regular verbs (godan/ichidan) are provided together.

tables.caption_tr: する — All Conjugation Forms
rows: ませんでした (kibar olumsuz geçmiş)
Bağlama, rica (してください), süreklilik
Emir; しろ konuşma dili, せよ yazı/edebî dili
'Yapabilmek' — TAMAMEN AYRI KELİME, しられる değil!
使役受身形[しえきうけみけい] (ettirgen-edilgen)
footnotes_tr: できる is a completely different verb (suppletive form) that replaces する's expected しられる/せられる form — this is the most commonly mistaken point on exams.
命令形 しろ is used in casual/masculine speech, while せよ is used in written, formal, or sports/military commands.
される can carry both passive meaning ('to be done') and, in some contexts, honorific (尊敬語) meaning.

tables.caption_tr: 来る[くる] — All Conjugation Forms
rows: ませんでした (kibar olumsuz geçmiş)
Bağlama, rica (来[き]てください), süreklilik
'Gelinmek' (aynı biçim, bağlamdan ayırt edilir — genelde rahatsızlık edilgeni: 雨に来[こ]られた 'yağmurdan muzdarip oldum')
使役受身形[しえきうけみけい] (ettirgen-edilgen)
footnotes_tr: 来[こ]られる can have three different meanings: (1) capability 'to be able to come', (2) passive/adversative passive, (3) honorific form (尊敬語) 'to come' (for teacher/customer). Meaning is derived from context.
来る on its own is generally written in hiragana (くる) in spoken language, but the kanji 来る is preferred in formal/written texts.

tables.caption_tr: Irregular Comparison: する / くる vs Godan / Ichidan Examples
footnotes_tr: In godan and ichidan verbs, the stem changes according to a single regular rule; in する and くる, however, each form uses a different stem that must be memorized — this is why they are called 'irregular verbs' (不規則動詞[ふきそくどうし]).

tables.caption_tr: 名詞[めいし]＋する Compound Verbs (Most Frequently Used)
footnotes_tr: In compound する verbs, ONLY the する part is conjugated: 勉強[べんきょう]しません, 勉強[べんきょう]した, 勉強[べんきょう]できる, etc.
を can be placed between the noun and the verb: 勉強[べんきょう]をする、電話[でんわ]をする — the meaning remains the same, only the noun is emphasized.

tables.caption_tr: Stem (Root) Sound Changes: する and くる
rows: ます, ない, た, て, たい, ながら (します, しない, した, して...)
来[き]ます, 来[き]て, 来[き]た, 来[き]たい
sözlük formu (する), ば formu (すれば)
sözlük formu (来[く]る), ば formu (来[く]れば)
しよう, させる, される, せよ
来[こ]よう, 来[こ]い, 来[こ]させる, 来[こ]られる, 来[こ]ない
footnotes_tr: This table shows which conjugation suffix is added to which stem form of the verb; studying by syllable group makes memorization easier.

examples.reading: すぐにきてください。

examples.reading: かんじはむずかしいから、できないとおもう。

examples.note_tr: できる — the capability form of する; not しられる, but a completely separate word.

kanji-radicals.intro_tr: 漢字[かんじ] radicals, that is 部首[ぶしゅ], are the fundamental building block pieces that make up kanjis. Each kanji is composed of one or several radicals, and radicals generally provide clues about the meaning category of the kanji; sometimes they also carry a hint about its pronunciation. For example, kanjis containing 氵(さんずい, "water" radical) usually relate to water/liquid: 海[うみ], 泳[およ]ぐ, 洗[あら]う. Radicals are also used for searching kanji in paper dictionaries (部首索引[ぶしゅさくいん]) and make it easier to memorize new kanjis by breaking them down into parts. On this page you will learn the 7 fundamental position types of radicals within kanji and the most frequently encountered radicals, along with their meanings and examples.

examples.target: 木[き]でできた家[いえ]に住[す]んでいます。
examples.reading: きでできたいえにすんでいます。
examples.translation_tr: I live in a house made of wood.
examples.note_tr: In the word 「家[いえ]」, the radical 宀(うかんむり) carries the meaning "house/roof", while in the word 「木[き]」, the radical 木(きへん similar root kanji) carries the meaning "tree".

examples.target: 毎日[まいにち]日本語[にほんご]を勉強[べんきょう]しています。
examples.reading: まいにちにほんごをべんきょうしています。
examples.translation_tr: I study Japanese every day.
examples.note_tr: The word 「語[ご]」 contains the radical 言(ごんべん) "word, speech".

examples.target: 川[かわ]で泳[およ]ぐのが好[す]きです。
examples.reading: かわでおよぐのがすきです。
examples.translation_tr: I like swimming in the river.
examples.note_tr: The word 「泳[およ]ぐ」 contains the radical 氵(さんずい) "water"; thanks to this, one can infer that the word is related to water.

examples.target: 花[はな]の茶[ちゃ]を飲[の]みます。
examples.reading: はなのちゃをのみます。
examples.translation_tr: I am drinking flower tea.
examples.note_tr: Both the words 「花[はな]」 and 「茶[ちゃ]」 contain the radical 艹(くさかんむり) "plant" at the top.

examples.target: 病気[びょうき]で学校[がっこう]を休[やす]みました。
examples.reading: びょうきでがっこうをやすみました。
examples.translation_tr: I couldn't go to school because of illness.
examples.note_tr: The word 「病[びょう]」 contains the radical 疒(やまいだれ) "illness"; the word 「休[やす]む」 contains the radical 亻(にんべん) "person".

examples.target: 近[ちか]い道[みち]を通[とお]って学校[がっこう]に行[い]きます。
examples.reading: ちかいみちをとおってがっこうにいきます。
examples.translation_tr: I go to school via the nearby path.
examples.note_tr: In the words 「近[ちか]い」 and 「道[みち]」, the radical 辶(しんにょう) "path, to go" wraps around from the left toward the bottom.

examples.target: 国[くに]の名前[なまえ]を漢字[かんじ]で書[か]きます。
examples.reading: くにのなまえをかんじでかきます。
examples.translation_tr: I write the country's name in kanji.
examples.note_tr: In the word 「国[くに]」, the radical 囗(くにがまえ) "enclosure, border" surrounds the kanji from all sides.

examples.target: 妹[いもうと]は忙[いそが]しいので忘[わす]れっぽいです。
examples.reading: いもうとはいそがしいのでわすれっぽいです。
examples.translation_tr: My younger sister is forgetful because she is busy.
examples.note_tr: The word 「忙[いそが]しい」 contains the radical 忄(りっしんべん), and the word 「忘[わす]れる」 contains the radical 心(こころ) "heart, emotion" — both derive from the same root.

nimo-kakawarazu.intro_tr: 〜にもかかわらず means "...despite, ...in spite of", a formal conjunction that emphasizes an unexpected result contrary to what was expected. It functions very similarly to のに, but is a more written/formal expression; it is frequently encountered in news texts, formal speeches, and business correspondence. It emphasizes the strong contrast between two situations (often accompanied by feelings of surprise, disappointment, or appreciation). The word かかわらず comes from the verb 関[かか]わる (to be related, to be connected); もかかわらず means "despite being related/connected". Note: にかかわらず (without も) has a completely different meaning — it means "...regardless of, without making a difference", and these two are frequently confused.

tables.caption_tr: Connection Patterns (By Word Type)
rows: 名詞[めいし] + にもかかわらず
雨[あめ]にもかかわらず (yağmura rağmen)
な-sıfat + であるにもかかわらず (resmî) / na-sıfat + にもかかわらず (konuşmaya yakın)
静[しず]かであるにもかかわらず (sessiz olmasına rağmen)
い-sıfat（辞書形[じしょけい]）+ にもかかわらず
忙[いそが]しいにもかかわらず (meşgul olmasına rağmen)
動詞[どうし]辞書形[じしょけい] + にもかかわらず
知[し]っているにもかかわらず (bildiği halde)
動詞[どうし]た形[けい] + にもかかわらず
頑張[がんば]ったにもかかわらず (çabalamasına rağmen)
それにもかかわらず、彼[かれ]は来[こ]なかった。(Buna rağmen o gelmedi.)
footnotes_tr: Past-tense event + にもかかわらず expresses an unexpected result that occurred in the past.
Adding である to な-adjectives and nouns gives a more formal/written tone; in everyday conversation である is often omitted.

tables.caption_tr: Comparison of 〜にもかかわらず with Similar Expressions
rows: Güçlü tezat, beklenmedik sonuç; genelde nesnel anlatım
努力[どりょく]したにもかかわらず失敗[しっぱい]した。
Beklenmedik sonuç + genelde şaşkınlık/hayal kırıklığı/sitem duygusu
Günlük konuşma ve yazı, her ikisinde de yaygın
頑張[がんば]ったのに失敗[しっぱい]した。
Aynı özne içinde iki çelişkili durumun bir arada olması
小[ちい]さいながらも立派[りっぱ]な家[いえ]だ。
Basit karşıtlık, 'ama'; duygusal vurgu daha zayıf
頑張[がんば]ったけど失敗[しっぱい]した。
'Fark etmeksizin, ilgisiz olarak' — FARKLI ANLAM, karıştırılmamalı
天気[てんき]にかかわらず、試合[しあい]は行[おこな]われる。
footnotes_tr: 〜にもかかわらず in the second part of the sentence generally implies the speaker's surprise or disappointment, but it is not as strong/emotional as のに.
にかかわらず is generally used with question words+も or contrasting compound structures (like 雨[あめ]天[てん]にかかわらず) and carries the meaning of 'regardless' rather than 'despite'.

tables.caption_tr: Usage Characteristics and Points to Note
rows: Ağırlıklı olarak yazı dili ve resmî konuşmada kullanılır; günlük sohbette のに veya のに/けど tercih edilir.
Genellikle şaşırma, hayranlık, eleştiri veya hayal kırıklığı gibi bir duyguyu ima eder — sadece nötr bir 'ama' değildir.
İkinci cümlecik genelde olumsuz/beklenmedik bir sonuç bildirir: 失敗[しっぱい]した, 遅刻[ちこく]した, 続[つづ]けられた gibi.
Cümle başında bağımsız bağlaç olarak kullanılır: 'buna rağmen' anlamında, önceki cümleyle bağlantı kurar.
にかかわらず ile karışma
にもかかわらず = '…-e rağmen' (tezat); にかかわらず (も’suz) = '…-e bakmaksızın' (ilgisizlik/kayıtsızlık) — anlamca tamamen farklıdır, sınavlarda sık karıştırılır.
〜にもかかわらず, てください veya ましょう gibi teklif/emir cümleleriyle doğrudan bitirilmez; olgusal bir sonucu bildirir.

examples.target: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っているにもかかわらず、試合[しあい]は続[つづ]けられた。

examples.target: 彼[かれ]は若[わか]いにもかかわらず、とても落[お]ち着[つ]いている。

examples.target: 何度[なんど]も注意[ちゅうい]したにもかかわらず、彼[かれ]はまた遅刻[ちこく]した。
examples.reading: なんどもちゅういしたにもかかわらず、かれはまたちこくした。

examples.target: 忙[いそが]しいにもかかわらず、会議[かいぎ]に参加[さんか]してくれてありがとうございます。
examples.reading: いそがしいにもかかわらず、かいぎにさんかしてくれてありがとうございます。

examples.target: 経済[けいざい]が不安定[ふあんてい]であるにもかかわらず、株価[かぶか]は上昇[じょうしょう]した。
examples.reading: けいざいがふあんていであるにもかかわらず、かぶかはじょうしょうした。

examples.target: それにもかかわらず、彼[かれ]は最後[さいご]まで諦[あきら]めなかった。
examples.reading: それにもかかわらず、かれはさいごまであきらめなかった。

examples.target: 努力[どりょく]したにもかかわらず、試験[しけん]に落[お]ちてしまった。

kara-koso.intro_tr: 〜からこそ and its classical/literary counterpart 〜ばこそ are patterns that emphasize the reason strongly by adding the emphatic particle こそ (precisely, exactly) to the normal conjunction 〜から (because). They carry the meaning "not just for this reason, but precisely for this reason" and the sentence generally ends with 〜のだ / 〜のです to reinforce the explanatory tone. While 〜からこそ is frequently used in everyday and written language, 〜ばこそ is more formal, literary, and somewhat old-fashioned; it is formed by adding こそ to the ば-form. Both patterns are generally used with a consequential clause expressing affirmation or appreciation (e.g., "it is valuable precisely because it is difficult"). At the N2 level, it is frequently encountered in speech and writing for emphasizing reasons, but should be learned as an alternative that is more "literary and impactful" than the simple 〜から.

footnotes_tr: The sentence generally ends with an explanatory expression such as 〜のだ / 〜のです / 〜と思う: 「〜からこそ、〜のです」.
The reason can also be in the past tense: 頑張[がんば]ったからこそ、合格[ごうかく]できた。

kake-kakeru.intro_tr: The ~かける suffix, when added to the ます-stem of a verb, conveys the meaning "started to do an action but stopped halfway/left unfinished" or "almost ...-ed, was just about to ...". Forms derived from the same root, ~かけの (modifies nouns) and ~かけだ (used as a predicate), express something or a state that is "half-done, unfinished". かける itself conjugates like a 一段[いちだん] verb, therefore it can be used in all forms such as て形, た形, ない形, etc. This structure, unlike 始[はじ]める in particular, carries the emphasis that the action remained HALF/INCOMPLETE or was interrupted; in patterns like 死[し]にかける, on the other hand, the meaning of "almost ...-ed, dangerously approached ..." comes to the fore.

ni-itaru.title_tr: 〜に至る / 〜に至って / 〜に至っては (…reaching a point)
ni-itaru.intro_tr: The 〜に至る group (に至る / に至って / に至っては / に至るまで) is an N1 level pattern in Japanese that expresses "reaching" a serious, extreme, or unexpected point at the end of a process, and is frequently used in formal and written language. The verb 至る[いたる] means "to reach, to arrive" in its dictionary sense; therefore 〜に至る is generally translated as "…reaching up to a point, …coming to" and mostly emphasizes a bad, serious, or irreversible result. 〜に至って, on the other hand, with the meaning "only when reaching that point, only then," indicates that something is noticed or realized late. 〜に至っては is used to bring to the foreground the most extreme, most excessive, or most criticizable among multiple examples or cases, and generally ends with a negative judgment. 〜に至るまで emphasizes that it includes even the farthest or most extreme point of a list or scope (meaning "…even up to"). This pattern is almost never used in spoken language; it appears in news articles, official reports, academic writings, and literary narratives.

bungo-relic-forms.title_tr: 文語[ぶんご] Residual Inflections: 〜ざる / 〜べき / 〜たる Adjective Usage
bungo-relic-forms.intro_tr: 文語[ぶんご] (classical written language), not spoken in modern Japanese, but some inflectional remnants in fossilized (化石化[かせきか]) form continue to persist in today's official writing, in idioms, and in newspaper headlines. On this page, three important remnants are examined: (1) 〜ざる — the 連体形[れんたいけい] (noun-modifying) form of the classical negation auxiliary verb「ず」, corresponding to modern「〜ない」; (2) 〜べき — the 連体形[れんたいけい] form of the classical necessity/supposition auxiliary verb「べし」, and is still actively used in modern Japanese; (3) 〜たる — the 連体形[れんたいけい] form of the copulative (断定[だんてい]) auxiliary verb「たり」derived from the classical particle「と」+「あり」, usually combines with two-character Sino-derived words (such as 堂々[どうどう], 厳然[げんぜん]) to form a magnificent/formal adjective. These three forms frequently appear at the N1 level; they are found in written formal texts, idioms, and literary expressions, not in everyday speech. In the tables below, the complete classical conjugation of each form, the most frequently used patterns, and modern equivalents are listed.

tables.caption_tr: ず (打消[うちけし], negation) Auxiliary Verb's Classical Conjugation — Origin of 〜ざる Form
rows: cümle sonu, edebi kalıp (例: 知らず)
isim niteler → MODERN 〜ざる buradan gelir (見えざる手)
koşul kökü, 〜ざれば gibi kalıntılarda görülür
footnotes_tr: 「ぬ」and「ざる」share the same 連体形[れんたいけい] cell; however, in modern times almost only 〜ざる is used as an attributive adjective pattern (許されざる, 知らざる).

tables.caption_tr: べし (推量[すいりょう]・当然[とうぜん], supposition/necessity) Auxiliary Verb's Conjugation — Origin of 〜べき Form
rows: べからず, べからざる gibi kalıpların kökü
〜べく edebi bağlaç olarak hâlâ kullanılır (合格すべく努力する)

isim niteler → MODERN 〜べき buradan gelir (考えるべき問題)
koşul kökü, günümüzde neredeyse hiç kullanılmaz
footnotes_tr: In modern Japanese, 〜べき can be used both as 連体形[れんたいけい] and as a standalone predicate (行くべきだ); this is a somewhat relaxed version of classical grammar rules.

tables.caption_tr: たり (断定[だんてい], derived from と+あり) Auxiliary Verb's Conjugation — Origin of 〜たる Form

isim niteler → MODERN 〜たる buradan gelir (堂々たる態度)

footnotes_tr: This「たり」should not be confused with another classical「たり」expressing 完了[かんりょう] (completion) (derived from つ+あり); the たり here only functions as an attributive adjective.

ya-ina-ya.title_tr: 〜や否や (as soon as … / no sooner … than …)
ya-ina-ya.intro_tr: 〜や否や is a rather literary and formal N1 pattern that expresses that "as soon as one action occurs, another action immediately follows." It corresponds exactly to the English structure "as soon as … / no sooner … than …" and is generally encountered in written language, in novels, newspapers, and news texts. It emphasizes that there is almost no time gap between the two events; in spoken language, the more natural 〜たとたん(に) or 〜とすぐに is preferred instead. The pattern is used with the dictionary form (辞書形) of the verb, and the second clause usually contains a past-tense, unexpected/sudden result; expressions such as requests, commands, or wishes are not used in the second clause.

tables.caption_tr: Yapı: Fiil (sözlük形) + や否[いな]や
footnotes_tr: The pattern is only added to the dictionary form (辞書形) of the verb; it is NOT used with the ta-form or the masu-form.
The action in the second clause occurs immediately after the first action, almost at the same moment.

In everyday conversation, these three are almost never used; instead, 〜たとたんに or 〜てすぐに is preferred.

made-no-koto-mo-nai.title_tr: 〜までもなく / 〜までもない (without the need to..., no need to even...)
made-no-koto-mo-nai.intro_tr: 〜までもなく (and its terminal form 〜までもない) is used to express that performing an action or a check is so obvious, evident, or insignificant that it is unnecessary; it corresponds to expressions such as "there's no need to even...", "without there being a need to...". It attaches to the dictionary form (辞書形) of a verb and is generally used together with verification verbs such as seeing, hearing, saying, and checking (like 見るまでもない, 言うまでもない, 聞くまでもない). 〜までもない functions as the predicate that ends a sentence, whereas 〜までもなく functions as an adverbial/connective form linking to the following clause. It is a fairly written and formal expression; it is encountered at the N1 level and is rarely used in everyday conversation. Although it is close in meaning to similar expressions such as 〜には及ばない, 〜べくもない, and 〜必要はない, there are nuance differences.

keigo-written.title_tr: Written Formal Language — 拝啓[はいけい]／敬具[けいぐ] and Letter Patterns
keigo-written.intro_tr: Formal letters and business correspondence in Japanese are written using fixed patterns that are completely different from everyday spoken language. Every letter begins with a "頭語[とうご]" (opening word) and ends with a corresponding "結語[けつご]" (closing word) — this pair is never chosen independently of each other. A letter follows a fixed order: opening, seasonal greeting, well-wishing for the other party, thanks, main text, and closing sentence. This register is generally used together with 敬語[けいご] (尊敬語/謙譲語) and appears at N1 level in formal correspondence, business letters, invitations, and congratulatory/condolence writings. The tables below summarize the letter skeleton, set phrases, and envelope/address writing rules.

A letter that starts with 拝啓 never ends with 草々; each opening matches its own closing.

formal-written-connectives.title_tr: 資格[しかく]文書[ぶんしょ]の接続[せつぞく]詞[し]：および／ならびに／または／かつ（Resmî Yazı Bağlaçları）
formal-written-connectives.intro_tr: および、ならびに、または、かつ; these are the formal written language (書[か]き言葉[ことば]) counterparts of conjunctions used in everyday speech such as と、や、か、そして. They appear in laws, regulations, official correspondence, contracts, and business documents; they are never used in everyday conversation. These four conjunctions are divided into two groups: および／ならびに carry the meaning of "and," listing nouns/items, while または／かつ carry the meanings of "or" and "both...and" respectively. The most critical point is that および and ならびに, and または and もしくは, have a hierarchical grouping rule when used TOGETHER: small groups are connected on the inside, large groups on the outside. This page covers the complete usage rules of these four conjunctions (and the related もしくは) for formal text reading/writing skills at the N1 level.

tables.caption_tr: General comparison of the four formal conjunctions
rows: isim, isim grubu (2 veya daha fazla öge)
および ile birlikte hiyerarşik sıralama
または ile birlikte hiyerarşik seçim
İki şartın eş zamanlı sağlanması gerektiğinde
footnotes_tr: All of these conjunctions belong to the 書き言葉 (written language) register; they are not used in spoken conversation, and if used, they sound artificial/comical.
および and または are usually placed between the second-to-last item and the last item: A、B、C および D.

tables.caption_tr: および vs ならびに — the hierarchical grouping rule
rows: Aynı kategorideki iki/daha fazla ögeyi birbirine bağlar
(A および B) ならびに (C および D)
Zaten oluşmuş iki grubu birbirine bağlar
Gruplama gerekmiyorsa sadece および yeterlidir; ならびに kullanılmaz
A ならびに B (grup yokken)
Tek seviyeli sıralamada ならびに kullanmak hatalıdır; sadece および kullanılmalıdır
footnotes_tr: Rule: if there is NO grouping, only および is used. If there IS grouping, および is used for the small group, and ならびに is used for the large/outer connection.

tables.caption_tr: または vs もしくは — the hierarchical selection rule (または／もしくは の使い分け)
rows: Aynı kategori içindeki alternatifleri birbirine bağlar
(A もしくは B) または (C もしくは D)
Zaten oluşmuş iki seçenek grubunu birbirine bağlar
Gruplama gerekmiyorsa sadece または yeterlidir
Üç veya daha fazla eş düzey seçenek
En yaygın ve nötr kullanım budur
footnotes_tr: In everyday correspondence, generally only または is used; もしくは is mostly seen in multi-layered official documents such as legal texts.

tables.caption_tr: かつ の kullanım kalıpları
rows: A であり、かつ B である
公正[こうせい]であり、かつ透明[とうめい]である
安[やす]く、かつ早[はや]く
A し、かつ B する
検討[けんとう]し、かつ承認[しょうにん]する
A、かつ B でなければならない
有資格[ゆうしかく]者[しゃ]であり、かつ経験[けいけん]者[しゃ]でなければならない
footnotes_tr: Unlike the て-form, かつ emphasizes not just sequencing but that two conditions must hold SIMULTANEOUSLY / TOGETHER.
It is generally written separated by a comma: 、かつ、

examples.target: 本[ほん]規則[きそく]は、教員[きょういん]および[および]職員[しょくいん]に適用[てきよう]される。

examples.note_tr: および is the written-language conjunction used in place of 'と' in official documents.

examples.target: 会員[かいいん]は、氏名[しめい]、住所[じゅうしょ]ならびに[ならびに]電話番号[でんわばんごう]および[および]メールアドレスを登録[とうろく]しなければならない。

examples.note_tr: Two-layered grouping: the small group (phone+email) is connected with および, and the large group with ならびに — the 'name, address' group and the 'phone, email' group are combined.

examples.target: 委員[いいん]は、専門[せんもん]知識[ちしき]を有[ゆう]し、かつ[かつ]公正[こうせい]な判断[はんだん]ができる者[もの]でなければならない。

examples.note_tr: かつ emphasizes that two conditions must be satisfied SIMULTANEOUSLY; it is a stronger and more formal connector than the て-form.

examples.target: 本[ほん]規定[きてい]に違反[いはん]した者[もの]は、警告[けいこく]または[または]除名[じょめい]の処分[しょぶん]を受[う]ける。

examples.target: 出席者[しゅっせきしゃ]は、会員[かいいん]本人[ほんにん]もしくは[もしくは]その代理人[だいりにん]、または[または]委任[いにん]を受[う]けた者[もの]とする。

examples.note_tr: In the または／もしくは pair as well, the same hierarchy rule as および／ならびに applies: options within a small group are connected with もしくは, and the choice between large groups is connected with または.

examples.note_tr: Typical contract language: および (the signature+seal group) and かつ (an additional mandatory condition) are used together.

o-verb-ni-naru.title_tr: お〜になる / お〜する Patterns — Keigo (Respectful Language) Verb Structures
o-verb-ni-naru.intro_tr: お〜になる and お〜する are two of the most common and regular patterns used in Japanese to produce 尊敬語[そんけいご] which expresses respect and 謙譲語[けんじょうご] which expresses humility. お〜になる elevates the action of the person before you (teacher, customer, superior) in expression; お〜する, on the other hand, lowers your own action to show respect to the other party — meaning お〜になる is never used for your own action, and お〜する is never used for the other party's action. Both patterns are formed together with the ます-stem (連用形[れんようけい]) of the verb; for two-syllable verbs of kanji origin (漢語[かんご]+する), the prefix ご is preferred over お. However, frequently used verbs like 行く[いく], 来る[くる], する, 言う[いう], 見る[みる], 食べる[たべる] have their own unique (special) keigo forms, and in these verbs the お〜になる/お〜する pattern is not used, and special forms are preferred instead.

tables.caption_tr: Creating お〜になる (尊敬語) — Elevating the action of others
footnotes_tr: This pattern is used only for the action of others (superiors, customers, teachers, etc.), never for your own action.

tables.caption_tr: Creating お〜する (謙譲語) — Presenting one's own action with humility
footnotes_tr: This pattern is used only if your own action is directed toward the other party; it is not used for the other party's action.

tables.caption_tr: ご〜になる / ご〜する — ご instead of お in 漢語+する (two-syllable kanji + する) verbs

footnotes_tr: General rule: 訓読み[くんよみ] (native reading) verbs take お, 音読み[おんよみ] (kanji reading) two-syllable verbs take ご. Exceptions exist (e.g. お電話[でんわ]する は is common usage).

koto-da.intro_tr: 〜ことだ is a versatile structure with two main functions at the N2 level. First, with the pattern verb dictionary form or ない form + ことだ, it gives strong and usually generally-applicable advice/counsel to the other party; it means "you should…, you must…" and often carries a slightly imperative tone, like "if you're smart, you should do this." Second, with the pattern い-adjective or な-adjective + (な) + ことだ, it forms an exclamatory sentence expressing a strong emotion such as surprise, admiration, or sorrow felt in the face of a situation; it means "how…!" The advice-meaning usage is frequently heard in spoken language and is generally directed not at third persons but directly at the listener or a general "person" subject. Compared to べきだ, it carries a less formal but more definite/imperative tone of advice than ほうがいい; the exclamatory usage, on the other hand, is more commonly seen in written and literary language.

In the exclamatory usage of な形容詞, な is mandatory: 静かな[しずかな]ことだ (How quiet!).

footnotes_tr: This usage generally has the nature of counsel directed at a general listener or the subject 'everyone/people'; it is not natural when talking about a specific third person.
In spoken language, よ is sometimes added at the end to strengthen the emphasis: 早く[はやく]寝る[ねる]ことだよ。

rows: 何[なん]と素晴らしい[すばらしい]ことだ!
合格[ごうかく]できて嬉しい[うれしい]ことだ。

な形容詞[けいようし] + な

な形容詞[けいようし] + な

情けない[なさけない]ことだ。

footnotes_tr: This usage is close to the 〜ことか pattern, but while 〜ことか indicates degree with more of a question/exclamation tone, 〜ことだ expresses a more fixed judgment/observation.
When used as an adverb in the form 〜ことに, it adds a comment directed at the sentence as a whole: 幸い[さいわい]なことに (fortunately, thankfully).

Genellikle genel bir muhataba/insan tipine öğüt; biraz resmî-didaktik hava

While the exclamatory meaning of 〜ことだ is heard in formal/written language, the advice meaning of 〜ことだ is also frequently heard in everyday speech.

to-omoimasu.title_tr: と思います (I think, in my opinion)
to-omoimasu.intro_tr: と思います is a very common N4 pattern used to politely express the speaker's personal opinion, prediction, or current thought, and corresponds to the Turkish "bence", "sanırım", "…-diğini düşünüyorum" expressions. Structurally, before the particle と, there is always the 普通形[ふつうけい] (plain form) of a verb, adjective, or noun+だ — it never combines with ます形 or です. The verb 思う itself, on the other hand, is conjugated as a separate verb in terms of tense and politeness (思います, 思いました, 思っています etc.). Negation is generally done in the clause before と (〜ないと思います); making the verb 思う negative (〜と思いません) is less natural. While と思います is used for the first person (私), when conveying the opinion of a third person, と思っています is preferred because this emphasizes that the person has a continuous/current opinion.

tables.caption_tr: Attachment Rule to と思います (普通形 by Word Type)
column_headers: 普通形[ふつうけい] (Plain Form)
rows: 明日[あした]、行[い]くと 思[おも]います。 (Yarın gideceğini düşünüyorum.)
彼[かれ]は 行[い]かないと 思[おも]います。 (Onun gitmeyeceğini düşünüyorum.)

行[い]かなかったと 思[おも]います。 (Gitmediğini düşünüyorum.)

高[たか]くないと 思[おも]います。 (Pahalı olmadığını düşünüyorum.)

With nouns and な-adjectives in the affirmative, だ must be written; it cannot be omitted: 学生[がくせい]だと思います (correct), 学生[がくせい]と思います (incorrect).

examples.reading: やまださんは いい せんせいだと おもっています。
examples.translation_tr: Yamada-san thinks he/she is a good teacher (this is his/her continuous/permanent opinion).
examples.note_tr: When conveying a third person's opinion, と思っています is more natural.

beshi-relics.title_tr: 〜べし / 〜べからず (Remnants of Classical Necessity and Prohibition)
beshi-relics.intro_tr: 〜べし and its negative form 〜べからず are necessity/prohibition expressions inherited from Classical (文語[ぶんご]) Japanese into the present day. They are no longer used productively in modern everyday speech, but they frequently appear in frozen forms (慣用句[かんようく]) on signs, proverbs, mottos, institutional rules, and literary/formal texts. べし is attached to the 終止形[しゅうしけい] of the verb in the classical language and, depending on context, can carry six different meanings such as "will definitely …", "must …", "can …", "it is appropriate to …"; べからず, on the other hand, is the negative of べし and expresses a strong prohibition meaning "never …", "… is absolutely forbidden". At N1 level, recognizing these patterns — especially on signs, in sayings, and in classical quotations — is important for reading/comprehension skills; they should be learned for recognition (受容[じゅよう]) purposes, not for productive speech.

tables.caption_tr: The six basic meanings of べし depending on context
rows: 明日[あした]は雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るべし
我[われ]、必[かなら]ず勝[か]つべし
当然[とうぜん]・義務[ぎむ] (gereklilik)
人[ひと]は学[まな]ぶべし
為[な]すべきことは為[な]すべし
静粛[せいしゅく]にすべし
footnotes_tr: In classical texts, the actual meaning is understood only from context (the preceding/following sentence); the dictionary meaning alone is not sufficient.

tables.caption_tr: The full classical conjugation table of べし (ク活用[かつよう] type)
footnotes_tr: 終止形「べし」→ cümle sonu bildirimi (現代語の「〜だ」に近い konum).
連体形「べき」→ isim niteler; modern Japoncada tek başına yaşayan form budur (例: 〜べき点).
已然形「べけれ」→ combines with 〜ば to give the meaning 'if it should be that one must …'; it is almost never used today.
べからず = べし's 未然形「べから」+ the classical negation suffix「ず」.

サ変動詞[へんどうし] する
すべし（現代語ではするべしも可）
すべからず（するべからずも可）
カ変動詞[へんどうし] 来[く]る
ラ変動詞[へんどうし] あり（古語専用）
footnotes_tr: する fiilinde すべし biçimi daha 'doğru' klasik形とされるが, modern kalıntı kullanımda するべし da yaygındır — ikisi de kabul edilir.

学[まな]ぶべし → 学[まな]ぶべきだ
だろう／に違[ちが]いない

勝[か]つべし → 勝[か]つだろう
てはいけない／禁止[きんし]

footnotes_tr: In exams (N1 reading section), these patterns are usually tested not through translation but through matching the correct meaning.

examples.target: 芝生[しばふ]に入[はい]るべからず。
examples.reading: しばふにはいるべからず。
examples.translation_tr: Do not step on the grass (entering is strictly forbidden).
examples.note_tr: This is a classical prohibition pattern frequently seen on park/garden signs; in everyday speech one would say 芝生[しばふ]に入[はい]らないでください.

examples.target: 初心[しょしん]忘[わす]るべからず。
examples.reading: しょしんわするべからず。
examples.translation_tr: Never forget your original intention (the resolve you had at the beginning).
examples.note_tr: This is a famous motto. 忘[わす]る is the classical 終止形[しゅうしけい]; in modern language 忘[わす]れる is used.

examples.target: 人[ひと]は大[おお]いに学[まな]ぶべし。
examples.reading: ひとはおおいにまなぶべし。
examples.translation_tr: A person should learn abundantly.
examples.note_tr: Here べし carries the meaning of 当然[とうぜん]・義務[ぎむ] (necessity/recommendation); it corresponds to the modern べきだ.

examples.target: 許可[きょか]なく立[た]ち入[い]るべからず。
examples.reading: きょかなくたちいるべからず。
examples.translation_tr: No entry without permission.
examples.note_tr: This is a fixed prohibition expression frequently used in official signs and warning notices.

examples.target: 明日[あした]は必[かなら]ず晴[は]れるべし。
examples.reading: あしたはかならずはれるべし。
examples.translation_tr: Tomorrow will definitely be clear.
examples.note_tr: Here べし carries the meaning of 推量[すいりょう] (strong conjecture); it is close to the modern だろう/に違いない.

examples.target: 男子[だんし]たるもの、かくあるべし。
examples.reading: だんしたるもの、かくあるべし。
examples.translation_tr: A person who is a man ought to be like this.
examples.note_tr: Here べし expresses 適当[てきとう] (appropriateness/expected behavior); together with たるもの it forms a literary sentence of admonition.

examples.target: 落書[らくが]きすべからず。
examples.reading: らくがきすべからず。
examples.translation_tr: Writing on walls/graffiti is forbidden.
examples.note_tr: The classical 終止形[しゅうしけい] of the verb する, す + べからず → すべからず (the modern するべからず is also accepted).
